Physics of Memory # 存储容量越大，访问速度越慢 进行一次主存访问大约需要消耗 300 个处理器时钟周期。这意味着如果没有优化，处理器在执行一条加载指令（如 lw）后需要闲置等待 300 个周期，软件运行将极其缓慢 为了解决上述矛盾，课件提出了核心洞察：小容量存储器比大容量存储器快。 解决方案： 在处理器和主内存之间放置一个“小而快”的存储器，即 Cache。 工作机制： 将**当前活跃（currently active）**的内存位置保留在 Cache 中，从而确保处理器发出的内存请求能得到快速响应。 Cache Memory # Locality of Reference # 缓存之所以有效，是因为大多数软件程序在特定时间内只使用主内存中有限的一部分数据。
定义： 处理器的读写操作（引用）在程序执行的较长时间内，往往集中在有限的一组地址范围内。 空间局部性 (Spatial Locality)： 指被访问的内存单元在地址空间上相互邻近（即访问了某个地址，很快可能会访问其附近的地址）。 时间局部性 (Temporal Locality)： 指同一个内存单元在时间上被重复访问（即刚才访问过的数据，很快又会被访问）。 Logic of Cache # 1. 缓存读数据的操作逻辑 # 当处理器请求读取地址 A 的数据时，流程如下：
情况 A：缓存缺失（Cache Miss） 缓存中没有地址 A 的副本。 动作： 缓存向主内存请求地址 A 的数据，并同时请求 A+1, A+2, A+3（这是一种基于未来可能需要的“猜测”）。 结果： 内存（缓慢地）做出响应。缓存将 A 的数据传给处理器，并将 A 到 A+3 的所有数据存入自己内部。 评价： 这个过程很慢，设计目标是尽量减少其发生频率。 情况 B：缓存命中（Cache Hit） 缓存中存有地址 A 的值。 动作： 缓存直接将数据发送给处理器。 效率： 仅需 1 或 2 个处理器周期。 评价： 速度极快，设计目标是让这种情况占据绝大多数时间。 Direct-Mapped Caches # Blocks of Bytes # 基本原理： 当缓存向主存（MM）请求数据时，它请求的是连续的一组字节，而不仅仅是一个地址。
内存组织： 主内存被划分为多个 Block。 示例： 假设块大小为 16 字节： Block 0： 包含字节 0 - 15 Block 1： 包含字节 16 - 31 Block 2： 包含字节 32 - 47 The Direct-Mapped Cache # 课件开始引入最简单的缓存结构：
结构视图： 可以将缓存想象成由“行”和“列”组成的表格。 Cache Line（缓存行）： 缓存中的每一行称为一个 Cache Line。 对应关系： 每一个缓存行包含的字节数与主内存的块大小完全相同。 术语区分： * 在主内存（MM）中，这一组字节被称为 Block。 当这组字节存入缓存后，它驻留在 Cache Line 中。 核心结论： MM 块大小（Block size）永远等于缓存行大小（Cache line size）。 课件提出了一个架构上的关键问题：主存块（MM Block）允许驻留在缓存的什么位置？
规则： 在直接映射缓存中，一个特定的 MM Block 只能进入一个特定的缓存行。 优点（Good）： 查找非常简单，处理器只需要检查一个固定的地方。 缺点（Bad）： 由于缓存行很少，不同的主存块会争抢同一个位置，导致频繁的“踢出（Kicked out）”操作。 Tag 来记录当前这里住的到底是哪位 ❗ 排序方式类似 Hash Table
❗ 一个块 16 Bytes，一个 Word 则是 4 Bytes，所以一个 Block 中有 4 个 Words
Ex. 0x00000054 # 我们将十六进制地址展开为 32 位二进制（重点看最后 8 位）：0000 ... 0000 0101 0100
右边第 1-4 位（Offset）：0100（十进制的 4）
意义：这告诉处理器，你要的数据在这个 16 字节块里的第 4 个字节位置。 ❗ Offset 告诉了一个 Word 在 block 中的位置
中间第 5-6 位（Index）：01（十进制的 1）
意义：这对应 $j \mod 4$ 的结果。它告诉硬件：这个地址只能存放在缓存的 Line 1（2 号房）。 左边剩余所有位（Tag）：0000 ... 01
意义：这是这个块的“唯一身份证号”。硬件会把它存入 Line 1 的 Tag 区域。 Processor Read Access # Write Policies # 当一个新的块要进来，必须踢走旧的行时，我们需要考虑：**这个旧行在“住在缓存期间”，有没有被处理器修改过（**即执行了 Store 操作）？ 逻辑： 如果没改过：直接扔掉，因为主内存里还有一份一模一样的。 如果改过：不能直接扔，否则你的修改就丢失了！必须先把它写回主内存。 Dirty Bit # 定义：这就是每个缓存行里 Dirty bit 的用途。 规则： ◦ 一旦缓存行中任何一个字被修改，Dirty bit 就会被置为 1。 ◦ 在驱逐时，硬件会检查这个位。如果 $D=1$，则将该行内容复制回主内存。 策略 Write-back（写回法） Write-through（写直方法） 核心逻辑 仅在被驱逐且“变脏”时才写回内存。 每次处理器写缓存时，同步写回内存。 脏位需求 需要（用来标记是否被改过）。 不需要（内存永远是最新的）。 性能 快（减少了访问慢速内存的次数）。 慢（如果写入频繁，主存访问会成为瓶颈）。 Hit Rate # Supermarket (超市) = Main Memory (主存)：货全、量大，但距离远，去一趟很慢。 Fridge at home (家里的冰箱) = Cache (缓存)：容量小，只能装常用的食物，但在厨房伸手就能拿到，速度极快。 理想状态：如果能把处理器想要的数据大部分都提前放进缓存，程序就会运行得飞快。命中率公式
$$ \text{Hit Rate} = \frac{\text{命中次数 (# hits)}}{\text{总访问次数 (# accesses)}} $$
Reprise of Read Access # Ex. Hit and Miss # Associative Caches # Direct-Mapped 的优缺点 # 规则：每个主存块（MM Block）只能存放在唯一固定的一个缓存行（Cache Line）中
Good（优点）：硬件实现简单、速度快。处理器只需要看一个地方就知道数据在不在。 Bad（缺点）：容易发生冲突（Conflict）。如果两个常用的块不幸映射到了同一个行，它们就会不停地互相“踢出（Eviction）”，导致性能大幅下降 Fully-Associative Cache # 规则：每个主存块可以存放在**任何（Any）**缓存行中。 Good（优点）：极大地减少了冲突。只要缓存还有空位，新块就能住进来，不需要踢走别人。 Bad（缺点）：硬件极其昂贵。 处理器不能再“一跳直达”，而是需要**同时搜索（Search）**整个缓存。 需要大量的**比较器（Comparators）**并行工作，同时对比地址 Tag 和缓存里所有的 Tag M-way Set-Associative Cache # 由于直接映射太死板，全关联太贵，于是有了这个“中间地带”：
规则：将缓存分成若干组，每个主存块被限制在一组较小的缓存行集合中（即 M 个位置）。 术语：如果一个块可以放在 M 个不同的位置，就叫 “M 路组相联”。 常见值：M 通常为 2 到 16（而总缓存行数可能有成千上万个） Ex. Example of M-way Set-Associative Cache # 课件给出了一个具体的缓存配置，我们需要通过计算来还原它的“设计图”：
Cache 总容量：$32\text{ KB}$（即 32,768 字节） 每行大小 (Line Size)：32 字节（意味着 MM Block 也是 32 字节）。 关联度 (M)：4-way（即每组有 4 条行）。 2. 结构推导计算 # 通过以上三个参数，我们可以得出：
总行数 (N)：$32\text{ KB} \div 32\text{ Bytes/Line} = 1,024$ 条行。
组数 (Sets)：$1,024\text{ Lines} \div 4\text{ Lines/Set} = 256$ 组。
意味着缓存被分成了 Set 0 到 Set 255。 规则：任何特定的 MM Block 只能进入它对应的那个 Set，但在该 Set 内的 4 个车位（Lines） 中可以随便停。 3. 映射逻辑图示 # 右侧的手绘图展示了这种多对多的映射：
• MM Block 0 映射到 Set 0。但在 Set 0 内部，它有 4 个位置（Line 0, 1, 2, 3）可以选择。
• 同理，MM Block 256 也会映射到 Set 0（因为 $256 \mod 256 = 0$）。
• 对比：在直接映射中，Block 0 和 256 会打架；但在 4 路组相联中，如果 Block 0 已经占了一个位，Block 256 进来时可以坐剩下的 3 个位中的任何一个。冲突大大减少！
Cache Replacement Policies # ❗ 如果一个组（Set）里的 4 个位置都住满了，新数据进来时到底该踢走谁
LRU 算法：最近最少使用 (Least Recently Used) # 它的逻辑是：如果一个数据很久没被访问了，那它未来被访问的概率也很低
Matric for Cache: Hit Time & Miss Penalty # AAC # $$ \text{AAC} = h \times c + (1-h) \times m $$
h (Hit Rate)：命中率（比如 0.9 代表 90% 的请求在缓存里找到了）。 c (Hit Time)：命中时的开销（例子中为 4 周期）。 1-h (Miss Rate)：缺失率（命中率剩下的部分）。 m (Miss Penalty)：缺失时的惩罚（例子中为 300 周期）。 L2 Cache # Multi-level Cache Hierarchy # 元素 访问周期 (#cycles) 容量 (Size) 关联度 (Organization) L1 (Data/Inst) 5 48K / 32K 12-way (非常灵活) L2 Cache 13 512K 8-way L3 Cache 41 8M 16-way (容量大，命中率高) Main Memory 391 16G n/a (极其缓慢) Conflicting accesses # Cache Thrashing # Trashing # 解决方案 # Cache 与外部设备的冲突 # CPU (Nios V)：它看世界是通过 Cache 的。它改了数据，可能只改在了 Cache 里。 VGA 控制器：它是一个外部硬件，它看不见 Cache，它只盯着 主内存 (MM) 看，并把内存里的内容画到屏幕上 “幽灵”是怎么产生的？ # 写回策略 (Write Back)：当你代码里“擦除”一个方块时，CPU 只是在 Cache 里把那块区域改成了黑色。 不同步：此时主内存里还是原来的旧颜色。VGA 控制器从主内存读数据，依然画出了原来的方块。 延迟生效：只有当这个 Cache 行因为太挤被“驱逐”回主内存时，屏幕才会突然变黑。 结论：这就是所谓的“幽灵”。在处理像显存（Frame Buffer）这种需要实时展示的数据时，通常我们要么关闭 Cache，要么使用 Write Through（写直通） 模式。

Faraday’s Law # $$ \Psi = \iint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{s} $$
Magnetic Flux is the integral of Magnetic Strength $B$ in area $s$
Electromotive Force (EMF) # $$ V_{emf} = - \frac{d}{dt} \Lambda = - \frac{d}{dt} (N \Psi) $$
Time-varying Magnetic Flux # Starting from Faraday’s Law $\Psi = \iint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{s}$, we can get there’s three term that can change
$$ V_{emf} = -N \left[ \iint \frac{d|\vec{B}|}{dt} ds \cos\alpha + \iint |\vec{B}| \frac{d(ds)}{dt} \cos\alpha - \iint |\vec{B}| ds \sin\alpha \frac{d\alpha}{dt} \right] $$
Stationary Loop in a Time-varying Magnetic Field # This is the can when loop doesn’t change, but field is
$$ V_{emf}^{tr} = -\iint \frac{d\vec{B}}{dt} \cdot d\vec{s} $$
Lenz’s Law # Based on Lenz’s Law, the induced current is to oppose the change of flux
Ex. # Faraday’s Law Relates Electric and Magnetic Fields # In Electrostatic, we have $\nabla \times \vec{E} = 0$, but its complete formula is $\nabla \times \vec{E} = - \frac{\partial \vec{B}}{\partial t}$, thus this meas that changing Magnetic Field will induced a Electric Field
$$ V_{emf}^{tr} = - \iint \frac{\partial \vec{B}}{\partial t} \cdot d\vec{s} $$
Moving Conductor in a Static Magnetic Field # This case is when a wire is moving in a uniform Magnetic Field
Moving Conductor on a Conducting Rail in a Static Magnetic Field # Motional EMF # Ex. Moving Loop # Electromagnetic Generator # When a loop is rotating with angular frequency of $\omega$ in a static magnetic field
Transformer & Motional EMF # When there’s two kind of EMF at the same time, then we have
$$ V_{emf} = V_{emf}^m + V_{emf}^{tr} $$
Eddy Currents # Eddy currents are circulating currents induced inside a conductor when it experiences a changing magnetic field
Ideal Transformer # Voltage and Current Relations # Displacement Current # Conduction & Displacement Current in PP Capacitor Circuit # Ex. Displacement Current Density # Angular Frequency # Ex. Electric & Magnetic Fields Between Capacitor Plates #

DT System # The DT system gets in a DT input and produces exactly one DT output
$T{x}[n]$ is the value of the output signal at time $n\in \mathbb Z$ While CT systems is more align to physics, DT system tend to come from engineering processes, such as
Discretisation of CT systems Digital filtering or signal processing Economic/ Financial models Properties of DT systems: Linearity and Causality # Linearity # A DT system $T$ is linear if for any two input signals $x, \tilde{x}$ and any two constants $\alpha, \tilde{\alpha} \in \mathbb{C}$ it holds that $T{\alpha x + \tilde{\alpha}\tilde{x}} = \alpha T{x} + \tilde{\alpha} T{\tilde{x}}$
Causality # A DT system $T$ is causal if for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, the output value $y[n]$ depends only on the present and previous input values ${ \dots, x[n-2], x[n-1], x[n] }$
Property of DT systems: Time-Invariance # A DT system T is time-invariant if for any input signal $x$ with output signal $y = T{x}$, it holds that $y_k = T{xk}$ for all possible time shifts $k \in \mathbb{Z}$
❗ Physical meaning: an experiment on the system tomorrow will produce the same results as an experiment on the system today
Ex. Time-invariance of reversal system # Properties of DT systems: memory and invertibility # Memoryless # ❗ Only depends on current value
A DT system T is memoryless if for all times $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, the output value $y[n]$ depends only on the input value $x[n]$
Invertible # A DT system T is invertible if there exists another DT system $T_{inv}$ such that $T_{inv}{T{x}} = T{T_{inv}{x}} = x$ for all inputs $x$
Property of DT system Stability (linear systems) # A signal is Bounded or having Finite Amplitude if $||x||\infty = \max{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |x[n]|$, i.e. the amplitude of the signal has a maximum over the whole period
Bounded-Input Bounded-Output Stable # If there’s a constant $K\geq 0$ s.t. $||y||\infty \le K||x||\infty$ for all $y = T{x}$
Properties of DT systems: LTI # The Impulse response of a LTI system # Impulse response $h$ of a DT LTI system $T$ is the response $T{δ}$ to a unit impulse δ input applied at $n = 0$, i.e., $h = T{δ}$
Get the Impulse Response by simply substitute the function into Impulse Function $\delta (t)$ Response of a DT LTI system # Known the input $x$ can be expressed in DT as $x = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k]\delta_k$, known its output is $y=T{x}$, thus we can sub in the input to get
$$ y = T{x} = T \left{ \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k]\delta_k \right} = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x[k]T{\delta_k} $$
and as this is a Time-Invariant System, we can get
$$ y[n]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h[n - k]x[k] $$
Properties of DT convolution # Ex. DT convolution and polynomial multiplication # LTI System Properties and the Impulse Response # Overall, to summarise, the output of DT LTI system is the convolution of impulse response with input signal $y = h * x$
$$ y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h[n - k]x[k] $$
And the Impulse Response $h$ actually determines a lot of properties for System
Ex. Bank Account Model # Finite impulse response (FIR) systems # Finite Impulse Response is a DT LTI system of the form
$$ y[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k x[n - k] = b_0 x[n] + b_1 x[n - 1] + \dots + b_M x[n - M] $$
$x[n]$: Present output $x[n-k]$: Past outputs This means that the current output value is a finite linear combination of past and present input values
Impulse response of FIR system # The impulse response of an FIR system is calculated to be
$$ h[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{M} b_k \delta[n-k] = \begin{cases} b_n & \text{if } 0 \le n \le M \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$
Conclusion: the number of nonzero terms for FIR system is limited, thus named Finite Impulse Response
Properties of LTI FIR system # Thus we can conclude this system is
Causal: As $h[n]=0$ for all $n<0$ BIBO stable: since $$ \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} |h[n]| = \sum_{k=0}^{M} |b_k|<\infty $$
Difference Equations and DT systems # In the following part, we are going to analysis the case of linear, inhomogeneous, constant-coefficient difference equations
We now called this long difference equation the LICC-DE, having the form
$$ a_0y[k] + a_1y[k-1] + \dots + a_ny[k-n] = b_0x[k] + \dots + b_mx[k-m] $$
$x$: Input Signal $y$: Output Signal $n,m$: Nonnegative Int $a_i,b_j$: Real Constant Coefficient we assume $a_0=1$ for not losing generality ❗ This system is depending on both past input and output
Now we define a operator $D^\ell y[k] = y[k - \ell]$, the power of $D$ is just the number of step $D$ going backwards, thus we can get two equation of left and right side
$$ Q(D) = 1 + a_1D + a_2D^2 + \dots + a_nD^n $$
$$ P(D) = b_0 + b_1D + b_2D^2 + \dots + b_mD^m $$
Now the LICC-DE then becomes
$$ Q(D)y[k] = P(D)x[k] $$
LICC-DEs define LTI DT systems # As LICC-ODEs for CT systems, we only consider right-sided inputs and outputs
Ex. Discretised RC circuit # DT LTI system with complex exponential inputs # Setting the input to be $x[n] = e^{j\omega_0 n}$, then
$$ y[n] = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h[k]e^{j\omega_0 (n-k)} = \left[ \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} h[k]e^{-j\omega_0 k} \right] e^{j\omega_0 n} $$
We can see the output of this Complex Exponential is
Also a complex Exponential Same Frequency Scaled by the DTFT of $h$ Here we define the DTFT as the frequency response of system, that $H(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} h[n]e^{-j\omega n}$
❗ Recall Frequency Response, that’s how system dealing with different system’s frequency scales
When the input is a Complex Exponential Signal $x[n] = e^{j\omega_0 n}$, the output will be
$$ y[n] = |H(e^{j\omega_0})| e^{j(\angle H(e^{j\omega_0}))} e^{j\omega_0 n} $$
Thus the conclusion is
❗ A LTI system will Scale the Amplitude and Shift the Phase for any Complex Exponential input

LTI System with Complex Exponential Inputs # Recall a LTI System with Impulse Response of $h$, its output in Time Domain is
$$ y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t-\tau)x(\tau) , d\tau\quad or\quad y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(\tau)x(t-\tau) , d\tau $$
Now if the input $x(t)$ is a Complex Exponential Signal $e^{st}$, then the output is
$$ y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(\tau)e^{s(t-\tau)} , d\tau = \left[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(\tau)e^{-s\tau} , d\tau \right] e^{st}=H(s)e^{st} $$
Whereas the $H(s)$ is being defined as the Transfer Function
Motivation for transfer function methods # The Transfer Function we just defined is in the form $H(s) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t)e^{-st} , dt$
Comparing it to the original CTFT one $H(j\omega)$ what’s the difference?
Mainly, the CTFT is not always well-defined (Case when the integral diverge), but $H(s)$ turns out can be existed in many situations where $H(j\omega)$ doesn’t
Although the Transfer Function can be developed, here we only analysis cases when
CT Signals that are Right-Sided CT Signals that are LTI and Causal Signals of Exponential Class # A Right Sided CT signal $x$ is of Exponential Class if $|x(t)| \le Me^{\sigma t}$ for $t\geq 0$, $M>0$, $\sigma\in \mathbb R$, where the smaller $\sigma$ is labelled $\sigma^*(x)$
The right-sided Laplace Transform # Suppose x is of exponential class, and let $\mathcal{R}_x = {s \in \mathbb{C} \mid \text{Re}(s) > \sigma^\star(x)}$. The Laplace Transform of $x$ is the complex-valued function
$$ X(s) = \int_{0^-}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-st} , dt $$
We used $0^-$ to include CT impulse at $t=0$ $X(s)$ is only defined for $s \in \mathcal{R}_x$, the Region of Convergence Existence of the Laplace Transform # Ex. LT of right-sided exponentials # For $a>0$, consider two signals $x_1(t) = e^{-at}u(t)$ and $x_2(t) = e^{at}u(t)$
Connection between LT and the CTFT # CTFT is the special case of LT in Imaginary Axis, only when system’s ROC contains the Imaginary Axis of Complex Domain, we can then use the algebric substitution to change LT into CTFT
Recall the previous example signal $x_1$, the ROC of that signal contains the whole Imaginary Axis, thus its legal to directly sub in the $s=j\omega$ into $X_1(s)$
$$ X_1(s) \Big|{s=j\omega} = \frac{1}{s+a} \Big|{s=j\omega} = \frac{1}{j\omega + a}=X_1(j\omega) $$
Important Laplace transforms # Properties of the Laplace transform # Response of a causal LTI System and the LT # The Response of a causal LTI System under LT is just the same as the case in CTFT in mathematic form, however there do exist some differences
If $T$ is a causal LTI, with impulse response $h$ and LT $H(s)$ and RoC $\mathcal R_h$, and $x$ is a right-sided signal with LT $X(s)$ and RoC $\mathcal R_x$, then the Response of the system is
$$ Y(s) = H(s)X(s), \quad s \in \mathcal{R}_y \supseteq \mathcal{R}_h \cap \mathcal{R}_x $$
And it’s Time-Domain Expression would then be a Convolution
$$ y(t) = \int_{0^-}^{t} h(t - \tau)x(\tau) , d\tau, \quad t \geq 0 $$
Ex. Use LT to find the response for RC circuit # Analysis of LICC-ODEs via Laplace Transform # Recall the LICC-ODE
$$ Q(D)y(t) = P(D)x(t) $$
For every unique input $x(t)$ it will give a unique output $y(t)$, whereas the $Q(D)$ and $P(D)$ are two Linear Differential Operators $Q(D) = D^n + a_{n-1}D^{n-1} + \dots + a_1D + a_0$ and $P(D) = b_mD^m + b_{m-1}D^{m-1} + \dots + b_1D + b_0$
Here we also defined $D\xi(t) = \frac{d\xi(t)}{dt}$ as the dervative operation
We are going to use Laplace Transform to compute the Impulse Response of this causal LTI System, and the key idea is to take the LT of both sides, thus we get
$$ (s^n + a_{n-1}s^{n-1} + \dots + a_1s + a_0)Y(s)=(b_ms^m + b_{m-1}s^{m-1} + \dots + b_1s + b_0)X(s) $$
Rearrange them to get
$$ H(s) = \frac{Y(s)}{X(s)} = \frac{b_ms^m + b_{m-1}s^{m-1} + \dots + b_1s + b_0}{s^n + a_{n-1}s^{n-1} + \dots + a_1s + a_0} = \frac{P(s)}{Q(s)} $$
Thus we can conclude that the transfer function of an LTI system defined by a LICC-ODE is very easy to find, and is often the preferred way for us
Furthermore, we want to translate this $H(s)$ back to Time Domain, as the $H(s)$ is now in rational form, we need to
Factoring the denominator Partial Fraction Expansion Inverse Laplace Transform term by term If $m\leq n$, then we will get the Impulse Response in the form of
$$ h(t) = b_0\delta(t) + \left[ \sum_{k=1}^{n} b_k t^{m_k} e^{p_k t} \sin(\omega_k t + \phi_k) \right] u(t) $$
Ex. The Series RLC circuit # Steady-State Interpretation of the frequency response # In the previous part, we defined Frequency Response $H(j\omega)$ as the response of a LTI System to two-sided Complex Exponential, i.e. $x(t) = e^{j\omega_0 t}$ is a two sided signal and its resposne is $y(t) = H(j\omega_0)e^{j\omega_0 t}$
But now the input has become right-sided and causal, like $x(t) = e^{j\omega_0 t}u(t)$
Here we first assume impulse response $h$ has finite action, so $T$ is BIBO stable ($x(t) = e^{j\omega_0 t}u(t)$), and its result would be
$$ y(t) = H(j\omega_0)x(t) - F(t)x(t) $$
$H(j\omega_0)x(t)$: The Steady-State Response, indicates that if the system has runed for enough time, then the output will be a signal with same frequency, amplitude scalling $|H(j\omega_0)|$ and Phasor shifting $\angle H(j\omega_0)$ $F(t)x(t)$: The Transient Response, as our signal is right-sided and causal, thus there need to be a transient feedback for system then it first get the input, and this term $F(t) \to 0$ as $t\rightarrow \infty$ The convergence of F(t) # As long as the system is BIBO Stable, we can prove that $F(t)$ will eventually become zero
Ex. Steady-state response of RC circuit # Steady-state interpretation of the frequency response # For a causal and BIBO stable CT LTI system
The response to a sinusoidal input is sinusoidal in steady-state the s.s. response has the same frequency as the input the s.s. response amplitude is the input amplitude times $|H(j\omega_0)|$ the s.s. response phase is the input phase plus a shift of $\angle H(j\omega_0)$ To measure that BIBO steady system, we can apply a sinusoidal input and record the output

Network function, Transfer function # Under Zero Initial Condition, the Network function is being defined as the ratio between input and output Laplace Transform
$$ T(s) = \frac{Y(s)}{X(s)} $$
This function can be extract into two parts, Natural Poles and Forced Poles
Natural Poles: Natural Response due to poles of $T(s)$ Forced Poles: Forced Response due to poles of $X(s)$ Observations # Stable Circuit: If a circuit’s Natural Response dies down to zero as time pass, then it’s a Stable Circuit This is equivalent to all the poles of $T(s)$ is on the Left-Half Plane of S-domain This is because $p = \sigma + j\omega$ is equivalent to $e^{pt} = e^{\sigma t}e^{j\omega t}$ in time domain, thus only a negative real part make this to zero eventually Forced Response & Steady-State # If the input signal $X(s)$’s poles is also on the left-half plane, then its Forced Response will also goes to zero
Otherwise, this will form a Steady-State Response for those Forced Poles Ex. Find the Zero-State Response for RC circuit # Transfer Function # One-port Network # This Port’s Transfer Function is normally a Impedance, as there’s only one port, thus no transfer inside, instead all we get is a element by itself
Two-port Network # For Two-port Network, there’s an input and an output, based on the type for in and output, there could be four types of Transfer Function
Voltage Transfer Function: $T_V(s) = \frac{V_2(s)}{V_1(s)}$ Current Transfer Function: $T_I(s) = \frac{I_2(s)}{I_1(s)}$ Transfer Admittance: $T_Y(s) = \frac{I_2(s)}{V_1(s)}$ Transfer Impedance: $T_Z(s) = \frac{V_2(s)}{I_1(s)}$ Forward and Reverse Transfer Function # ❗ The logic is that, where ever the input source is, the element beside it will be neglect
Forward Transfer Function # If we use $v_1(s)$ as input, then $C_1$ is neglectable in this case, what’s remaining is then only a series circuit between R and C
$$ T(s) = \frac{V_2(s)}{V_1(s)} = \frac{\frac{1}{C_2 s}}{R + \frac{1}{C_2 s}} = \frac{1/RC_2}{s + 1/RC_2} $$
Reverse Transfer Function # Now we take $v_2(s)$ as the input, then $C_2$ is being discarded, thus
$$ T’(s) = \frac{\frac{1}{C_1s}}{R + \frac{1}{C_1s}} = \frac{1/RC_1}{s + 1/RC_1} $$
❗ Generally Speaking: $T(s) \neq T’(s)$
Examples of Transfer Functions # Voltage Divider Circuit # Its Voltage Transfer Function is: $T_V(s) = \frac{V_2(s)}{V_1(s)} = \frac{Z_2}{Z_1 + Z_2}$
Its Driving Point Admittance is then: $Z_{eq} = Z_1 + Z_2$
Current Divider Circuit # Its Current Transfer Function is $T_I(s) = \frac{I_2(s)}{I_1(s)} = \frac{Y_2}{Y_1 + Y_2}$
Its Driving-Point Admittance is $Y_{eq} = Y_1 + Y_2$
Op-amp Circuits # There’s a lot kind of Op-amp, here we only analysis Inverting and Non-Inverting ones, but the key to analysis both of them is by Virtual Short that $(V_p=V_n, i_p=i_n=0)$
Inverting Amplifier # Known the closed gain for Inverting Amplifier is $T_V(s) = \frac{V_2(s)}{V_1(s)} = -\frac{Z_2}{Z_1}$
Whereas the Driving Impedance is $Z_{eq} = Z_1$
Non-Inverting Amplifier # Its Transfer function is $V_1 = \frac{Z_1}{Z_1 + Z_2} V_2 \implies T_V(s) = \frac{Z_1 + Z_2}{Z_1} = 1 + \frac{Z_2}{Z_1}$
Ex. Finding Transfer Function for a Circuit # Cascade Connection # Known that a Two-port Network has the Transfer Function of $V_2(s) = T_V(s) V_1(s)$, however, this is under a open circuit configuration, if there’s a Load on the output port, it will created a divider port then
$$ V_2(s) = \underbrace{V_1(s) T_V(s)}{\text{Open Response}} \times \underbrace{\frac{Z_L}{Z_T + Z_L}}{\text{Divider Factor}} $$
This can be solved by adding a Buffer
Impulse Response, Convolution # Definition of Impulse Function # Impulse function has the following property
When $t\neq 0$, $\delta(t)=0$ Integral containing origin is always 1 Sifting Property of Impulse Function # Impulse function can sifting a point’s value of a function at given time $t_0$
$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) \delta(t-t_0) dt = f(t_0) $$
Laplace Transform of Impulse Function # $$ D(s) = \mathcal{L}{\delta(t)} = \int_0^\infty \delta(t) e^{-st} dt=1 $$
Notice this integral is just the Sifting of function $e^{-st}$ at $t=0$, thus is equal to one
Thus we can also get $\mathcal{L}^{-1}{1} = \delta(t)$
Impulse response of a circuit # Known in a circuit, with $\delta (t)$ as the input, the output $h(t)$ shall be the Impulse Response
Then take both side for Laplace, we get the two S-domain function $D(s)$ and $H(s)$, notice $\mathcal L{\delta (t)} = D(s)=1$, thus we have the output as
$$ H(s) = T(s) \cdot D(s)=T(s)\cdot 1\Rightarrow H(s)=T(s) $$
❗ The circuit transfer function is just the impulse response in S-domain
Circuit response in S-domain # Based on the property $H(s)=T(s)$, we get $Y(s) = T(s)X(s) = H(s)X(s)$
Circuit response in Time-domain # Taking the Inverse Laplace on both side to get
$$ y(t) = \mathcal{L}^{-1}{Y(s)} = \mathcal{L}^{-1}{H(s)X(s)} $$
Ex. Finding the Time Domain output of LTI System using Laplace Transform # Direct time-domain solution # This part contains a derivation, and its final claim is
$$ Y(s) = H(s)X(s) \iff y(t) = h(t) * x(t) $$
Convolution Integral # $$ h(t) * x(t) = \int_{0}^{t} h(t-\tau) x(\tau) d\tau $$
Property of convolution # Commutative: $f(t) * g(t) = g(t) * f(t)$ Associative: $f(t) * [g(t) * w(t)] = [f(t) * g(t)] * w(t)$ Distributive: $f(t) * [g(t) + w(t)] = [f(t) * g(t)] + [f(t) * w(t)]$ Convolution with an impulse: $f(t) * \delta(t-t_0) = f(t-t_0)$ Ex. Finding the time domain output of LTI System using Convolution # The meaning of convolution # Result of convolution is an addition of weighted function sampled points
Step Response # The $u(t)$ is a kind of classic step function
$$ G(s) = T(s) \cdot \mathcal{L}{u(t)} = T(s) \cdot \frac{1}{s} $$
Known that $T(s)$ is normally a fraction with Poles $p_1,p_2,\dots,p_n$m, that can be extract into
$$ G(s) = \frac{k_0}{s} + \frac{k_1}{s-p_1} + \dots + \frac{k_n}{s-p_n} $$
Taking the inverse Laplace Transform to get
$$ g(t) = k_0 u(t) + (k_1 e^{p_1 t} + \dots + k_n e^{p_n t}) u(t) $$
This Time domain output contains two parts, Forced Response and Natural Response
Forced Response: $k_0 u(t)$, caused by the input signal Natural Response: $(k_1 e^{p_1 t} + \dots + k_n e^{p_n t}) u(t)$, determined by the poles of Transfer Function Stable System # For a Stable System, the Natural Response will decay to zero as time passes, so that means as time $t\rightarrow \infty$, $g(\infty)\rightarrow k_0$
And $k_0$ can be found using the Cover-up Algorithm $k_0 = s G(s) \big|{s=0} = T(s) \big|{s=0} = T(0)$, thus eventually the Step Response can be represented by
$$ g(t) = T(0) u(t) + (k_1 e^{p_1 t} + \dots + k_n e^{p_n t}) u(t) $$
Relationship between Step response and Impulse response # ❗ In Time Domain, Step Function is the integral of Impulse Function, and Impulse Function is the derivative of Step Function
In Frequency Domain, there’s a s term difference between Impulse and Step Function
By this relationship, we can get that, if we want the Impulse Response $h(t)$ of the System which can reveal the behavior of the System, we can
Start with a Step Function input to get the Step Response of the System Then use a Differentiator Circuit to get the Impulse Response $h(t)$ Ex. Find the Step Response # Ex. # Sinusoidal Response # Here we are trying to analysis when the input is a Sinusoidal Signal, in the form of $x(t) = X_A \cos(\omega t + \phi)$, base on the Laplace Transform pair, we can get $X(s)$
$$ X(s) = X_A \left[ \frac{s \cos \phi - \omega \sin \phi}{(s - j\omega)(s + j\omega)} \right] $$
Notice the poles are $(s - j\omega)(s + j\omega)$ on Complex Plane
Recall the Response contains Forced Poles and natural Poles
Forced Poles: $s = j\omega$ and $s = -j\omega$, in the form of $\frac{k}{s - j\omega} + \frac{k^*}{s + j\omega}$, taking the Inverse Lapalce will give us $y(t) = k e^{j\omega t} + k^* e^{-j\omega t}$ Natural Poles: Due to the System itself Steady-State Response: When Natural Response decay to zero, then we get $$ y_{ss}(t) = k e^{j\omega t} + k^* e^{-j\omega t} $$
Then we shall we Cover-up Algorithm to calculate $k$, that will be $k = (s - j\omega) Y(s) \big|_{s = j\omega}$, and the result will be
$$ y_{ss}(t) = X_A |T(j\omega)| \cos(\omega t + \phi + \theta) $$
$X_A |T(j\omega)|$, Amplitude: Determine by Input Amplitude and System Gain $\phi + \theta$, Phase Angle: Determine by Input Phase and System Shifting ❗ Recall, a System only have a Scaling of Amplitude and Shifting of Phase on input
Ex. # Frequency Response # Recall the Transfer Function, with input as Various Frequency Components, the Transfer Function contains Amplitude $|T(j\omega)|$ and Phase Change $\angle T(j\omega)$ two parts
What this Transfer Function does is called the Frequency Response which is a “profile” that capture how circuit “process” signal component to different frequencies
Low Pass Filter # By setting a Cut Off Frequency $\omega_0$, we set up this Low Pass Filter, as this is not an Ideal LPF, we set up the frequency out of the band with a decay model
Different Filter will have there own passband Area
Low-pass：$[0, \omega_c]$ High-pass：$[\omega_c, \infty)$ Band-pass：$[\omega_{c1}, \omega_{c2}$ Band-stop: $[0, \omega_{c1}] & [\omega_{c2}, \infty)$ The Bode Diagrams # There’s two kind of Bode Diagrams, Magnitude Plot and Phase Plot, they both have horizontal unit of frequency, and with different Vertigo Components
Magnitude Plot: $20 \log_{10} |T(j\omega)| \text{ decibel (dB)}$, use Decibel Phase Plot: $\angle T(j\omega) \text{ degree}$, use Angle Cascaded Systems # The overall Transfer Function is the multiplication of all Transfer Functions, in the form
$$ T(j\omega) = T_1(j\omega) \times T_2(j\omega) \times \dots \times T_n(j\omega) $$
Advantage of dB Scale # dB scale is a good way to compactly express both very large and very small values
First-order Low Pass response # Given a RC circuit, the Voltage Transfer Function will be given as
$$ T(s) = \frac{V_2(s)}{V_1(s)} = \frac{1/sC}{R + 1/sC}= \frac{1}{1 + sRC} $$
General form of First-order low pass response # Known the General form of First-order low pass response is $T(s) = \frac{K}{\alpha + s}$
$s$: Complex Frequency $\alpha$: Poles, Cut off Frequency $K$: Gain Coefficient Frequency Response of First order low pass response # If the only thing we care is how circuit deal with frequencies, then we can simplify the term $s = \sigma + j\omega$ into $s=j\omega$, which is the Frequency Response of the system, now we get
$$ T(j\omega) = \frac{K/\alpha}{1 + j\omega/\alpha} = \frac{T(0)}{1 + j\omega/\alpha} $$
Bode Plot of the Magnitude # Start with the Transfer Function $T(j\omega) = \frac{K}{\alpha + j\omega}$, its Amplitude shall be the mod $|T(j\omega)| = \frac{|K|}{\sqrt{\alpha^2 + \omega^2}}$, then change into $|T(j\omega)| = \frac{|T(0)|}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega/\alpha)^2}}$
There’s three important region on this Graph
$|T(j\omega)|_{\omega=0}$: The DC term, is equal to $|T(0)|$ $|T(j\omega)|_{\omega=\alpha}$: At the cut off frequency, is equal to $\frac{|T(0)|}{\sqrt{2}}$ $|T(j\omega)|_{\omega=high~\omega}$: At the region of cut off frequency, is equal to $\frac{|K|}{\omega}$ For region larger than the cut off frequency, it is followed by the equation
$$ 20\log |T(j\omega)| = |K|_{\text{dB}} - 20\log\omega $$
this was approached by taking $log$ on both side of equation
Plot of the phase angle # Also start with $T(j\omega) = \frac{K}{\alpha + j\omega}$, then overall phase is $\angle T(j\omega) = \angle K - \arctan(\omega/\alpha)$, we can also analysis this overall phase under three frequencies
$T(j\omega)|_{\omega=0}$: If $K$ is $+ve$, then its 0, else is $\pm 180$ $T(j\omega)|_{\omega=\alpha}$: Phase is $\angle K - 45^{\circ}$ $T(j\omega)|_{\omega\rightarrow \infty}$: Phase is $\angle K - 90^{\circ}$ Current Interpretation # Recall the RC circuit,
At Low Frequency, the Impedance $\frac{1}{j\omega C}$ is very large that it’s an open-circuit, thus $V_{out} \approx V_{in}$, $T(j\omega) \approx 1$, $\angle T(j\omega) = 0^{\circ}$ At High Frequency, Impedance is small that is a short circuit, $T(j\omega) \approx \frac{1}{j\omega RC}$, $V_{out} \to 0$, $\angle T(j\omega) = 90^{\circ}$ Bandwidth (BW) # For the First Order Low Filter $T(j\omega) = \frac{T_o}{1 + j\omega/\omega_c}$, its Bode plot is
Whereas $T_0$ is the DC gain and $\omega_c$ is the Corner Frequency (AKA Bandwidth, Cut off Frequency, 3dB Frequency)
It’s called 3dB frequency because it’s 3dB lower than $T_0$
Gain-Bandwidth Product (GBW) # ❗ Gain-Bandwidth Product (GBW) = DC gain $\times$ BW
This means that in a given First Order System, the product of gain and BW is a constant
Op Amp’s Bandwidth # Based on the Gain-Bandwidth Product, we can get the Op Amp’s gain and Bandwidth once we know the other
Open-loop # Open Loop Op amp has high gains, with $A_0=10^5-10^6$, this makes it’s $\omega_c$ really small
Closed-loop # Known that the feedback coefficient is $\beta = \frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}$, thus we can get the closed-loop gain from the formula $V_o = A(j\omega)(V_p - V_n)$
$$ \text{Closed-loop gain} = \frac{A(j\omega)}{1 + \beta A(j\omega)} $$
Now sub in the formula for First order low filter $A(j\omega) = \frac{A_o}{1 + j\omega/\omega_c}$ to get
DC gain: $T_0=\frac{A_o}{1 + \beta A_o}$ Cut off Frequency: $\omega_c(1 + \beta A_o)$ now we can get the new GBW formula as
$$ \text{GBW}_{closed} = \left( \frac{A_o}{1 + \beta A_o} \right) \times \left( \omega_c(1 + \beta A_o) \right) = A_o \omega_c $$
The blue line is the Frequency Response for the open loop gain, it’s also the limit of the op amp, whereas the orange one $\omega_{clo}$ is the closed loop gain in which, 1. manually decrease the amplitude, 2. but having a widther bandwidth
First-order high-pass response # The Standard form of First-order high-pass response is
$$ T(s) = \frac{Ks}{s + \alpha} = \frac{Ks/\alpha}{1 + s/\alpha} \quad (\alpha > 0) $$
$\alpha$ : Cut off frequency ($\omega_c$) Magnitude Response # Taking the mod of the Transfer function to get
$$ |T(j\omega)| = \frac{|K|\omega}{\sqrt{\alpha^2 + \omega^2}} = \frac{|K|\omega/\alpha}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega/\alpha)^2}} $$
$\omega \ll \alpha$: $|T(j\omega)|= \frac{|K|\omega}{\alpha}$, under log scale, it’s increasing with the slope of $+20\text{dB/dec}$ $\omega \gg \alpha$: $|T(j\omega)|=|K|$, the magnitude is approaching constant $K$ Phase Response # Taking the phase of the Transfer function to get
$$ \angle T(j\omega) = \angle K + 90^\circ - \tan^{-1}(\frac{\omega}{\alpha}) $$
$\omega = 0$: $\angle T(j\omega) =\angle K + 90^\circ$ $\omega = \alpha$: $\angle T(j\omega) =\angle K + 45^\circ$ $\omega \to \infty$: $\angle T(j\omega) =\angle K + 90^\circ - 90^\circ = \angle K$ Frequency Response # By letting $s=j\omega$, we get the Frequency Response as
$$ T(j\omega) = \frac{j\omega K}{\alpha + j\omega} $$
High-pass circuit example # High-pass and Low-pass cascade # The overall system is formed by a series connection of High-pass and Low-pass filter
Thus we can get the overall Transfer function as the multiplication of two functions
$$ T(s) = T_1(s) \cdot T_2(s) = \frac{K_1 s}{s + \alpha_1} \cdot \frac{K_2}{s + \alpha_2} $$
Whereas its Frequency response is
$$ T(j\omega) = \frac{K_1 j\omega}{j\omega + \alpha_1} \cdot \frac{K_2}{j\omega + \alpha_2} $$
Magnitude Response of the Cascade Transfer function # Starting with the low frequency:
****$\omega \ll \alpha_1$: $|T(j\omega)|=\frac{|K_1|\omega}{\alpha_1} \cdot \frac{|K_2|}{\alpha_2}$, $|T(j\omega)|{\text{dB}} = \left| \frac{K_1 K_2}{\alpha_1 \alpha_2} \right|{\text{dB}} + 20 \log \omega$ Then the high frequency:
$\omega \gg \alpha_2$: $|T(j\omega)|=\frac{|K_1|\omega}{\omega} \cdot \frac{|K_2|}{\omega} = \frac{|K_1 K_2|}{\omega}$, $|T(j\omega)|{\text{dB}} = |K_1 K_2|{\text{dB}} - 20 \log \omega$ Lastly the band pass region $\alpha_1 \ll \omega \ll \alpha_2$:
$T_1(j\omega)\rightarrow \frac{|K_1|\omega}{\omega} = |K_1|$ $T_2(j\omega)\rightarrow \frac{|K_2|}{\alpha_2}$ Thus the overall Magnitude response is
$$ |T(j\omega)| \to \frac{|K_1 K_2|}{\alpha_2},\quad G = |K_1 K_2|{\text{dB}} - |\alpha_2|{\text{dB}} $$
Circuit Realization of Band-pass filter # The series connection of a RC circuit and Op Amp forms a Band-pass filter
Whereas the High-pass part is the RC filter, and low-pass is the Non-inverting Amplifier, thus the overall Transfer function is
$$ T(s) = T_1(s) \cdot T_2(s) $$
High-pass part # Transfer function: $T_1(s) = \frac{R}{R + \frac{1}{sC}} = \frac{s}{s + \frac{1}{RC}}$ Frequency Response: $T_1(j\omega) = \frac{j\omega}{\frac{1}{RC} + j\omega}$ Cut-off Frequency: $f_{c_1} = \frac{\omega_{c_1}}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}$ Low-pass part # Frequency Response: $T_2(j\omega) = \frac{\text{DC gain}}{1 + j\omega / \omega_{cl_0}} = \frac{A_0 / (1 + \beta A_0)}{1 + j\omega / (\omega_c(1 + \beta A_0))}$ Cut-off Frequency (Angular): $\omega_{c_2} = \omega_c(1 + \beta A_0)$ Cut-off Frequency: $f_{c_2} = \frac{\omega_{c_2}}{2\pi} = f_c(1 + \beta A_0)$ Thus the overall Transfer Function (Frequency Response) is then
$$ T(j\omega) = T_1(j\omega) T_2(j\omega) = \frac{j\omega}{\frac{1}{RC} + j\omega} \times \frac{A_0 / (1 + \beta A_0)}{1 + j\omega / (\omega_c (1 + \beta A_0))} $$
When the whole system is in the band-pass region ($\frac{1}{RC} \ll \omega \ll \omega_c(1 + \beta A_0)$), this becomes
$$ |T(j\omega)|_{\text{mid-range}} \approx 1 \times \frac{A_0}{1 + \beta A_0} = \text{Passband Gain} $$
Ex. Band-pass Filter Example # Band-stop Response # Band-stop response is a parallel connection for a High-pass and Low-pass filter, and the overall Transfer function becomes
$$ T(s) = T_1(s) + T_2(s) $$
Notice: Series Cascade is multiplication, Parallel Cascade is addition
We can also get the Frequency response and the Magnitude response
$$ T(j\omega) = \frac{j\omega K_1}{\alpha_1 + j\omega} + \frac{K_2}{\alpha_2 + j\omega},\quad |T(j\omega)| = \frac{\omega K_1}{\sqrt{\alpha_1^2 + \omega^2}} + \frac{K_2}{\sqrt{\alpha_2^2 + \omega^2}} $$
Then we can start analysing Transfer function under different frequencies
Staring with Low Frequency:
$\omega \ll \alpha_2$: $|T(j\omega)| \approx |T_2(j\omega)| = \frac{K_2}{\alpha_2}$ Then is the High Frequency:
$\omega \gg \alpha_1$: $|T(j\omega)| \approx |T_1(j\omega)| = K_1$ Design choice, it’s suggested if we can make two band’s gain the same, in which $K_1 = \frac{K_2}{\alpha_2}$ Lastly the Mid Frequency:
$\alpha_2 < \omega < \alpha_1$: $|T_1(j\omega)| = |T_2(j\omega)|, \quad \frac{K_1 \omega}{\alpha_1} = \frac{K_2}{\omega}, \quad \frac{K_1 \omega}{\alpha_1} = \frac{K_2}{\omega}, \quad \omega = \sqrt{\alpha_1 \alpha_2}$, thus the stopband gain is $\frac{K_1 \sqrt{\alpha_1 \alpha_2}}{\alpha_1} = K_1 \sqrt{\frac{\alpha_2}{\alpha_1}} \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{K_2}{\sqrt{\alpha_1 \alpha_2}}$ Circuit Realization for Band-stop Response # LEc 31

In the previous cases, we used transfer from Time Domain to Phasor Domains to analyze circuit with Sinusoidal Steady-State, but we suggest this method is too limited. To use Laplace Transform, we are able to deal with more general ones
Laplace Transform: Transfer circuit in Time Domain into Frequency Domain (s-Domain)
In time domain the circuit is described by Differential Equations and in Frequency Domains they are Algebraic Equations We first use Laplace Transfer to change it into Frequency Domain, then get the result in Frequency Domain, and change it back to time Domain using Inverse Laplace Laplace Transform # $$ F(s) = \mathcal{L}{f(t)} = \int_{0^{-}}^{\infty} f(t) e^{-st} dt $$
Notice the Interval of the Integral, with 0 as the lower bond, this means we assume $f(t)=0$ for all $t<0$
The Inverse Laplace Transform # $$ f(t) = \mathcal{L}^{-1}{F(s)} = \frac{1}{2\pi j} \int_{\sigma-j\infty}^{\sigma+j\infty} F(s) e^{st} ds $$
We actually never use this, instead we follow the Laplace Transform Pairs
信号名称 (Signal) 时域波形 f(t) 复频域变换 F(s) Impulse (单位冲击) $\delta(t)$ 1 Step (阶跃函数) $u(t)$ $1/s$ Ramp (斜坡函数) $t u(t)$ $1/s^2$ Exponential (指数) $e^{-\alpha t} u(t)$ $1/(s+\alpha)$ Sine (正弦) $\sin(\beta t) u(t)$ $\beta/(s^2+\beta^2)$ Damped Sine (衰减正弦) $e^{-\alpha t}\sin(\beta t) u(t)$ $\beta/[(s+\alpha)^2+\beta^2]$ Uniqueness Property of Laplace Transform # Laplace Transform is a one to one function that
$$ If\quad \mathcal{L}{f(t)} = F(s)\quad then\quad \mathcal{L}^{-1}{F(s)} = f(t) $$
Linearity of Laplace Transform # $$ \mathcal{L}{a f_1(t) + b f_2(t)} = a F_1(s) + b F_2(s) $$
Integration # Taking Integration in Time Domain equals to divided by s in s Domain
$$ \mathcal{L}{\int_0^t f(\tau) d\tau} = \frac{F(s)}{s} $$
Differentiation # Taking differentiation in Time Domain equals to timing s and subtract initial value din s domain
$$ \mathcal{L}{\frac{df(t)}{dt}} = sF(s) - f(0^-) $$
Translation Properties # There’s two shift for Laplace, one is shifting in Time Domain, the other is shifting in Frequency Domain
Frequency Damian Translation:
$$ \mathcal{L}{e^{\alpha t} f(t)} = F(s - \alpha) $$
Time Domain Translation
$$ \mathcal{L}{f(t-\alpha) u(t-\alpha)} = e^{-\alpha s} F(s) $$
Poles and Zeros # For linear Circuits, the Frequency Domain $F(s)$ tends to be a Rational Fraction
$$ F(s) = K \frac{(s - z_1)(s - z_2) \dots (s - z_m)}{(s - p_1)(s - p_2) \dots (s - p_n)} $$
Whereas there are to kind of discontinuity in this Fraction, Zeros and Poles
Zeros: When Nominator is zero Poles: When Denominator is zero Ex. Laplace Transform and their Discontinuity # Finding the Inverse Laplace Transform # As indicated, most of the Laplace Function we seen will have the form of
$$ F(s) = k \frac{(s-z_1)(s-z_2) \cdots (s-z_m)}{(s-p_1)(s-p_2) \cdots (s-p_n)} $$
and there could be several cases for this function, but we need to make sure the degree of nominator must be smaller than degree of denominator to begin
Case 1: Distinct Poles # When all poles are the degree of one, thus we will have the function in the form of
$$ F(s) = \frac{k_1}{s-p_1} + \frac{k_2}{s-p_2} + \cdots + \frac{k_n}{s-p_n} $$
Where the coefficients $k_1, k_2, \dots, k_n$ here are called Residues
And Covering Up Method is what we used for finding Residues
Special Case 1: Complex Roots # Case 2: Repeated Roots # When one poles exist more than one times, then its a repeated root with the form
$$ F(s) = \frac{N(s)}{(s-p_1)^r (s-p_2) \cdots} $$
In this case, for that $(s-p_1)$ term, we need to expand it into r terms, which is
$$ F(s) = \frac{k_{11}}{(s-p_1)^r} + \frac{k_{12}}{(s-p_1)^{r-1}} + \cdots + \frac{k_{1r}}{s-p_1} + \text{others} $$
And in this case, we can’t use the Cover up method anymore, instead we need derivatives
$$ k_{1j} = \frac{1}{(j-1)!} \frac{d^{j-1}}{ds^{j-1}} \left[ (s-p_1)^r F(s) \right] \Bigg|_{s=p_1} $$
Special Case 2: Two Complex Double Poles # When there’s Complex Root and there time is more than one, in the form of
$$ F(s) = \frac{K}{(s-p_j)^2(s-p_j^*)^2} = \frac{k}{(s+\alpha-j\beta)^2} + \frac{k^*}{(s+\alpha+j\beta)^2} $$
It’s Laplace Inverse in time domain will then be a sinusoid signal with time linear decay
$$ f(t) = 2|k| t e^{-\alpha t} \cos(\beta t + \theta) u(t) $$
Case 3: Improper Rational Function # Use long division first to get the fraction in the form of a Polynomial + a Real Fraction

Techniques applicable in S-domain # There’s some same techniques we used in time domain that can be also apply on the S-domain

Self Inductance # When the Coil has a current change, it will create a induced emf and induced current
due to current change in coil itself
$$ L = \frac{N\Phi}{i} \quad \text{or} \quad N\Phi = Li $$
The Self Inductance in a Coil # In a coil with length $l$, Cross-Sectional Area $A$ and $N$ turns, its Magnetic Flux will be
$$ \Phi = B \cdot A = \mu_0 \frac{N}{l}iA $$
Which sub in L will get
$$ L = \frac{N}{i} \left( \mu_0 \frac{N}{l} i A \right) = \frac{\mu_0 N^2 A}{l} $$
Faraday’s Law # Faraday’s Law states once there’s a Change in Magnetic Flux, a Induced voltage will be created in inductor against that change
$$ v(t) = \frac{d(N\Phi)}{dt} $$
Also sub in $N\Phi = Li$ to get
$$ v(t) = \frac{d(Li)}{dt} = L\frac{di}{dt} $$
Mutual Inductance # On top of Faraday’s Law, if two Coil is very close
When there’s current change in one Inductor, it will cause the Magnetic Flux to change, in which make the second coil has a current change, that is
$$ v_{21} = N_2 \frac{d\phi_{21}}{dt} = M_{21} \frac{di_1}{dt} $$
$v_{21}$: Means that this voltage is occur on Coil 2 due to Coil 1
$N_2 \frac{d\phi_{21}}{dt}$: Faraday’s Law
$M_{21}$: Mutual Inductance Coefficient
So basically what happened is that
There’s a current change in Coil 1, $\frac{di_1}{dt}$ The current change cause the Magnetic Field in coil 1 changed, that influence the Magnetic Flux in coil 2 which is near coil 1 Thus based on Faraday’s Law, there will be a Induced Voltage in Coil 2 due to Coil 1’s current change, and that’s $v_{21}$ If Magnetic Medium in the coil is linear, then
$$ M_{21}=M_{12}=M $$
Energy # The two Inductor forms a system with total energy of $W(t)$, and as energy can’t be negative, that gives us
$$ M \le \sqrt{L_1 L_2} $$
Coupling Coefficient # Coupling Coefficient is from $[0,1]$ which measures how close was two coils
$$ k = \frac{M}{\sqrt{L_1 L_2}} $$
Perfect Couling is when $k=1$
Total Voltage # When there’s two inductors that are close, the voltage on the first inductor doesn’t simply depends on itself, but in the equation
$$ v_1(t) = L_1 \frac{di_1}{dt} \pm M \frac{di_2}{dt} $$
Sign Connection # When the Magnetic Flux from Coil 1 and Coil 2 are in the same direction, then use addition, otherwise apply the subtraction
Seen in this image, two Magnetic Flux are having the same direction (CW), thus is an additive
The Dot Convention # By drawing the coils, it makes the problem too hard, so we can simplify using Dot Convention
Addition # When dots are on the same Node
Subtraction # Ex 1. Mutual Inductance # Ex 2. Mutual Inductance # Ideal Transformer # In ideal Transformer, we assume perfect coupling, making $k=1$, also $\Phi_1 = \Phi_2 = \Phi$, and there’s no heat loss
Recall Coupled Coils # Coupled Coils has the property that
$$ \Phi_1 = \Phi_{11} + \Phi_{12} $$
The main function for Transformer is
Isolation: There’s no connection between primary and secondary winding Replication: The signal can be transform from one side to the other Scaling: Resize the magnitude of Voltage or Current Turn Ratio # $$ n = \frac{N_2}{N_1} $$
The ratio of Turns, this decided Transformer is raising of decreasing voltage
Dot Convention # Voltage Ratio
$$ \frac{v_2(t)}{v_1(t)} = \pm n $$
Current Ratio
$$ \frac{i_2(t)}{i_1(t)} = \mp \frac{1}{n} $$
Transformer in Phasor Domain # In Phasor Domain the Turn Ratio has the same equation
$$ \frac{\bar{V}_2}{\bar{V}_1} = \pm n,\quad \frac{\bar{I}_2}{\bar{I}_1} = \mp \frac{1}{n} $$
Types of Transformer # Based on the Turn Ratio, we can get three kinds of Transformer
Type Turn Ratio Physical Behavior Isolation n = 1 i and V stay the same Step-up n > 1 $V \uparrow$, $I \downarrow$ Step-down n < 1 $V \downarrow$, $I \uparrow$ Impedance in Phasor Domain # Based on the Secondary, $Z_L = \frac{\bar{V}_2}{\bar{I}_L}$, also we known that $\bar{V}_2 = n \bar{V}_1$ and $\bar{I}_L = \frac{\bar{I}_1}{n}$, thus
$$ Z_L = \frac{n \bar{V}_1}{\bar{I}_1 / n} = n^2 \frac{\bar{V}_1}{\bar{I}1}=n^2 Z{IN} $$
Ex.1 Finding Voltage and Current in Phasor Domain # Ex 2. # Circuit Transformers # Transformer is the real element we used for resizing the voltage, whereas circuit transformer is the way we used to use a circuit to simulate the behavior of Transformer, and this is done by using Thevenin Equivalent Circuit
In the Circuit Transformer, we divided the circuit into left and right which are primary and secondary half, then we can either do Thevenin on the left side or the right side
Thevenin Equivalent Circuit on Primary Side # Thevenin Equivalent Circuit on Secondary Side # The same can be applied on the Secondary Side, having
Root-Mean-Square Value # RMS is the value used to evaluate the Average Power of the Signal
As for the Instant Power, it’s $p(t) = v(t)i(t) = Ri^2(t) = \frac{v^2(t)}{R}$ Then we can use the Average Formula to find the RSM value
$$ P_{ave} = \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} p(t) dt=R( \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} i^2(t) dt)=\frac1R( \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} v^2(t) dt) $$
$$ \Rightarrow P_{ave} = R \cdot I_{rms}^2=\frac{V_{rms}^2}{R} =V_{rms} \cdot I_{rms} $$
Special Case for Trig Functions # For those commonly seen Trig Functions, it’s RSM Value can be simplified to
$$ V_{rms} = \frac{V_A}{\sqrt{2}} $$
Transformer Design Example # Known the Voltage Source is $13.8kV$ and Wire is $R_{line}=5\Omega$, whereas the Secondary Requirement is $V_2= 240V$, with maximum current $I_L=200A$
Linear Transformers in Phasor Domain # Starting with the Voltage in Time domain, we have the equation
$$ v_1(t) = L_1 \frac{di_1(t)}{dt} \pm M \frac{di_2(t)}{dt} $$
eThe first term is Self-Induction and Second term is Mutual Induction
Notice this is a Differential Equation, we wish to transform this into phasor domain to simplify the question, thus we will have
$$ \overline{V}_1 = j\omega L_1 \overline{I}_1 \pm j\omega M \overline{I}_2,\quad \overline{V}_2 = j\omega L_2 \overline{I}_2 \pm j\omega M \overline{I}_1 $$
Now setting the Reactance to let $X_1 = \omega L_1$, $X_2 = \omega L_2$, and $X_M = \omega M$, we will then get
$$ \bar{V}_1 = jX_1 \bar{I}_1 \pm jX_M \bar{I}_2,\quad \bar{V}_2 = jX_2 \bar{I}_2 \pm jX_M \bar{I}_1 $$
Coupling Coefficient in Phasor Domain # $$ k = \frac{M}{\sqrt{L_1 L_2}} = \frac{X_M}{\sqrt{X_1 X_2}} $$
Ex. Magnetically Coupled Circuits # Instantaneous and Average power # Giving a reference current with $i(t) = I_A \cos \omega t$, analyze the behavior of other elements’ ins and avg power
Impedance has two parts $Z=R+jX$
$R$: Resistance (Real), the part really consuming energy Has the same phase for Current and Voltage $X$: Reactance (Imaginary), caused by the Electronic Field or Magnetic Field, Has a Phase difference as over a period, the average of it will be induced back Load Instantaneous Power Average power Resistor $\frac{V_A I_A}{2} [1 + \cos 2\omega t]$ $\frac{V_A I_A}{2} = V_{rms} I_{rms} = R I_{rms}^2$ Inductance $-\frac{\omega L I_A^2}{2} \sin 2\omega t$a 0 Capacitor $-\frac{\omega C V_A^2}{2} \sin 2\omega t$ 0 Average Power of Inductance and Capacitor over a period will be zero out, the Average Power is then zero Where as the Instantaneous Power will have a phase difference of 90 AC Power System # Having a System of Sinusoidal Source $i(t) = I_A \cos(\omega t)$ and $v(t) = V_A \cos(\omega t + \theta)$, we are going to calculate its Ins and Average Power
Instantaneous Power # Start with the equation $p(t) = v(t) \cdot i(t)$
We can define two Power, Active and Reactive Power
Active Power: $P = \frac{V_A I_A}{2} \cos \theta$ , the power being consumed Reactive Power: $Q = \frac{V_A I_A}{2} \sin \theta$ , the power transferring in Electro Field and Magnetic Field As indicated, the Blue one will be wasted, while orange one has the average of zero
Average Power # The average is given by the Integral divided by Period, thus is
$$ P_{ave} = \frac{1}{T} \int_{0}^{T} p(t)dt = \frac{V_A I_A}{2} \cos \theta $$
❗ Notice Average Power is just Active Power
Here we can use the concept of RMS, and the fact that $V_{rms} = \frac{V_A}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $I_{rms} = \frac{I_A}{\sqrt{2}}$ to get
$$ P_{ave} = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos \theta $$
In this equation, the term $\theta$ is the only one deterring the number of Actual Work, analyze it in different values
Theta = 0 # In this case, the Power is always on the top of t axis that makes the magnitude of Average Power to maximum
Theta = 45 # Part of the Power will be moved blow t axis, that means the power is return from the load to the source
Average Power vs. Theta # This is the graph of $cos\theta$ in the range from $[-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2]$
Lagging and Leading # $\theta$ basically tells if the system has a lagging or leading in signal
$\theta>0$: Voltage Phasor is larger than Current Phasor $\theta <0$: Current Phasor is large than Current Phasor Ex. Calculate the Power of System # Complex Power # Here we are going to summarize thing above, starting with the formula of Instantaneous Power
$$ p(t) = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\theta [1 + \cos 2\omega t] - V_{rms}I_{rms}\sin\theta [\sin 2\omega t] $$
We now define the Complex Power as $\overline S=P+jQ$, whereas
$P$ is the Real Power, and the Average Power $Q$ is the Reactive Power Their magnitude $|\bar{S}| = \sqrt{P^2 + Q^2} = V_{rms} I_{rms}$, is the Apparent Power, that’s the capacity of power device have to have to make everything run $pf=\cos \theta$ is the Power Factor that determine the phase Analogy of beer # A good analogy for this Complex Power would be the beer
The Foam is the Reactive one and Real Beer is the Real (Active) one, whereas the size of the cup has to be S to hold both the fuzz and beer
Complex Power in Phasor Domain # Now we can analysis the Instantaneous Power $p(t) = V_{rms}I_{rms}\cos\theta [1 + \cos 2\omega t] - V_{rms}I_{rms}\sin\theta [\sin 2\omega t]$ in Phasor Domain, as defined, the Complex Power is $\overline S=P+jQ$
$$ \Rightarrow \bar{S} = V_{rms} I_{rms} e^{j\theta} = V_{rms} I_{rms} \angle \theta= V_{rms} I_{rms} \angle (\phi_v - \phi_I) $$
$$ \Rightarrow \overline S=V_{rms} \angle \phi_v \cdot I_{rms} \angle -\phi_I $$
Known that $I_{rms} \angle -\phi_I = I^*_{rms}$, thus we get the final formula is
$$ \bar{S} = \bar{V}{rms} \cdot \bar{I}{rms}^* $$
The Power Triangle # We can use a triangle on the complex plane to represent this Complex Power
Ex. Calculating the Power Triangle for the system # Conservation of Complex Power in a System # Power Flow # Recall the ways we express the Power Flow, to begin with, we have four Powers
P: Active Power Q: Reactive Power $S_L$: Complex Power $|S_L|$: Apparent Power $\cos \theta$: Power Factor Given Active and Reactive Power # $$ \bar{S}_L = P_L + jQ_L $$
Given Apparent and Power Factor # $$ \bar{S}_L = P \pm jQ $$
Given Active and Power Factor # Use Active Power to find the Apparent Power $|\bar{S}_L| = \frac{P_L}{pf}$, then find the Reactive Power $|\bar{S}_L| = \frac{P_L}{pf}$
Given Impedance and RMS # $$ \bar{S}L = Z_L \cdot I{rms}^2 = \frac{V_{rms}^2}{Z_L^*} $$
Ex. Source Voltage and Complex Power # Power Factor Correction # For most of time, the low Power Factor is not good, as the Real Power will be reduced, in order to transfer the same Real Power, it will need to transfer a larger transparent Power
On top of that, a larger current will increase the lose in the power line, thus we need to find a way to resize the Power Factor
Power factor correction: design feature that increases the pf without changing the real power
And the method we will apply is to parallel a Capacitor beside the Load Impedance
The Impedance for Load is $Z_L = R + jX_L$, and its Complex Power formula is
$$ \bar{S}_L = P + jQ_L = R|\bar{I}_L|^2 + j\omega L \frac{|\bar{V}_L|^2}{|Z_L|^2} $$
And for Capacitor, its Impedance is $X_C = -\frac{1}{\omega C}$, and its Complex Power Formula is
$$ \bar{S}_C = -j\omega C |\bar{V}_L|^2 $$
By adding them up, we will get
$$ \bar{S} = \bar{S}_L + \bar{S}_C = \underbrace{R|\bar{I}L|^2}{P} + \underbrace{j\omega \left( \frac{L}{|Z_L|^2} - C \right) |\bar{V}L|^2}{Q} $$
Now, we would like to eliminate the $Q$ term to make the Charge Wire leave entirely to the Real Power, that’s the case when we need $C$ to be $C = \frac{L}{|Z_L|^2}$
Now we have complete the Power Factor Correction
without influencing the Power of Real Power Using Capacitor to eliminate the Reactive Power in Capacitor Make the Impedance into Resister Ex. Power Factor Correction # Ex. Design Example for Power Factor Correction #

LTI systems with Complex Exponential Inputs # Known that a for a LTI system $T$, its output is the Convolution of input and Impulse Response
$$ y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(\tau)x(t-\tau) d\tau $$
Now we are considering case where the input is a Complex Exponential $x(t) = e^{j\omega_0 t}$
Complex Exponential Inputs # Sub in the $x(t) = e^{j\omega_0 t}$ to get the output as
$$ y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(\tau) e^{j\omega_0(t-\tau)} d\tau= \left[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(\tau) e^{-j\omega_0 \tau} d\tau \right] e^{j\omega_0 t} $$
Which is just $h(t)$’s CTFT at $\omega_0$, $H(j\omega)$
This helps us conclude some property of the System
If input is with frequency $\omega_0$, then output is still $\omega_0$ There will be a shift for Magnitude and Phase of the input Frequency response of a LTI system # $$ H(j\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t)e^{-j\omega t} \text{d}t $$
This is Frequency Response of the system, that can be represent in Polar Form which is
$$ H(j\omega) = |H(j\omega)| e^{j\angle H(j\omega)} $$
$|H(j\omega)|$: Magnitude, determine Amplitude scaling of input Frequency $\angle H(j\omega)$: Phase, the Phase Change to the input frequency ❗ The Effect of LTI system to a input frequency is only Scaling its amplitude and Shifting its Phase
Ex. RC Circuit # Car suspension System # Response of a LTI System to a periodic Input # Starting with a Periodic CT Signal with period $T_0 = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}$, its CTFS is
$$ x(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} a_k e^{j k \omega_0 t} $$
Then use CTFT to transfer it into Frequency Domain
$$ X(j\omega) = 2\pi \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} a_k \delta(\omega - k\omega_0) $$
Multiply it to the System to get its output $Y(j\omega) = H(j\omega) X(j\omega)$ which is
$$ Y(j\omega) = H(j\omega) X(j\omega)= 2\pi \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} a_k H(j k \omega_0) \delta(\omega - k\omega_0) $$
Then do the inverse CTFT to get back in Time Domain
$$ y(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \underbrace{a_k H(j k \omega_0)}_{b_k} e^{j k \omega_0 t} $$
Now take a look at this output $y(t)$, it means, the output of the LTI system is the Scaling and Shifting of Components one by one based on their frequency
Response of a LTI system and the CTFT # Notice in the previous part “Response of a LTI System to a periodic Input”, we used the CTFT and i-CTFT to only do calculations in Frequency Domain, this is because it’s more easy to do multiplication in Frequency Domain than do Convolution in Time Domain, as
$$ y(t) = (h * x)(t) \iff Y(\mathbf{j}\omega) = H(\mathbf{j}\omega)X(\mathbf{j}\omega) $$
Ex. Computing the output for the RC circuit # LTI System and Invertibility # A LTI system with impulse response h is invertible if there exists an impulse response $h_{inv}$ such that $h ∗ h_{inv} = \delta$
It’s kind of strange for the condition $h ∗ h_{inv} = \delta$, but if we take CTFT, this then becomes
$$ H(j\omega) H_{\text{inv}}(j\omega) = 1 $$
Thus we can get the Frequency Response for Inverse Response as
$$ H_{\text{inv}}(j\omega) = \frac{1}{H(j\omega)} $$
Condition for LTI System to be Invertible # As $H_{\text{inv}}(j\omega) = \frac{1}{H(j\omega)}$, this means if and only if $H(j\omega)\neq 0$, then the system is Invertible
Ex. Invertible LTI System # Ex. Invertibility and Feedback Interconnections # Filtering via LTI systems # Filter is the progress of selecting desired frequencies, and there’s basically four kinds of filters
Low-Pass Filters (Remove all high frequency content) High-Pass Filters (Remove all low frequency content) Band-Pass Filters (Remove all content outside a band) Band-Stop Filters (Remove all content inside a band) Filters can be conveniently designed using LTI systems through an appropriately chosen Frequency Response
That being said, as the input signal was $x(t)$, and the Response of System is $H(j\omega)$, then the output spectrum $Y(j\omega)$ is $Y(j\omega) = H(j\omega)X(j\omega)$, in this case, if we want to design a Low-Pass Filter, we just need a LTI System having $|H(j\omega)| \approx 1$ and $|H(j\omega)| \approx 0$
The Ideal Low-Pass Filter # For $\omega_c>0$ consider the Frequency Response
$$ H(j\omega) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } -\omega_c \le \omega < \omega_c \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$
This System perfectly passes frequencies $|\omega|<\omega_c$, while its Impulse Response is
$$ h(t) = \frac{\sin(\omega_c t)}{\pi t} $$
Not Causal Problem # Notice the Filter in Time Domain, which is a sinc function
Notice there’s value at $t<0$, this makes the LTI System a Not Causal, thus this can’t be apply in Real Time application
Instead of Ideal Filter, we often prefer Non-ideal but Causal filters for two reasons
Can be modelled using Differential Equation Can be easily implemented in hardware/software for real-time use In addition, the use of Ideal Low Pass Filer makes the output signal Oscillates as it’s a sinc function, that creates Gibbs Phenomenon
❗ The more Perfect on Frequency Domain, the more Complicated on Time Domain
Non-Ideal LPF - RC circuit # RC Circuit is a non-Ideal but Causal Low-Pass Filter, known that it have a Frequency Response
$$ |H_{\text{RC}}(j\omega)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (RC\omega)^2}} $$
Notice on the top we define the Cut-off Frequency as $\frac{1}{RC} = \omega_c$
This Frequency Response is just $h_{\text{RC}}(t) = \frac{1}{RC}e^{-t/RC}u(t)$ in time domain
From the figure, notice all parts before $t=0$ is just 0, this makes the function a Causal System
Comparison of RC circuit and Ideal LPF # Here we are going to use a example to show the difference of Ideal & Non-Ideal Filter
The Cut Frequency has been set to $\omega_c=2~rad/s$
Ideal Filter # Anticipate the input change (As it’s not Causal) Perfectly removes the oscillatory component above $\omega_c$ RC Circuit # Reacts only after the input changes Attenuates (decay) the oscillatory component, but can’t remove it The Ideal High-Pass Filter # The HPF has the Frequency Response
$$ H(j\omega) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } |\omega| > \omega_c \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$
While this HPF has the Impulse Response of $h(t) = \delta(t) - \frac{\sin(\omega_ct)}{\pi t}$
Non-Ideal HPF - RC circuit # Still using RC circuit, known that A Capacitor will block the high frequency and pass the low frequency, thus if we use the Resistor Voltage as output instead of Capacitor Voltage, then this RC circuit will become a High-pass Filter
The High-pass Filter’s Frequency Response is
$$ |\tilde{H}(j\omega)| = 1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + (RC\omega)^2}} $$

The former course is about to use Assembly and C language to view the processor in terms of a programmer, now the course has been switched into view processor hardware using digital design knowledge
Computer Architecture # Recall the architecture we have, what the processor does is
Fetch from the memory to get Machine Code instructions Execute the instructions Interact with memory Now we are going to use logic gates to rebuild this
Simple Processor Design # The processor we are working on will be a 8 bit one, with one 4 Registers, R0 - R3
By setting the processor to 8 bit, it means that its word size is 8 bits As the memory address also only have 8 bits, thus there’ll be $2^8=256$ memories The same applies to pc Instruction Set # There’s gonna be 10 kinds of instruction, with also fixed size of 8 bits
And the instruction is going to look like add R1, R2 # R1 = R1 + R2 Condition Flags # There’s going to be two 1 bits flag
Z Bit (Zero): If the last instruction result is zero, z = 1 , else is z = 0 N Bit (Negative): If the last instruction result is negative, N = 1 , else N = 0 Nios V doesn’t use this method
Datapath # Before starting, here’s some part of the processor that we have to get
PC Memory Register ALU Data Flows # Fetch Path # Starting from pc , it send the required address to memory Then memory output the Instruction to Instruction Register and Memory Data Register Execution Path # Then Register File will choose to read one of regA and regB Then using Multiplexers to decided which data to pass through Lastly use ALU to get the final result Instruction Formats # As indicated, there’s 8 kinds of instructions, where they can be extracted into two types
Reg - Reg ones # The operation between two Registers, i.e. add R1, R2 , inside the instruction, there will be
Opcode (4 bits): Choosing operation regA (2 bits): Target Register regB (2 bits): Source Register Immediate ones # The operation between Register and Constants, i.e. addi R1, 5
Opcode (4 bits): Choosing Operation regA (2 bits): Target Register regB (2 bits): Immediate Number (Notice the range is $2^2$ which is $0-4$ Semantics # Regardless of add Ra, Rb or sub Ra, Rb , they are having similar operations
Arithmetic Operation # Calculate the operation result first
Flags # Then update two status bits, Zero and Negative
Then update pc = pc + 1
Encoding of Machine Code # One instruction will be extract into three parts in a 8 bit Register
Or immediate Operation # The General Form of Or Immediate Operation is ori imm5 , notice
There’s NO Given Register for this command There’s 5 bits on immediate number Firstly the Register issue, we fix the Register of this operation to R1 to save two 2 bit of space
Secondly, as there’s only 3 bits for Opcode and it’s 111 ,thus we have 5 bits for this constant
Execution Steps # $R1 \leftarrow R1 \ OR \ ZE(Imm5)$ Here ZE means Zero Extend, add three zero in front of 5 immediate to make it 8 bits Update the Z and N bit Update PC : $PC \leftarrow PC + 1$ Ex. ori 0x7 # Memory Instructions # There’s two Memory Instructions used load and store , it’s similar to lw and sw , but notice for the Memory Instructions, the Z and N bit won’t be set as there’s no ALU logic
Load Operation # The general form of Load Operation is load Ra, (Rb) , and will be encoded in the form of
Store Operation # The general form of Store Operations is store Ra, (Rb) , will be encoded in the form of
Conditional Branches # Recall the instruction bne r5, r0, loop , this is a branch if not zero instruction, that branch to a different address (other than pc+1) if result of last operation in ALU is not zero
In this Simple Processor, we can tell this by using the Z bit, thus here’s the full step for Branch
Running the instruction bnz Imm4
Check the Z bit, if Z == 0 (The result is not zero), then JUMP If Z == 1 (The result is zero), then PC <- PC + 1 Jumping process is using an offset that PC <- PC + SE(Imm4) , here SE is Sign Extension Here we are using Relative Addressing This having the Encoding of
There’s up four bits for Imm4 - 4 bits constant, and lower 4 bits Opcode with bnz = 1001
While there’s also an Instruction bpz imm4 which is Branch if Positive with Opcode of 1101
Design Example # Here’s a full code comparing two value in Memory and see if they subtract to zero
Address Label Instruction Comment Encoding 0 loop: load R2,(R0) R2 <- [R0] 0x80 1 load R3,(R1) R3 <- [R1] 0xd0 2 sub R2, R3 R2 <- R2 - R3 0xb6 3 bnz loop 0xd9 The hardest thing here is to calculate Imm4 for Encoding bnz , notice loop is at address 0 , when running til bnz loop , PC is already 3 m thus we want
$$ PC + Imm4 = Target\rightarrow3 + Imm4 = 0 $$
Thus we get $Imm4 = -3$, in 2’s Complement, -3 is just 1101 , thus this Encoding code will be 1101 1001 = 0xd9
❗ Notice in this part, PC is pointing to current Instruction address instead of next instruction’s
Register # Recall the implementation of a Register, its fundamental unit is a D Flip-Flop
D Flip-Flop # This Flip-Flop contains an input D, output Q, clock and a Enable , this Flip-Flop will update when there’s a positive edge of clock, then check if Enable = 1 , then Q <- D , otherwise the output Q will remains the same
In this Processor, as we indicated is a 8 bit register, there’s gonna be 8 Flip-Flops together, sharing the same Enable and Clock
The Clock ’s frequency depends on the device we are running at, its $50MHz$ for Nios V, and $2GHz$ for normal computers
Multiplexer # Instructions # add # Recall the execution of the add instruction add Ra, Rb # Ra <- Ra + Rb , with the encoding of
Suppose the add R1, R2 is being coded into 01 10 0100 , which is 0x64 in HEX, and this instruction is stored at address 0x05 , there’ll be six steps for this instruction
Fetch: Read from memory of what PC is pointing to, then activate MemRead and IRLoad Decode: Recognise which instruction is inside Read: Read the value of R1 and R2 , turn on ABld Compute: Set the ALUop into additional mode, and calculate ALUout = R1 + R2 , the signals are ALU_A = 1 , ALU_B = 0 , ALULoad = 1 . After computed, set the Z and N bit based on the result (need to enable Flagwrite = 1 ) Write: Write back the result of ALUout back to Ra (RFwrite = 1 ) Compute PC: Update the PC sub # Fetch and Increment PC: MemRead=1 , PCwrite=1 Decode & register fetch Compute: Use ALU_Op=001 to tell ALU to do subtraction, and store it in ALUOut , at the same time, it will update the Flags ( zero or negative) Write: RFWrite=1 OR Immediate # Unlike sub , there’s a Immediate Value now, and it requires one more period than sub
Fetch: Then same, active MemRead , IRload PC <- PC + 1 ALU_A=0, ALU_B=1, ALU_Op = add = 001 PCwrite=1 Decode & register fetch: Read Ra and Rb from the Register File 这次读取是浪费的 (Wasted) 对于 ori 指令，我们需要读的是寄存器 R1（通常对应编码中的某个位置），而硬件逻辑在这一步还没准备好。 Load # Store # BNZ # Shift L/R Ra, Imm2 # FSM Cycles # Load # BNZ Imm4 # Processor elements # Register File # 通过 regA 和 regB 两个 2-bit 输入信号，分别从 dataA 和 dataB 端口同时输出两个 8-bit 数据 通过 regw（2-bit）选择目标寄存器，在 RFWrite 信号有效且时钟 CLK 到达时，将 dataw（8-bit）的数据写入 regA 信号作为上方 Mux 的选择端，决定 dataA 输出哪个寄存器的值 regB 信号作为下方 Mux 的选择端，决定 dataB 输出哪个寄存器的值 左侧的 2-bit 输入 regw 连接到一个译码器，将其转换为四条选通线（00, 01, 10, 11）。 每条选通线与 RFWrite 全局信号通过一个 AND 门 相连。 使能控制：只有当 RFWrite 为 1 且译码器选中该寄存器时，对应寄存器的 Enable（使能） 端才会被激活。 数据输入：dataw（橙色线）连接到所有四个寄存器的输入端，但只有被使能的那个寄存器会在时钟触发时保存该值 ALU # 输入输出：拥有两个 8-bit 输入端口（A 和 B），一个 8-bit 输出端口（ALUout）。 控制信号：ALUop 是一个 3-bit 的选择信号，决定当前的运算类型 并行运算层：输入 A 和 B 同时进入所有的运算模块（加法器、减法器、或门、与非门、移位器）。这意味着所有运算是同时发生的。 ALUop 信号连接到 Mux 的选择端。它的作用是从上方所有运算模块的结果中，只选出一个作为最终的 ALUout 输出 FSM & Memory # 读 (Memread = 1)：地址输入后，数据在同一个时钟周期内从 DATAout 输出。 写 (MemWrite = 1)：地址和 DATAin 输入后，数据在时钟周期结束时完成更改。

Intro to Low-Level Graphics # Starting from the structure of the De1-SoC, different parts have own role on Graphics
Processor: Take and decided where and which to show on each pixel Memory (Frame Buffer): A specific space in Memory to store the value of each pixel VGA: Continuously read from the Frame Buffer and send it to screen Coordinate System # The screen has been divided into boxes with 320 x 240 pixels
And the origin is at the left top, this means that the right down corner is then $(319,239)$
Pixel Encoding - RGB565 # On the screen, each box is representing one pixel, while each pixel is encoded using 16 bits
The 16 bits components are R: 5 bits, G: 6 bits, B: 5 bits This is because human are more sensitive to green
Address Mapping # As memory is 1 Dimension but Screen is 2D, so we’ve design a way to representing 2D
So as the De1-SoC is a 32 bit system, we will divided this 32 bits into
Base: 14 bits Y Coordinate: 8 bits, cause $2^8=256$ X Coordinate: 9 bits, cause $2^9=512$ Ending 0: 1 bit, this 0 is always here, as there’s 2 bytes representing one pixel, this means that the starting address of each pixel has to be an even number By leaving a 0 in the end of the bit is equivalent to timing a 2 in decimal number Thus overall we can conclude the formula for calculating the Address’s corresponding pixel
$$ \text{address} = \text{base} + (y \ll 10) + (x \ll 1) $$
Ex. Calculating the Pixel Address # $(0,0)$: Origin, is the base address 0x08000000 $(1,0)$: One pixel to the right, that’s x =1, which is 0x08000002 $(1,1)$: One pixel to the right, then down, is 0x08000402 (1024 = 0x400 ) $(319,239)$: Right Down Corner, is 0x0803be73 Code Example # /* program to draw four green pixels into the middle of the screen */ void plot_pixel(int x, int y, short int line_color); // plots one pixel void clear_screen(); // clears whole screen int pixel_buffer_start; // global variable location of frame buffer int main(void) { volatile int * pixel_ctrl_ptr = (int *)0xFF203020; // pointer to the base register of controller /* The default base of the frame buffer is int VGA controller */ /* That default address is stored in the base register of the VGA controller port/interface */ /* so the next statement gets it, leaving pixel_buffer_start = 0x08000000 */ pixel_buffer_start = *pixel_ctrl_ptr; clear_screen(); plot_pixel(160, 120, 0x07E0); plot_pixel(161, 120, 0x07E0); plot_pixel(162, 120, 0x07E0); plot_pixel(163, 120, 0x07E0); } // code not shown for clear_screen() and draw_line() subroutines void plot_pixel(int x, int y, short int line_color) { volatile short int *one_pixel_address; one_pixel_address = pixel_buffer_start + (y << 10) + (x << 1); *one_pixel_address = line_color; } void clear_screen() { int y, x; for (x = 0; x < 320; x++) for (y = 0; y < 240; y++) plot_pixel(x, y, 0); } Drawing Lines on Screen # Known that the boxes one screen are discrete, thus drawing a straight lines are hard
Things like this case will occur which is called aliasing, but that’s already the best approximation
The way we calculate it is by the slope $slope = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}$
This method best work for steep lines with slope less than 1 Animation # The animation is just 1. Draw lines, 2. Erase Lines, 3. Repeat, here’s more detail of approach
Buffer Register # Front Buffer stores the starting address of the current image
The Screen’s image can be changed immediately by changing Buffer Register Flickering # If there’s no new image after the old one has been removed, then flickering will occur that there’s a blank or broken image
Vertical Synch # The VGA controller will scan the screen from left to right, up to down
Vertical Retrace: While there’s a delay after the whole progress was done and return to origin Thus the updates can be done during the Vertical Retrace period, and there’ll be a register called status register in charge of the state Double Buffering # The ultimate solution for animation, thus set two buffer regions, Front Buffer and Back Buffer , and the update steps will be
Remove and draw the new shape inside Back Buffer Wait for the Vertical Synch Signal Swap VGA Controller Memory Mapped Registers # Front Buffer Address Register: Storing the current image’s starting address It’s a read-only reg that only change when there’s a swap instruction Back Buffer Address Register: Storing the starting address of back buffer Its a write reg Status Register: The lowest bit is S (Status Bit) When we write a 1 into the Front Buffer Reg , a swap will occur and this Status Bit will be set to 1 representing the change is in progress Whereas after the swap is finished, then S bit will return to 0 again Note that the De1-SoC’s VGA controller can only access the SDRAM address staring with 0x00 , while can’t access the DDR3 starting with 0x04 Process of swapping to avoid Flickering # Initiate # At the beginning, the processor will send a 1 into the Front Buffer Reg that tells VGA controller to swap when ready
While in this case, the S bit in Status Reg will swap to 1, meaning the swapping is in progress
Wait for V-Sync # The swap won’t happen immediately, that’s because if the screen is at its middle of scanning, the upper and lower part of the screen will occur flickering
Thus only run swap when V-Sync is ready
C Language Code for wait_for_vsync() # void wait_for_vsync() { // Base Address for VGA Controller volatile int * pixel_ctrl_ptr = (int *) 0xff203020; int status; // Wrtite a 1 into the Front Reg *pixel_ctrl_ptr = 1; // Read the status Reg status = *(pixel_ctrl_ptr + 3); // Polling until the last bit becomes 1 while ((status & 0x01) != 0) { status = *(pixel_ctrl_ptr + 3); } // If it goes to 0, auto break } Poll # The processor will then use polling to check the bit S to see when the swapping is finished, so it can start drawing the next frame
Frame Per Second # So 60 FPS means the processor can render one frame less than $1/60$ s, if something went wrong that it requires more than $1/60$ s to render a frame, then we want to keep the frame frequency lower but keep the overall animation contingence
