Magnetic Dipole # As Magnetic Field is created by Current, the Magnetic Dipole is thus a Closed Loop Current
This is equivalent to a Magnetic as the $+z$ direction is N, $-z$ direction is S
While ideally, we assume the radius of Loop to be infinite small thus it becomes a point By setting the radius of the loop to $a$, we can get $$ \vec{H} = \frac{I \pi a^2 \hat{z}}{2 \pi (\sqrt{a^2 + z^2})^3} = \frac{\vec{m}}{2 \pi (a^2 + z^2)^{3/2}} $$
Whereas the $\vec m$ is Magnetic Dipole Moment having $\vec m = IS\hat n$
This moment indicate the Normal direction of Loop, and the Magnitude of the Field There’s basically two kinds of Magnetic Field we have
Case 1: Point at center of Loop # $$ \vec{H}(0) = \frac{I}{2a} \hat{z} $$
Case 2: Point that’s far away on Z-Axis # $$ \vec{H}(z \gg a) \approx \frac{\vec{m}}{2 \pi z^3} = \frac{I a^2}{2 z^3} \hat{z} $$
Case 3: Any point in the space # Now consider the point at any point of the space, start with Biot-Sacart too
$$ \vec{H} = \int \frac{I d\vec{l} \times \vec{R}}{4\pi |\vec{R}|^3} $$
Duality Between Magnetic Dipole & Electric Dipole # Magnetic Materials # Nature of Magnetic Materials # There’s two kinds of movement for electrons in atoms
Orbiting Electron: That’s electron spinning around Core and create $m_o$ Spinning Electron: The self spin of the electron, creating $m_s$ As the magnetic Moment is $m_o = IA_{loop}$, for a circular orbit with radius $r$, it have $A= \pi r ^2$
Whereas the current is the Charge’s rate of change of time, electron has the charge of $-e$, and the time spinning one circle is $\Delta t = \frac{2\pi r}{u}$, that will be $I = \frac{-e}{\Delta t} = \frac{-eu}{2\pi r}$, so we can get
$$ m_o = \frac{-eu}{2\pi r} \cdot \pi r^2 = -\frac{eur}{2} $$
Having the Plank Constant and Angular Momentum sub in, our finial conclusion will be
$$ |m_s| = |m_o| \approx 9 \times 10^{-24} , \text{A} \cdot \text{m}^2 $$
❗ This indicates that the Magnetic from material is from the Orbiting and Spinning of electrons which creates current
Magnetization # Now we are viewing Magnetism under macro perspective
Firstly recall the two kinds of current we have, 1. Free Current and 2. Bounding Current
Free Current is the charges moving inside wires Bounding Currents are then the Spinning ones inside atom When we are analysing a material with $\Delta V$ as the volume, we assume there’s N Dipoles inside , thus the $m_{total}$ will then be
$$ \vec{m}{total} = \sum{i=1}^{N\Delta V} \vec{m}_i $$
Magnetization # This is used to describe the extend how material has been Magnetized
$$ \vec{M} = \lim_{\Delta V \to 0} \frac{1}{\Delta V} \sum_{i=1}^{N\Delta V} \vec{m}_i $$
It’s definition is the net Magnetic Dipole in unit volume
Magnetization of Magnetic Materials # Before describing the Magnetic Field inside a Magnetic Material, we shall summarize all things first
$M$: Magnetization, describe the magnetic field created by the material own $H$: External Magnetic Field Now we define $\chi_m$ to be the Magnetic Susceptibility, which is the response of material under magnetic field
So the total Magnetic Flux Density inside the material will be
$$ \vec{B} = \mu_0 (\vec{H} + \vec{M}) $$
This means that the total Flux will be the External plus Internal, now sub in $\vec{M} = \chi_m \vec{H}$ to get
$$ \vec{B} = \mu_0 (\vec{H} + \chi_m \vec{H}) = \mu_0 (1 + \chi_m) \vec{H} $$
Now we define $(1 + \chi_m)$ to be $\mu_r$, Relative Permeability, now we can get
$$ \vec{B} = \mu_0 \mu_r \vec{H} $$
This means that the existence of Magnetic Material changed the distribution of Magnetic Field
Types of Magnetic Materials # Magnetic Domains # Imagine the internal structure of material is formed by numbers of chambers which are called Domains
When the Domains are having different Magnetic Force directions, externally the $M=0$
Whereas then Domains are aligned, this creates a Magnetic Field
Magnetic Hysteresis of Ferromagnetic materials # Basically, the Magnetic Material’s Internal magnetic Field has the property of Hysteresis which is like FSM that the current stage depends on previous stage
Magnetic Field Boundary Conditions # When Magnetic Field coming across two materials, here analyze how it change
Magnetic Field Boundary Condition - Normal Components # Based on a long derivation, we get that Normal Component of Magnetic Flux is continuous, but the Magnetic Field is not as
$$ \mu_1 H_{n1} = \mu_2 H_{n2} $$
Magnetic Field Boundary Condition - Tangential Components # Based on derivation, we get the Magnetic Field is continuous, but Magnetic Flux isn’t
$$ \frac{B_{t1}}{\mu_1} = \frac{B_{t2}}{\mu_2} $$
Magnetic Field Boundary Condition when having Surface Current # This occur when there’s a perfect conductor that makes
$$ H_{t1} - H_{t2} = J_s $$
Thus the Magnetic Flux will have
$$ \frac{B_{t1}}{\mu_1} - \frac{B_{t2}}{\mu_2} = J_s $$
Revisiting Toroidal Magnetic Field # For a Toroid with radius r, it’s Magnetic Field $H$ will distribute in
$r<a$: 0 as no current is passing $a<r<b$: $\vec{H} = \frac{NI}{2\pi r} \hat{\phi}$ $r>b$: 0 as the current into is same as out of Now use the B.C. to calculate that again, starting from $H_{t1} - H_{t2} = J_s$, we can get there’s two interfaces, $r=a$ and $r=b$
$r=a$: $H_{air}=0$, $H_{core} = \frac{NI}{2\pi a}$, and Surface Charge is $J_s = \frac{NI}{l}$ $r=b$: $H_{core} = \frac{NI}{2\pi b}$, $H_{air}=0$ Ex. Calculating the Magnetic Field in Boundary Condition # Magnetic Flux # The Magnetic strength is $\vec{H} = \frac{NI}{2\pi r} \hat{\phi}$, whereas the Magnetic Flux Density will be $\vec{B} = \frac{\mu NI}{2\pi r} \hat{\phi}$, thus the Magnetic Flux will be the integral of B, which is
$$ \Psi = \iint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{s} = \iint \frac{\mu NI}{2\pi r} \hat{\phi} \cdot d s \hat{\phi} = \frac{\mu NI}{2\pi} \iint \frac{ds}{r} $$
Self-Inductance # Recall that Capacitor stores Energy inside Electric Field, whereas Inductor stores Energy in Magnetic Field
The Self-Inductance Coefficient is being defined as
$$ L = \frac{\Lambda}{I} = \frac{N\Psi}{I} $$
$\Lambda=N\Psi$: Flux Linage, is the Flux through all Turns We can extract this formula into
$$ L = \frac{N \iint \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{s}}{I}=\frac{N \iint \mu \vec{H} \cdot d\vec{s}}{I} $$
Self Inductance of a Toroid # First we need to use Amperes Law to get the Magnetic Field Strength in Toroid, which is
$$ \vec{H} = \frac{NI}{2\pi r} \hat{\phi} $$
Then sub this into the integral to get
$$ \Psi = \int_a^b \frac{\mu NI}{2\pi r} \cdot h , dr = \frac{\mu NIh}{2\pi} \ln\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)\Rightarrow L = \frac{\mu N^2 h \ln(b/a)}{2\pi} $$
Effect if Air Gap in Toroid # Self Inductance of a Solenoid # Self-inductance of a Solenoid – Special Case # Inductance of a Parallel-wire Transmission Line # Self-inductance of Infinitely Long Coaxial Cable # Mutual-Inductance # Mutual inductance describes the magnetic coupling between two coils
$$ M = L_{12} = \frac{\Lambda_{12}}{I_1} $$
Mutual-Inductance between Wire and Loop # Mutual-inductance in Solenoid with Two Solenoids # Mutual-inductance in Solenoid with Two Discrete Loops # Magnetic Energy #

Continuous-Time System # A CT system takes a CT input and produces a CT output
Pointwise Definition of CT system # Given the output of the system $y(t)=T{x}(t)$ it’s determined by an explicit formula from ${x(t)}_{t\in \mathbb R}$
Ex. Pointwise CT System # $$ y(t) = (x(t))^2 $$
CT System Property: Linearity # ❗ NOT all System are Linear
A Linear System has two properties, 1. Homogeneity and 2. Additivity, which can be written as
$$ T{\alpha x + \tilde{\alpha}\tilde{x}} = \alpha T{x} + \tilde{\alpha} T{\tilde{x}} $$
Zero input in Linear System # Based on Homogeneity: $T{0 \cdot x} = 0 \cdot T{x}$, thus a zero input always have a zero output
Example: The Squaring System # A squaring System is $y(t) = (x(t))^2 \text{}$, sub in to get
$$ T_{\text{sq}}{\alpha x + \tilde{\alpha}\tilde{x}}(t) = (\alpha x(t) + \tilde{\alpha}\tilde{x}(t))^2 \text{}= \alpha^2(x(t))^2 + \tilde{\alpha}^2(\tilde{x}(t))^2 + 2\alpha\tilde{\alpha}x(t)\tilde{x}(t) \text{} $$
This is not equal to adding their output separately
$$ \alpha T_{\text{sq}}{x}(t) + \tilde{\alpha}T_{\text{sq}}{\tilde{x}}(t) = \alpha(x(t))^2 + \tilde{\alpha}(\tilde{x}(t))^2 \text{} $$
CT System Property: Time-Invariance # A time delay in CT system is defined as $x_\tau(t) = x(t - \tau)$, a system is Time-Invariance if
$$ y = T{x} \implies y_\tau = T{x_\tau} $$
Physical meaning: an experiment on the system tomorrow will produce the same results as an experiment on the system today
Example: The Squaring System # Sub in the time delay in the Squaring System $y(t) = (x(t))^2$, notice
$$ T_{\text{sq}}{x_\tau}(t) = (x_\tau(t))^2 = (x(t - \tau))^2 $$
Thus that the Squaring System is a Time-Invariance System
CT System Property: Causality # A CT System is causal if for all $t\in \mathbb R$, the output $y(t)$ depends only on the past and present input values ${x(\tau)}_{\tau\leq t}$
Equivalent Definition # A CT system T is causal if for any time $t_0$ and any two inputs $x$, $\tilde{x}$ satisfy $x(t)=\tilde{x}(t)$ for all $t\leq t_0$, then their ouputs $y=T{x}$ and $\tilde{y}=T{ \tilde{x} }$ should also be the same
CT System Property: Memoryless # A CT System is memoryless if for all time $t\in \mathbb R$, the output $y(t)$ only depends on input $x(t)$ at the same time
❗ Memoryless is a special case for Causality
CT System Property: Invertibility # A CT system is invertible if
$$ T_{\text{inv}}{T{x}} = T{T_{\text{inv}}{x}} = x $$
CT System Property: Stability (Linear System Only) # Recall Bounded Signal # A CT signal is bounded if $|x|\infty = \max{t \in \mathbb{R}} |x(t)|$ is a finite value, thus it’s max amplitude will be a finite value
BIBO Stable # A linear CT system T is Bounded-Input Bounded-Output if there’s a constant $K\geq 0$ such that $|y|\infty \leq K|x|\infty$
Ex. Stable CT system # A Integrator is not a BIBO Stable System, as if the input is a step function, the output goes to infinity, which is not bounded
Summarize # Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) System # LTI system are both Linear and Time-Invariant
Recall: CT unit Impulse # $$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\delta_\tau(t) , dt = x(\tau) \text{} $$
The Impulse Response for a LTI System # Given the CT unit Impulse as the input of the LTI System, we can then get the $h(t)$ which is the Impulse Resposne for the System
The Response of an LTI System # As we know the LTI system’s Impulse Response, we can then calculate its response under any input signal, here’s proof
Known that $x(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)\delta(t-\tau) d\tau$, $x(\tau)$ represent the Magnitude of signal at that time, and $\delta(t-\tau)$ selected that time, by adding those all together, we can recover the original signal
Secondly, we are going to apply the Linear Property that
$$ y(t) = T\left{ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)\delta_\tau d\tau \right} = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau) T{\delta_\tau} d\tau $$
If we define the Response of LTI System under Impulse as $h(t)$, then based on the Time-Invariant Property, we get
$$ T{\delta(t-\tau)} = h(t-\tau) $$
Put this back into the $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau) T{\delta_\tau} d\tau$, we can then get
$$ y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)h(t-\tau) d\tau $$
Which is just he Convolution Integral
❗ This implies that, once we give LTI system a Unit Impulse Signal $\delta(t)$, to get its response $h(t)$, we can then use this $h(t)$ to get all the its output using the Convolution
Convolution # The convolution of two signals can be defined as
$$ y(t) = (h * x)(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t - \tau)x(\tau) \text{d}\tau $$
Observations of Convolution # Convolution is about Period # At any time t, the output $y(t)$ depends on the input $x$ and $h$’ s entire signal instead of pointwise property
Steps to Calculate Convolution # Time Reverse h Shift Forward Multiply Pointwise Integrate over all $\tau$ Property of CT Convolution # Limitation of Convolution # A case where Convolution doesn’t work can be $v(t)=1$, and
$$ (v * v)(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (1)(1) , d\tau = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} 1 , d\tau = +\infty $$
A result of Infinite doesn’t make sense, such is then undefined
Conditions for existence of Convolution # Convolution Example: Integrator System # Now using the Step Function as the input of an Integrator, we have $x(t)=u(t)$, also known that the Impulse Response of an Integrator is $h(t)=u(t)$, thus this a convolution between two Step Functions, we can thus get
$$ y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau)h(t-\tau) , d\tau = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} u(\tau)u(t-\tau) , d\tau $$
As Step function is piecewise function, we are analysing in two segments
For $t<0$: No Value For $t\geq0$: $y(t) = \int_{0}^{t} (1 \cdot 1) , d\tau = \tau \Big|_0^t = t$ Thus we have
$$ y(t) = \begin{cases} 0, & t < 0 \ t, & t \ge 0 \end{cases} $$
Convolution Example: Gaussian and Wavelet # LTI system properties and the impulse response # ❗ Basically Summary for above
The key property for LTI system is that the output of any LTI system is given by the convolution of the impulse response with the input signal
$$ y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} h(t - \tau)x(\tau) \text{d}\tau $$
Whereas we can use $h(t)$ to classify the system property
Causality # Causal if and only if $h(t) = 0$ for all $t < 0$
Memoryless # Memoryless if and only if $h(t) = αδ(t)$ for some $\alpha \in \mathbb R$
The Response only depends on current input, a scalar
BIBO Stable # BIBO Stable if $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |h(t)| \text{d}t < \infty$, equivalently
$$ |y|_\infty \le |h|1 |x|\infty $$

Learning Assembly is about to know what happens underneath, while C Language is more readable and faster
Compilation of C # Starting from C Language, it have the file type of .c , we use gcc to compile it into Assembly
Then we have Assembly with .s , we use gnuas to make it to Machine Code
Then we have Machine Code with all 1 and 0, that have file type of .o
Linker # If there’s more than one file for C language, then we need to link all the .o files together into one machine code
Start Up Code # Actually the program doesn’t start at the main function, instead it has a start up code , it
Set up stack pointer Set un-initialised variables Using I/O Devices in C # Recall the way we did in Assembly to copies the things on Switches into LEDs
.equ LEDs, 0xFF200000 .equ SW, 0xFF200040 _start: la t0, LEDs # get LED address into t0 la t1, SW # get SW address into t1 # loop to copy from the switches into the LEDs loop: lw t2, (t1) # load the 10 switches value into t2 sw t2, (t0) # store the 10 values into the LEDs j loop # do it over and over The same can be done in a better way in C
int main (void) { volatile int *SW_ptr = (int *) 0xFF200040; volatile int *LEDR_ptr = (int *) 0xFF200000; int value; while (1) { // infinite loop value = *SW_ptr; // Get Switches - dereference SW_ptr - lw t2,(t1) *LEDR_ptr = value;// Put to LEDs - dereference LED_ptr - sw t2, (t0) } } Notice there’s a volatile inside, this tells the compiler to keep reading the memory instead of the register as the Compiler will think keep reading Register is easier, but the truth is that the things in memory will change
Audio In and Output # Starting from the Original Sound, microphone will transfer those into Voltage Signal, then go through Amplifier, then goes to Analog to Digital Converter
That is sampling in short intervals, and this is a 24-bit Digital Values
Sample Rate # If we are sampling 10000 times in one sec, that’s a 10kHz sampling rate, and the samples are
just voltage values for each time
Sound Output Process # The processor will transfer the same 24 bit thing back (24 bits means 8kHz), then D/A will convert the discrete voltages into continuous voltage, then go through amplifier then to speaker
Buffering # There’s two problem for CPU when dealing with microphone and speaker
For input microphone, it’s generating new signal every $100\mu s$ For output speaker, it’s requiring signal every $100\mu s$ too Thus if the CPU is busy doing other things and forget to deal with those two, then a lag will occur
The way we overcome this issue is then by FIFO Hardware
The size of FIFO however, isn’t infinity large, with only 128 sampling points, thus if there comes the 129’s signal, it will be discard
FIFO # There’s only two operation for FIFO, Load and Store Even though FIFO is a hardware circuit, system will give it a virtual address, thus accessing this FIFO is same as accessing the memory The Processor only talks to the input FIFO and output FIFO instead of directly to the A/D, or D/A Audio Memory Mapped Registers # Left and Right data Register # The Leftdata and Rightdata are connected to the FIFO, that getting one sample from queue
The same holds for storing, it stores a sample into the Output FIFO
Fifospace Register # Indicates how empty or full the in/output FIFOs are
RALC: Number of Input Left FIFO used RARC: Numbers of Input Right FIFO used WSLC: Numbers of Output Left FIFO empty WSRC: Numbers of Output Right FIFO empty Thus we can see, if it’s clear, then Input FIFO RALC = RARC = 0 , and the Output FIFO WDRC = WSLC = 128 Control Register # A status Register
Write 1 into CR clears the Left and Right Input FIFO Write 1 into CW clears the Output FIFO RE and WE bits are about interrupt that we don’t need RI if the input FIFO is 75% full or more, shows up 1 WI if the output FIFO is less than 25% full, shows up 1 Code Example # #define AUDIO_BASE 0xFF203040 int main(void) { // Audio codec Register address volatile int * audio_ptr = (int *) AUDIO_BASE; // intermediate values int fifospace; // This is an infinite loop checking the RARC to see if there is at least one // entry in the input FIFOs. If there is, just copy it over to the output fifo. // The timing of the input FIFO controls the timing of the output, which // makes this easier than the other parts of the lab. while (1) { fifospace = *(audio_ptr + 1); // read the audio port fifospace register if ((fifospace & 0x000000FF) > 0) // check RARC to see if there is at least one sample input { // load both input microphone channels - just get one sample from each int left = *(audio_ptr + 2); // read the leftdata register - input FIFO int right = *(audio_ptr + 3); // same for rightdata // note that these removes the samples from the FIFO // store both of those samples to output channels *(audio_ptr + 2) = left; // storing to the leftdata adds to output FIFO *(audio_ptr + 3) = right; } } }

Magnetic Force # Lorentz Force # $$ \vec{F}_m = q \vec{u} \times \vec{B} $$
$\vec u$: The Velocity Vector of the charge
Recall that Cross Product’s magnitude is $|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \sin(\theta)$ Work Done by Magnetic Force # Start with reviewing the work done by Electric Force first
$$ W_e = \int \vec{F}_e \cdot d\vec{l} = q\int \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l} $$
Apply the same to Magnetic Field
$$ W_m = \int \vec{F}_m \cdot d\vec{l} = \int q(\vec{u} \times \vec{B}) \cdot (\vec{u} dt) $$
Known that the Crossed Vector $\vec{u} \times \vec{B}$ has to be perpendicular to $\vec{u}$
Thus the Work Done by Magnetic Field is ALWAYS zero Magnetic Force on a Straight Current Carrying Wire # In a Current Carrying Wire, there’s Current $I = \frac{dq}{dt}$, as the speed is $\vec{u} = \frac{d\vec{l}}{dt}$, thus we can get $I d\vec{l} = dq \vec{u}$
Thus there will be a curve for those Current Carrying Wire then
Magnetic Force on a Current Carrying Wire # Starting from Lorentz Force Equation $d\vec{F}_m = dq (\vec{u} \times \vec{B})$, use the equation mentioned above $dq \vec{u} = I d\vec{l}$, we can get $d\vec{F}_m = I d\vec{l} \times \vec{B}$
Thus if we want to know the total Lorentz Force on the wire, we just need to take the integral
Any Counter # $$ \vec{F}m = \int{a}^{b} I d\vec{l} \times \vec{B} $$
Under an uniform Magnetic Field, the integral is path independent, meaning the Integral only depends on the starting and ending point
Closed Loop # $$ \vec{F}_m = \oint_C I d\vec{l} \times \vec{B} $$
Under a uniform Magnetic Field, the total force will always be zero
But it will create a Torque, this will be cover later
Ex. Lorentz Foce on a Semicircle # Note: In a uniform Magnetic Field, the total Lorentz Force should be zero in a Closed Contour
Types of Current Distributions # Line Current # $$ I d\vec{l} $$
Surface Current # $$ I d\vec{l} = \left( \int \vec{J_s} \cdot d\vec{w} \right) d\vec{l} $$
Volume Current Density # $$ I d\vec{l} = \left( \iint_S \vec{J} \cdot d\vec{s} \right) d\vec{l} $$
Linear Integrals to Calculate Magnetic Force # Known that the basic Magnetic Force current have inside magnetic field is $\vec{F}_m = \int I d\vec{l} \times \vec{B}$
This formula will be $\vec{F}_m = I \left( \int d\vec{l} \right) \times \vec{B}$ if B is a uniform field Whereas $\int_a^b d\vec{l} = \vec{L}$, thus we then get $$ \vec{F}_m = I \vec{L} \times \vec{B} $$
Magnetic Force in a System # Total Magnetic Force on a Closed Current - Case 1 # Total Magnetic Force on a Closed Current - Case 2 # Total Magnetic Force on a Closed Current - General Case # When we put a Closed Current inside the Magnetic Field, it usually created a Torque that make itself spin inside the Magnetic Field
$$ \vec{\tau}_m = \vec{m} \times \vec{B} $$
$m$: Normal Vector of the Closed Current plane, $m=I\cdot A$ $B$: External Magnetic Field Thus the Magnetic Torque can be represented by
$$ |\tau| = Iab \cdot B_0 \sin\theta $$
❗ All things above are about how Closed Current response under the Magnetic Field, whereas things below will describe how Current Create Magnetic Field
Biot-Savart’s Law # In Coulomb’s Law, it describe how Charges creates the Electric Field, whereas the Biot-Savart’s Law describe how Current creates the Magnetic Field
Electric Field Magnetic Field Source Point Charge Q Small Current I$d\vec{l}$ Filed Equation $\vec{E} = \frac{Q \hat{R}}{4\pi\epsilon R^2} = \frac{Q \vec{R}}{4\pi\epsilon R^3}$ $d\vec{H} = \frac{Id\vec{l} \times \hat{R}}{4\pi R^2} = \frac{Id\vec{l} \times \vec{R}}{4\pi R^3}$ ❗ This indicate that Magnetic Field is formed by moving charge, and it’s a curl shape from current
Thus having the formula of
$$ d\vec{H} = \frac{Id\vec{l} \times \hat{R}}{4\pi R^2} = \frac{Id\vec{l} \times \vec{R}}{4\pi R^3} $$
Magnetic Filed of an Infinite Current Line # Ex. Magnetic Field of a Finite Current Line # Ex. Magnetic Field of two Semi-Infinite Current Traces # Ex. Magnetic Field of Circular Current Loop on Its Axis # Magnetostatic Maxwell’s Equations # There’s two basic physic principle for Magnetic Field
Gauss’s Law for Magnetism # $$ \nabla \cdot \vec{B} = 0 $$
This states that the divergency of Magnetic Field is zero, thus by Divergency Theorem we knows that any closed Integral’s Magnetic Field will be zero $\oint_S \vec{B} \cdot d\vec{s} = 0$
This reflect that the magnetic equivalence of an electric point charge doesn’t exist in nature
Amphere’s Law for Magnetism # $$ \nabla \times \vec{H} = \vec{J} $$
This indicates that the Magnetic Field’s strength is formed by the Current Density $\vec J$, thus current is the source that produce Magnetic Field
By Stokes’ Theorem, we can get that
$$ \oint_C \vec{H} \cdot d\vec{l} = \iint_S \vec{J} \cdot d\vec{s} = I_{enc} $$
Which means that the Line Integral along Magnetic Field is equal to the Net Current $I_{enc}$ crossed the surface
Ampere’s Law # $$ \oint_C \vec{H} \cdot d\vec{l} = \iint_S \vec{J} \cdot d\vec{s} = I_{enc} $$
Ampere’s Law Contour Choice # To make the calculation simple, there’s four suggestion on choosing the Contour
Choose Contour parallel to Magnetic Field H that makes $H\cdot dl=1$ If parallel is not possible, then choose perpendicular ones to make it zero Make sure the Magnetic Field $H$ is Equivalent among the contour, so the H can be get out of the Integral Use RHR to get directions Magnetic Field Calculation Summary # Biot-Savart # Similar to Colomb’s Law, where there’s no symmertry
$$ \vec{H} = \int_{\vec{r}’_{source}} \frac{I d\vec{l} \times \vec{R}}{4\pi R^3} $$
Ampere’s Circuital Law # Similar to Gauss’s Law
$$ \oint_C \vec{H} \cdot d\vec{l} = I_{enc} = \int \vec{J} \cdot d\vec{s} $$
The key of this Law is to use Symmetry to get $H$ out of the integral Magnetic Field of Infinite thick wire with uniform J # Magnetic Field of Infinite thick wire with non-uniform J # Magnetic Field of an Infinite Current Sheet # Magnetic Field of Toroidal Coil in xy-Plane #

Sampling # Sampling means to collect a measurement of a signal
If there’s too few samples, then there’s a little we can learn If there’s “enough”, then we may be able to figure out the original one The sampling function # The sampling function is defined as
$$ s(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t - nT_s) $$
Where $T_s>0$ is the Sampling Period
Mathematically, sampling is done by multiplying the original signal and the sampling function
$$ s(t)x(t) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t - nT_s)x(nT_s) $$
This will give a product of a weighted sum of impulses
CTFS of the Sampling Function # Firstly having $s(t)$ as a Impulse Train, with the period of $T_s$, we can get its harmonic angular frequency as $\omega_s=\frac{2\pi}{T_s}$, then we can get CTFS Coefficient to be
$$ \alpha_k = \frac{1}{T_s} \int_{-T_s/2}^{T_s/2} s(t)e^{-j k \omega_s t} dt $$
Where as here $s(t)$ is $\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t - nT_s)$, that is
$$ \alpha_k = \frac{1}{T_s} \int_{-T_s/2}^{T_s/2} \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(t - nT_s)e^{-j k \omega_s t} dt $$
As the outer Integral only contains the period from $T_s/2$ to $-T_s/2$, the inner n can only be zero, in such way, the CTFS Coefficient will be simplified into
$$ \alpha_k =\frac{1}{T_s} \int_{-T_s/2}^{T_s/2} \delta(t) e^{-j k \omega_s t} dt\Rightarrow a_k = \frac{1}{T_s}e^{-jk\omega_s(0)} =\frac{1}{T_s} $$
Notice this Coefficient is no long depend on k, thus every harmonic will have the same amplitude, and such the $s(t)$ can be represented by
$$ s(t) = \frac{1}{T_s} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} e^{j k \omega_s t} $$
CTFT of the sampling function # Known before that CTFT of a periodic signal is
$$ x(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \alpha_k e^{\mathbf{j} k \omega_0 t} \implies X(\mathbf{j}\omega) = 2\pi \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \alpha_k \delta(\omega - k \omega_0 $$
Therefor we can get the same for $s(t)$
$$ s(t) = \frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{s}}} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} e^{\mathbf{j} k \omega_{\mathrm{s}} t} \implies S(\mathbf{j} \omega) = \frac{2\pi}{T_{\mathrm{s}}} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(\omega - k \omega_{\mathrm{s}}) $$
❗ Notice the CTFT of the Sampling Function is also a Sampling Function
This is then called Picket Fence Miracl
Picket Fence Miracle # Band-Limited Signals # Definition # A CT signal is band limited with bandwidth B > 0 if its CTFT Spectrum satisfies $X(j\omega)=0$ for all $|\frac{\omega}{2\pi}|\geq B$
This $|\frac{\omega}{2\pi}|\geq B$ requirement also means that the Spectrum is zero outside $[-2\pi B,2\pi B]$
Now if we sampled this Band_Limited siganal
Sampling of Band-Limited Signals # As we have use mathematic ways to describe Sampling Function, and we interoperate the action of “sampling” as multiplication, in such way, recall the property that Multiplication in time-domain is convolution in frequency-domain
Thus the Spectrum of Sampled Signal $x_s(t)=x(t)s(t)$ is then
$$ \begin{aligned} X_{\mathrm{s}}(\mathbf{j}\omega) &= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} S(\mathbf{j}\nu) X(\mathbf{j}(\omega - \nu)) ,\mathrm{d}\nu \ &= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left[ \frac{2\pi}{T_{\mathrm{s}}} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \delta(\nu - k \omega_{\mathrm{s}}) \right] X(\mathbf{j}(\omega - \nu)) ,\mathrm{d}\nu \ &= \frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{s}}} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} X(\mathbf{j}(\omega - k \omega_{\mathrm{s}})) \end{aligned} $$
the spectrum of the sampled signal is a periodised version of the spectrum of original signal, with period ωs in the frequency domain Thus if $\omega_s \geq 4\pi B$, then there won’t be overlapping in frequency domain to make the signal aliasing
Nyquist-Shannon Sampling Theorem # Let $x$ be a bandlimited CT signal with bandwidth B. If $x$ is sampled with sampling period of $T_s$ satisfying $T_S<\frac{1}{2B}$, then $x$ can be exacly recoved from the samples in the way of
$$ X(j\omega) = T_s \cdot X_s(j\omega) \cdot [u(\omega + 2\pi B) - u(\omega - 2\pi B)] $$
Nyquist Frequency # The sampling frequency satisfied Nyquist-Shannon is then
$$ \omega=4\pi B $$
Aliasing # As the Sampling Frequency is too slow, it no longer recovers the original spectrum

In a linear circuit, a sinusoidal input with frequency $\omega$ always produces sinusoidal steady-state outputs with the same frequency
Thus we can only analyze the Amplitude an Phase of elements, and the key of it is
If there’s multiple inputs, they must have the same frequency No transient information will be given (only at steady state) Have to use complex numbers Complex Number # Rectangular Form # Polar Form # $$ z = |z|e^{j\theta} = |z|\angle\theta $$
We can’t add or subtract in Polar Form, has to convert first
Sinusoids # $$ v(t) = V_A \cos(\omega t + \theta) $$
$V_A$: Amplitude
$\omega$: Angular Frequency
$\theta$: Phase
$f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi}$: Frequency
$T = \frac{1}{f}$: Period
Euler’s relationship # The complex number can be expressed by
$$ Me^{j\phi} = M\cos\phi + jM\sin\phi $$
Notice that this is one Real and one Imaginary term, and we only want the Real one
In phasor analysis, we prefer Cosine function more
Thus we can get
$$ V_A \cos(\omega t + \theta) = Re{ V_A e^{j(\omega t + \theta)} }=Re{ V_A e^{j\theta} \cdot e^{j\omega t} } $$
Phasor # The phasor term contains the Amplitude and Phase of a wave, which is the two variables we want, while getting rid of the Angular Frequency which stays the same for whole time
Phase can be expressed in several ways
Exponential form: ****$V_A e^{j\theta}$ Polar form: $V_A \angle \theta$ Rectangular form: $V_A \cos\theta + jV_A \sin\theta$ Convert between Time and Phasor Domain # Time Domain Phasor Domain $i(t) = I_A \cos(\omega t + \alpha)$ $\overline{I} = I_A \angle \alpha$ $v(t) = V_A \sin(\omega t + \psi)$ $\overline{V} = V_A \angle (\psi - 90^\circ)$ Complex Number Calculus # Addition/Subtraction # It’s hard to calculate $V_1 \cos(\omega t + \theta_1) + V_2 \cos(\omega t + \theta_2)$, thus we can convert to Phasor Domain for simplification, that
$$ \overline{V} = \overline{V}_1 \pm \overline{V}_2 $$
Derivatives # Getting the derivative of $\frac{dv(t)}{dt}$, we can get
$$ \frac{dv(t)}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt} { Re [ \overline{V} e^{j\omega t} ] } = Re { \overline{V} \frac{d}{dt} e^{j\omega t} } = Re { j\omega \overline{V} e^{j\omega t} } $$
Can see that this is same to times a $j\omega$ in Phasor Domain
While getting the second derivative, we can get
$$ \frac{d^{2} v(t)}{dt^{2}} = \frac{d}{dt} [ Re { j\omega \overline{V} e^{j\omega t} } ] = Re [ j\omega \overline{V} \frac{d}{dt} e^{j\omega t} ] = Re [ (j\omega)^{2} \overline{V} e^{j\omega t} ] $$
That is timing a $(j\omega)^2$ in Phasor Domain
If we bring back the result of Derivatives of Voltage back to RLC Circuit, we can then get
$$ LC v’’(t) + RC v’(t) + v(t) = v_s(t) $$
is then equals to
$$ LC(j\omega)^2 \mathbf{V} + RC(j\omega) \mathbf{V} + \mathbf{V} = \mathbf{V_s} $$
This totally get rid of the time and simplified the differential equation into an equation
Time Domain vs. Phasor Domain # As the circuit change from Time Domain into Phasor Domain, the elements change too
Resistor # Capacitor # Inductor # Admittance # $$ Y = \frac{1}{Z} $$
Is useful in Parallel Circuit
Impedance vs. Frequency # From the element’s Impedance formula, we can see their relation with $\omega$
Ex. RC Circuit # $$ \mathbf{\bar{V}} = 4\angle 0^\circ \times (10 - j20) $$
Further using $tan$ and Mod formula we can get
$$ \mathbf{\bar{V}} \approx 89.44\angle -63.43^\circ $$
Which is $v(t) = 89.44\cos(5000t - 63.43^\circ) \text{ V}$ in time domain
Ex. RLC Circuit # Parallel and Series Connection # The Impedance of Z is the same as the Resistor
Series # The Impedance in Series Circuit is
$$ Z_{eq} = \sum_{j=1}^{n} Z_j $$
While the Voltage Division Rule will be
$$ \overline{V}k = \frac{Z_k}{Z{eq}} \overline{V} $$
Parallel # The Impedance in Parallel is
$$ Z_{eq} = \frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{Z_j}} $$
And the Voltage Division rule is
$$ \overline{I}k = \frac{Z{eq}}{Z_k} \overline{I} $$
Thevenin/Norton equivalent circuits in phasor domain # Ex. # Energy and Power # Energy and Power for a Resistor # Known there’s a AC Current through Resistor with $i_R(t)=I_A\cos\omega t$, the power formula is then
$$ P_R(t) = R \cdot i_R^2(t) = R I_A^2 \cos^2(\omega t)= \frac{R I_A^2}{2} [1 + \cos(2\omega t)] $$
Thus we can conclude
The Average Power of Resistor is $P_{avg} = \frac{R I_A^2}{2}$ as cosine’s avg in a period is zero Always dissipating energy: Unlike Capacitor or Inductor, Resistor only convert energy into heat Double in frequency: The frequency of Power is double of Current Energy and Power for an Inductor # The same current $i_R(t)=I_A\cos\omega t$ pass through the Inductor, and the Energy formula will be
$$ W_L(t) = \frac{1}{2} L I_A^2 \cos^2(\omega t)= \frac{L I_A^2}{4} [1 + \cos(2\omega t)] $$
Find the Derivative of W (Energy) of time to get Power
$$ P_L(t) = -\frac{\omega L I_A^2}{2} \sin(2\omega t) $$
Thus we can conclude that
The Energy Inductor absorb in a period is equal to the one it released, thus average Power is zero Energy and Power for a Capacitor # The Capacitor will have a AC Voltage across is $v_c(t) = V_A \cos\omega t$, using the same approach
$$ W = \frac{1}{2} C v^2 = \frac{C V_A^2}{4} [1 + \cos 2\omega t] $$
Finding the Derivative of it to get
$$ P_c(t) = -\frac{\omega C V_A^2}{2} \sin 2\omega t $$
Thus we can get
The average Power is zero Capacitor Absorb Energy in the Positive Power Cycle and return it back in the Negative Cycle Maximum Power Transfer # We first simplify the whole circuit into a Thevenin Equivalent circuit
In this case, there will be two Impedance, $Z_T$ Theveinin Impedance and $Z_L$ Load Impedance
We need to find a condition of $Z_L$ to make it have the maximum power
Known that only the Resistor is consuming Power in a AC source, while the formula is $P_{ave} = R_L \frac{|\bar{I}|^2}{2}$, based on the formula $|\bar{I}| = \frac{|\bar{V}_T|}{|Z_T + Z_L|} = \frac{|\bar{V}_T|}{\sqrt{(R_T+R_L)^2 + (X_T+X_L)^2}}$, we can get
$$ P_{ave} = \frac{\frac{R_L}{2}|\bar{V}_T|^2}{(R_T+R_L)^2 + (X_T+X_L)^2} $$
To make this formula largest, we can reduce the denominator
Let $X_T + X_L = 0$ and $R_L = R_T$ (This is achieved by finding derivative) Thus we can get, to maximum the power, we need a pair of Conjugate Impedance
$$ Z_L = Z_T^* $$
Thus the final Power formula will become
$$ P_{max} = \frac{|\bar{V}_T|^2}{8R_T} $$

Linear Ordinary Differential Equation, ODE # $$ a_n x^{(n)} + a_{n-1} x^{(n-1)} + \dots + a_1 x^{(1)} + a_0 x = g(t) $$
$x^{(n)}$: x’s n th derivative for t
$g(t)$: Forcing Term, if $g(t)\neq 0$, then this ODE is a Non-Homogeneous Function
Complementary Function # If $g(t)$ is zero, in which the ODE is a Homogeneous Function, then the function is aka Complementary Function
$$ a_n x^{(n)} + a_{n-1} x^{(n-1)} + \dots + a_1 x^{(1)} + a_0 x = 0 $$
It describe the behavior of function when no outer influence
Whereas the solution to this function is then called the Complementary Solution $x_c(t)$
$$ x_c(t) = C_1 x_1(t) + C_2 x_2(t) + \dots + C_n x_n(t) $$
The Complementary Solution is the n th solution’s Linear Combination
Whereas the Coefficient C is determined by the Initial Conditions
Particular Solution # The solution satisfied when $g(t)\neq 0$
The Particular Solution can be solved using Superposition, that is analysis two terms of $g(t)$ individually and add up later
Pick solution for particular type of g(t) # Ex. Finding Coefficient for Particular Solution # Suppose having function $x’’ - 2x’ + 3x = 3t^2 + 2t$
Based on the table, we guess the solution is in the form of $x_p(t) = At^2 + Bt + C$, this solution has the first derivative as $2At+B$ and second derivative as $2A$, thus
$$ (2A) - 2(2At + B) + 3(At^2 + Bt + C) = 3t^2 + 2t $$
Arrange LHS and we can get $x_p(t) = t^2 + 2t + \frac{2}{3}$
Exception for Particular Solution # If the assumed Particular Solution has already been mentioned in Complementary solution, then we need to time the guess to a $t^k$ (k normally = 1) until it’s not equal to Complementary solution
General Solution # $$ x(t) = x_c(t) + x_p(t) $$
First-order homogeneous ODE # A Particular ODE in the form of
$$ ax’ + bx = 0 $$
This function is being solved by the characteristic function, by letting $x(t) =e^{st}$
$$ a(se^{st}) + b(e^{st}) = 0\Rightarrow as + b = 0 $$
First-order RC/RL circuits # RC Circuit # Starting with the KVL, we get $R \cdot i(t) + v(t) = v_s(t)$, then known the relationship between Capacitor and current $i(t) = C \frac{dv(t)}{dt}$, sub in this to get the Differential Equation
$$ RC \frac{dv(t)}{dt} + v(t) = v_s(t) $$
RL Circuit # In RL Circuit we use KVL instead to get $\frac{v(t)}{R} + i(t) = i_s(t)$, knowing the relation between Inductor’s Voltage and Current to get
$$ \frac{L}{R} \frac{di(t)}{dt} + i(t) = i_s(t) $$
Those two RC and RL Circuit are just 1st Order Non-Homogenous ODE
Now we can first analysis the case when it’s Homogenous to find complementary solution
RC circuit zero input response # When the outer battery has been removed, the equation is now
$$ RC v’(t) + v(t) = 0 $$
With the Initial Condition that $v_c=0$, we can get the solution which is
$$ v(t) = V_0 e^{-t/RC} \quad (t \ge 0) $$
Notice that there’s a Coefficient $RC$ shifting the response rate of circuit which is $\tau = RC$
A key point is when $t=\tau$, $v_o$ will goes to 0.37 $v_0$ at this stage
RC circuit step response # Now going back to case when the external Voltage Source exist, as we want to analysis a source which only occur then $t>0$, thus we will need a Unit Step Function $u(t)$
$$ RCv’(t) + v(t) = V_s u(t) $$
And this equation will have the solution of $v(t) = v_c(t) + v_p(t)$, where $v_c$ is the Natural Response, and $v_p$ is $v_f$, the Force Response
Natural Response $v_n$: Has the form of $v_n(t) = K e^{-t/RC}$ Forced Response $v_f$: As $t\rightarrow \infty$, the particular solution will then be $V_s$ Thus the general solution will then be
$$ v(t) = K e^{-t/RC} + V_s $$
This K is just the coefficient C in ODE, that can be determined by sub in $v(0) =v_0$, so we get
$$ v(t) = (V_0 - V_s)e^{-t/RC} + V_s $$
Different Interpertations # We can treat this Reaction in two different perspectives
Natural + Forced # $$ v(t) = \underbrace{V_0 e^{-t/\tau}}{\text{Zero-Input (ZIR)}} + \underbrace{V_s(1 - e^{-t/\tau})}{\text{Zero-State (ZSR)}} $$
This form is more like a mathematic interpretation, that this is Complementary + Particular
Zero Input + Zero State # $$ v(t) = \underbrace{V_0 e^{-t/\tau}}{\text{Zero-Input (ZIR)}} + \underbrace{V_s(1 - e^{-t/\tau})}{\text{Zero-State (ZSR)}} $$
Describe the Capacitor under Initial Condition and Outer Input Source
We can conclude this RC Circuit by one formula
$$ v(t) = (v_{\text{initial}} - v_{\text{final}}) e^{-t/\tau} + v_{\text{final}} $$
Response to exponential input # Now that $g(t)$ has become a exponential function
$$ RC v’(t) + v(t) = V_s e^{-\alpha t} $$
Solving this by Complementary + Particular can get
$$ v(t) = \left( V_0 - \frac{V_s}{1 - \alpha RC} \right) e^{-t/RC} + \frac{V_s}{1 - \alpha RC} e^{-\alpha t} $$
A special case is given by when $\alpha =1/RC$m this can be solved by timing a t at Forced Response, that is
$$ v(t) = V_0 e^{-t/RC} + \frac{V_s}{RC} t e^{-t/RC} $$
2nd-Order DE # The standard 2nd Order DE formula is given by
$$ ax’’ + bx’ + cx = 0 \quad (a \neq 0) $$
This equation can also be solved by using the Characteristic Equation
$$ as^2 + bs + c = 0 $$
Known that this equation will have the solution of $(s_1, s_2) = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$
There will be several different kind of solutions based on the Sign of $D = b^2 - 4ac$
Case 1: Over-damped # Two District Real Roots: $b^2 - 4ac > 0$, having the General Solution of
$$ x(t) = c_1 e^{-\alpha_1 t} + c_2 e^{-\alpha_2 t} $$
This means that the Damp is high that the System won’t Oscillate, and it will goes to equilibrium
Case 2: Critically Damped # Two Identical Real Roots: $b^2 - 4ac = 0$, having General Solution of
$$ x(t) = c_1 e^{-\alpha t} + c_2 t e^{-\alpha t} $$
The fastest condition for system to go back to equilibrium
Case 3: Underdamped # One Conjugated Complex Roots: $b^2 - 4ac < 0$, having General Solution of
$$ x(t) = c_1 e^{-\alpha t} \cos(\beta t) + c_2 e^{-\alpha t} \sin(\beta t) $$
The system will Oscillate and then goes to Equilibrium
Series RLC Circuit # Now we can use the 2nd Order DE to analysis the Series RLC Circuit
Known the KVL is $v_L(t) + v_R(t) + v_C(t) = V_s(t)$
There’s 3 Circuit Element in the RLC Circuit, and we can analyse their voltage one by one
Firstly we know in this series Circuit the current is $i = C \frac{dv_c}{dt}$ Inductor: $v_L = L \frac{di}{dt}$, as $i = C \frac{dv_c}{dt}$, we have $v_L = LC v_c’'$ Resistor: $v_R = Ri = RC v_c'$ Then add up everything to get
$$ LC v_c’’(t) + RC v_c’(t) + v_c(t) = V_s(t) $$
Process of Solving # Find the Complementary Solution # Letting Force to be zero
$$ LC v_c’’ + RC v_c’ + v_c = 0 $$
This have the characteristic equation of
$$ as^2 + bs + c = 0 $$
Find the Particular Solution # A Forced Solution when $V_s\neq 0$
Use the Initial Condition # Use the Initial Condition to find the coefficient
Ex. Zero-Input Response # The Zeta and Omega Notation # From above we known that the Homogeneous ODE is
$$ ax’’ + bx’ + cx = 0 $$
Now we substitute $\omega_0^2=\frac{c}{a}$ and $\zeta = \frac{b}{2\sqrt{ac}}$, we can get
$$ x’’ + 2\zeta\omega_0 x’ + \omega_0^2 x = 0 $$
As the a,b,c coefficient only represent the Physical Quantity, it doesn’t tells us about the system’s status, thus we introduce Zeta and Omega, whereas
Zeta is the Phase Omega is the Speed So now we can describe the system as
State Condition Nature of Roots Phenomenon Description Overdamped $\zeta > 1$ Two distinct negative real roots The system returns slowly to the equilibrium position without any oscillation. Critically Damped $\zeta = 1$ Two equal negative real roots The system returns to the equilibrium position in the shortest possible time without oscillation. Underdamped $\zeta < 1$ A pair of complex conjugate roots The system oscillates around the equilibrium position, but the amplitude gradually decays over time. Now we can sub in the RLC to get $\omega_0 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{LC}}$, and $\zeta = \frac{R}{2}\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}}$

Electric Field Boundary Conditions # Dielectric – Dielectric Interface – Tangential Components # Known that Electric Field has the Conservative Property, that is
$$ \nabla \times E=0 $$
Thus based on Stokes’ Theorem, this means that $\oint_C \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l} = 0$
In order to analysis the condition around the margin, we first construct a square contour
This is just the sum of four contours, and known that their sum is zero
$$ \int_{l_1} + \int_{l_2} + \int_{l_3} + \int_{l_4} = 0 $$
Notice that both $l1$ and $l3$ is equal to zero if we make the height h to be zero, thus
$$ \int_{l_2} \vec{E}2 \cdot d\vec{l} + \int{l_4} \vec{E}_1 \cdot d\vec{l} = 0 $$
As they are in different directions, thus
$$ -E_{2t} \cdot a + E_{1t} \cdot a = 0\Rightarrow E_{1t} = E_{2t} $$
This is saying that when entering from one material to another, the Perpendicular Electric Field might change, but the Parallel one won’t
Dielectric – Dielectric Interface – Normal Components # Known that $\nabla \cdot \vec{D} = \rho_v$, which is $\oiint \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} = Q_{enc}$
Now we are using a model of a Pillbox
We are assuming that $h\rightarrow 0$, to get the Normal Boundary condition
Notice that when this cylindrical is now a circle having Surface Charge Density which only have flux on the top and bottom
$$ \iint\limits_{\text{Top}} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} + \cancel{\iint\limits_{\text{Side}} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s}} + \iint\limits_{\text{Bottom}} \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} = Q_{\text{enc}} $$
As all the Area is just $\Delta s$,the equation can be simplified to
$$ \varepsilon_2 E_{2n} - \varepsilon_1 E_{1n} = \rho_s $$
Example # Assuming two Electric Fields
$$ \vec{E_1}=E_{1x}\hat x+E_{1y}\hat y+E_{1z}\hat z $$
$$ \vec{E_2}=E_{2x}\hat x+E_{2y}\hat y+E_{2z}\hat z $$
The x and y component are always the same as the Tangent, whereas the Normal one have
$$ \varepsilon_2 E_{2n} - \varepsilon_1 E_{1n} = \rho_s $$
If we assume $\rho_s = 0$, then $\varepsilon_2 E_{2n} = \varepsilon_1 E_{1n}$
Dielectric – Perfect Conductor Interface – Tangential Components # A special case for conductor is that it’s interior Electric Field is zero, that is $E_1= 0,D_1=0$
Thus if the boundary is between a conductor and a Perfect Conductor, thus
The 1st B.C, $E_{1t}=E_{2t}=0$ The 2nd B.C. $E_{2n}=\frac{\rho_s}{\varepsilon _2}$ Conductor – Conductor Interface # As the previous ones $E_{1t}=E_{2t}$ for the 1st B.C., however as there’s current passing by in the Conductor, we need to take care of Current Density J, as $J=\sigma E$, we have
$$ \vec{J}{2t} = \frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1} \vec{J}{1t} $$
For the 2nd B.C., as $D_{2n} - D_{1n} = \rho_s$, and $D = \varepsilon E$, $E = J/\sigma$, thus we have
$$ \varepsilon_2 \frac{J_{2n}}{\sigma_2} - \varepsilon_1 \frac{J_{1n}}{\sigma_1} = \rho_s $$
Whereas at the steady state, we have $J_{1n} = J_{2n}$, thus
$$ J_{1n} \left( \frac{\varepsilon_2}{\sigma_2} - \frac{\varepsilon_1}{\sigma_1} \right) = \rho_s $$
Capacitance # In this course, Capacitance is being defined as the place where any two conductors sperate by insulator
In this course we start with formula $C=Q/V$, by Gaussian’s Law we define Q as
$$ Q_{enc} = \oint_S \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} = \oint_S \epsilon_r \epsilon_0 \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s} $$
While we can use the Line Integral to define V as
$$ V = -\int_-^+ \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l} = V_+ - V_- $$
And we can get he formula of C as
$$ C = \frac{\oint_S \epsilon \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s}}{-\int_-^+ \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l}} $$
Property of Capacitance # Capacitance only depends on following properties
Shape of the conductors Distance b/w the conductors Permittivity ($\epsilon$) RC Coefficient # Recall # Based on the Conductivity $\sigma$ we can classify the materials
Nevertheless, there’re no perfect Capacitor in real life, thus we need to analyse the real behavior
There’s two ideal material, Conductors and Dielectrics, one have the $R=0$, the other have $R=\infty$, as the Capacitance is not ideal in real life, we treat it with as a identical Parallel Capacitor and Resistor
Since we define the Resistor R as $R=V/I$, we can write it as
$$ R = \frac{V}{I} = \frac{-\int \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l}}{\iint \vec{J} \cdot d\vec{s}} $$
In the same way, we can write Capacitor as
$$ C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{\iint \epsilon \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s}}{-\int \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l}} $$
Notice if we multiply those two we will then get
$$ RC = \left( \frac{-\int \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l}}{\iint \sigma \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s}} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{\iint \epsilon \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s}}{-\int \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l}} \right)=\frac{\epsilon}{\sigma} $$
❗ Using this equation, we can get the R and C of the Capacitor as long as we know one of those
Ex. Parallel-Plate Capacitor # As indicated, in real life we deal with non-ideal Capacitor, and we wish to find that Leakage Resistance and the Capacitance
In this given example, we can start with $C=Q/V$
$$ C = \frac{Q}{V} = \frac{\iint \varepsilon \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{S}}{-\int_{-}^{+} \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l}} $$
As both integral requires Electric Field, we can find E first, and there’s basically two methods
Using the known formula for parallel plates Using Laplace’s Equation and B.C. Now we can sub in $\vec{E} = -\frac{\rho_s}{\varepsilon} \hat{z}$ $$ C = \frac{\iint \varepsilon \left( -\frac{\rho_s}{\varepsilon} \hat{z} \right) \cdot dS (-\hat{z})}{-\int_{0}^{d} -\frac{\rho_s}{\varepsilon} \hat{z} \cdot dz \hat{z}}= \frac{\rho_s \cdot A}{\frac{\rho_s}{\varepsilon} \cdot d} = \frac{\varepsilon A}{d} $$
Once known the Capacitance, we can then find R using the RC formula
$$ R = \frac{\epsilon}{\sigma} \cdot \frac{d}{\epsilon A} = \frac{d}{\sigma A} $$
Ex. Coaxial Cable Capacitor # As usual, find the C first using $C=Q/V$, then we need the Electric Field Again, and this Example we can approach by either Laplacian or Gauss’s Law, and it will be
$$ \vec{E} = \frac{-\rho_s a}{\epsilon r} \hat{r} $$
Sub in this E back and we will get
$$ C = \frac{\rho_s \cdot 2\pi a \cdot l}{-\int_{a}^{b} \frac{-\rho_s a}{\varepsilon r} \hat{r} \cdot dr \hat{r}} = \frac{\rho_s \cdot 2\pi a \cdot l}{\left. \frac{\rho_s \cdot a}{\varepsilon} \ln r \right|_a^b} = \frac{2\pi l \varepsilon}{\ln(\frac{b}{a})} $$
And using we RC formula we can also get
$$ R = \frac{\epsilon}{\sigma} \cdot \frac{1}{C} = \frac{\ln(b/a)}{2\pi \sigma l} $$
Capacitor with Stacked Dielectrics # When we put two Capacitors in Series or Parallel, its ability to store charge will change, based on the formula
$$ C = \varepsilon \cdot \frac{A}{d} $$
Where in this formula, the coefficient $\varepsilon$ is used to describe the scale of that ability, but if we still want to use the same formula after stacked two capacitors, we need to adjust this $\varepsilon$
Similar to mixing the juice, say we have apple juice and orange juice each has their own scale of sugar, if we combine them together, we will need a new way to describe the mixture of their sugar under the volume v.s. sugar
Stacked in Series # $$ \frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} = \frac{d_1}{\varepsilon_1 A} + \frac{d_2}{\varepsilon_2 A} \Rightarrow C = \frac{A \varepsilon_1 \varepsilon_2}{d_1 \varepsilon_2 + d_2 \varepsilon_1} $$
Now we want this formula back to the form of $C = \varepsilon \cdot \frac{A}{d}$, thus we divided by $A/d$
$$ \varepsilon_{eff,s} = \frac{\varepsilon_1 \varepsilon_2 (d_1 + d_2)}{d_1 \varepsilon_2 + d_2 \varepsilon_1} $$
Stacked in Parallel # $$ C = C_1 + C_2 = \frac{1}{d} (\varepsilon_1 A_1 + \varepsilon_2 A_2) $$
In Parallel, the Capacitance is simply addition, and the adjusted coefficient will be
$$ \varepsilon_{eff,p} = \frac{\varepsilon_1 A_1 + \varepsilon_2 A_2}{A_1 + A_2} $$

The Input and Output are the connection between the virtual world and the physical world
Recall on DE1-Soc Board, we have I/Os
10 LEDs 10 Slider Switches 4 Buttons 6 Seven Segment Displays Memory Mapped I/O # Recall the Computer Structure
The three main parts of Computer are communicating with the Bus , and there are address bus, which the lw will call when processor want to load something from the memory to the registers
The majority of address are associated to the memory that are being reserved for processors
They are bing classified by a circuit (the orange box) before entering While there are few of addresses that are mapped to connect to the Input/Output
For example, the state (ON/OFF) of LEDs are mapped to the low order 10 bits at address oxFF20000 , and that is just what we called the memory mapped I/O
Code Example: Using of I/O # # Define hardware register addresses .equ LEDs, 0xFF200000 # Base address for the 10 LEDs (Output) .equ SW, 0xFF200040 # Base address for the 10 Slider Switches (Input) _start: la t0, LEDs # Load the memory-mapped address of LEDs into register t0 la t1, SW # Load the memory-mapped address of Switches into register t1 # Main loop to synchronize switches and LEDs # In Memory Mapped I/O, the hardware uses the address to determine if # lw/sw refers to actual memory or a hardware device. loop: lw t2, (t1) # Read the current state of the 10 switches into register t2 sw t2, (t0) # Write the value from t2 to the LEDs, turning them ON/OFF j loop # Jump back to 'loop' to repeat indefinite Memory in Subroutines # Recall the Nested Subroutines which used the ra register to store the return address, there’s actually an issue with the Registers
If both the caller and the callee want to use one same register t0 , then an overwrite will occur Thus we make rules for everyone and follows them Transmission of Parameters # Recall in C, the function prototype is int Your_Sub(int a, int b){
This defines the input and output Argument Registers # In Assembly, to send parameters from caller to callee, we begin with first 8 parameters into register a0, a1 … a7
If there’s more than 8 of them, then use the stack The caller is responsible for both the pushing and popping While when returning, put to the a0,a1 … a7 too
Temporary Registers # The registers we frequently used t0 - t6 are the Temporary, the caller is responsible to preserve them for use
Callee Saved Registers # As for the s0-s11, those are called the saved Register, that if the callee want to make use, they will need to
Saved those on stack Then use them Make sure to restore everything before giving back to caller, so that for the caller, those are the same before and after calling Interrupt # In the previous code example, we used the way of polling to get the change of Keys, that is keep while loop to detect the change
This Polling method is bad as its keep wasting the processor source, so we need a better way, and that is just interrupt
Interrupt means that the processor will keep doing it own task, until some thing interrupt it
Special Registers # Data Reg (0xFF200050 ) # Only the last 4 bits is valid
Reflects the key status When Key 0 is pressed , the bit 0 set to 1 When Key 0 released, then set to 0 Edge Capture Reg (0xFF20005C) # Saved the pressed status
If key 0 is pressed, then set key 0 to 1 And it keeps to be 1 until Explicit Reset This Reg is designed as the CPU’s operating rate might be slower than the press operation, thus we want to record that action of pressing
To reset the bit to 0, send a 1 into it, otherwise it remains Detect the Key change # Thus there will be two ways for detecting the key change
Data Reg Edge Capture Reg Polling using Data Reg # .equ KEY_BASE, 0xFF200050 # Define the base memory-mapped address for the KEY pushbuttons la t0, KEY_BASE # Load the base address of the KEY port into register t0 # Polling loop: Wait here until Key 1 is detected as pressed poll: lw t1, (t0) # Read the current state of the Data Register into t1 andi t1, t1, 0x2 # Bitwise AND with 0x2 (binary 0010) to mask all bits except Bit 1 # This isolates the status of Key 1 beqz t1, poll # If t1 is 0 (Key 1 is not pressed), branch back to 'poll' # Execution reaches this point only after Key 1 is pressed Polling using Edge Capture Reg # .global _start .equ KEY_BASE, 0xFF200050 # Base address for the Pushbutton KEY parallel port .equ LEDs, 0xFF200000 # Base address for the Red LED parallel port _start: la t0, KEY_BASE # Load address of the KEY port into t0 la t1, LEDs # Load address of the LED port into t1 li t2, 0x1 # Initialize LED pattern: start with LED 0 turned ON # Main polling loop to check for edge capture events poll: lw t3, 0xC(t0) # Load the Edge Capture Register (offset 0xC from base) into t3 andi t3, t3, 0x4 # Mask Bit 2 to specifically check the status of Key 2 beqz t3, poll # If result is 0 (Key 2 not pressed/released), continue polling # Reaching here means Key 2 was pressed and released sw t2, (t1) # Store the current pattern in t2 to the LED data register xori t2, t2, 0x1 # XOR with 1 to toggle the state of Bit 0 for the next press # Critical Step: Reset the Edge Capture bit li t4, 0x4 # Prepare a value with Bit 2 set to 1 sw t4, 0xC(t0) # Write 1 to Bit 2 of the Edge Capture Reg to clear it (Write-1-to-Clear) j poll # Return to the start of the loop to wait for the next event Hardware Timer # There are several ways to time
Software Delay Loop: use loop to approximate time Notice as CPU frequency change, this will change Hardware Timer: Use specific hardware for timing There are two things needed, a Crystal Oscillator and a Counter Reg
Example # Consider a counter with $100MHz$, it’s period is then
$$ T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{100 \times 10^6 \text{ Hz}} = 10 \text{ ns} $$
To count to one, we will need
$$ 100,000,000 \text{ times} \times 10 \text{ ns} = 1 \text{ s} $$
which is 100 million times
So what we do is to start with 100 million and subtract one after each period
On Memory # As indicated, the I/O are being mapped on Register, there’s a Internal Timer that has six memory-mapped Registers which are 16 bits each
But we are operating everything in 32 bits, that means we need to do everything twice
After knowing the structure, here’s how to make it work
1. Split High and Low # Split Everything into high and low 16 bits
2. Set and Start # Change the Control Reg bit 2 (START) to 1, and bit 1 (CONT) to 1
START : Start CONT : Repeat after count to zero Can be done one simply write 0x6
3. Polling # Polling to check if T0 == 1 , if its true, then the time is up
4. Reset # Load 1 to T0 to reset it
Code Example: Hardware Counter # # -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # Program: LED Blinking with Hardware Interval Timer # Platform: DE1-SoC (Nios V / RISC-V) # Function: Toggles LED0 every 1 second using a 100MHz hardware timer. # -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- .global _start # Memory-mapped register addresses and constants .equ TIMER_BASE, 0xff202000 # Base address of the Interval Timer .equ LEDS, 0xff200000 # Base address of the Parallel Port for LEDs .equ COUNTER_DELAY, 100000000 # 100,000,000 ticks = 1 second at 100MHz _start: la t5, TIMER_BASE # Load timer base address into t5 la t6, LEDs # Load LEDs base address into t6 # 1. Initialize Timer sw zero, 0(t5) # Clear the TO (Time Out) bit in the Status register li t0, COUNTER_DELAY # Load the 32-bit delay value (100M) into t0 # 2. Split and Store the 32-bit counter value into 16-bit hardware registers # The hardware requires writing the Low 16 bits and High 16 bits separately. sw t0, 0x8(t5) # Store bits [15:0] to Counter Start Value (Low) srli t1, t0, 16 # Shift right by 16 bits to align the upper bits sw t1, 0xc(t5) # Store bits [31:16] to Counter Start Value (High) # 3. Configure and Start the Timer # We write 0b0110 (0x6) to the Control register: # Bit 2 (START) = 1: Starts the timer # Bit 1 (CONT) = 1: Enables continuous mode (auto-reload) li t0, 0b0110 # Load configuration bits sw t0, 0x4(t5) # Write to the Control register li t2, 1 # Initial state for LED0 (1 = ON) tloop: # 4. Update the LED state sw t2, (t6) # Store the current value to the LED register xori t2, t2, 1 # Flip the LSB of t2 (Toggle between 0 and 1) # 5. Polling Loop: Wait for 1 second to pass ploop: lw t0, 0(t5) # Load the Timer Status register andi t0, t0, 0b1 # Mask all bits except the TO bit (bit 0) beqz t0, ploop # If TO == 0, keep checking (timer still counting) # 6. Reset the Timer Status # Once TO is detected as 1, it must be manually cleared by writing 0 to it. sw zero, 0(t5) # Clear the TO bit for the next cycle j tloop # Jump back to toggle LED and wait again Interrupts # Polling is a kind of Mindless Loop that keep the processor keep tracking the change of button
This executed a lot and has a very low efficiency
Interrupt-Driven Input/Output # In the Computer organization, there will be several wires called Interrupt Request Lines that directly interrupt the Processor
Flow Chart # After getting the interrupt instruction, the main loop will first finish the current instruction, then goes to the Interrupt Request Handler and then come back
One thing need to make sure is that we can’t overwrite the registers that the main loop is using, thus we have to find a way to store them
mtvec Register # Under Nios V, we need to let FSM knows where to switch to when the interruption happens, and that’s provided by the mtvec Regester
mtvec having the full name of Machine Trap Vector, it stores the address of Interrupt Handler the main loop should jump to
While interruption is included inside Trap, Exception is also a kind of trap mepc Register # If we are jumping into somewhere else, we also need to find the path to go back after the interruption handler finished, and mepc does that
Unlike the pc Register, mepc is called Machine exception program counter that specifically response for the Counter related to machines
Stack # As indicated, we always need to store registers on stack before going into interruptions, and restore it after jumping back
This need to be implemented manually by code
Enable & Mask # Some details for interruption to works include
Enable the Interrupt function (this will be include later) while making sure there’s no interruption happens between Enable the interrupt and setting the mevec , otherwise FSM doesn’t know where to jump to and will make it crush The Input will have their own instruction of where to go to Privilege # In real world, mepc has a large power, thus user normally can’t get such power
Control Registers # Interrupt Request # There will be wires from input to FSM to help it figure out which device is sending the interrupt
Each Hardware is connected to its own IRQ The Interrupt Sequence # Initialisation # Before Everything happens, we need initialize things first
Enable Interruption (still not covered yet) Set up which device we want to used for interruption Starting with the Instruction * , so the interrupt happens since
The external hardware will pull up the IRQ wire to 1 to request the interrupt Processor check mstatus reg to see the mie is 0 or 1 Check the mie reg to see if the required device is being enable Set mstatus.MIE to zero to avoid interruption during interrupt First the processor will finish the current instruction * Then store the next address into the mepc Register Store the reason for interruption to mcause Looking at the mtvec Register to find the address of interrupt handler Since now we have jump into the Handler
goes to the address mtvec is pointing to Stack Protection, we store every register used in main loop into stack Execute things inside the Handler Then comes to the return stage
mret run, change the pc to address in mepc Reset mstatus.MIE to 1 Control and Status Register Command # Similarly, those special registers in memory can’t be operated by normal instructions, instead they should be called by csr, commonly seen commands are
csrr : Read csrw : Write csrs/csrc : Set/Clear MIE Register # Machine Interrupt Enable Register, is correspond to the IRQ, setting the given digit to one can make the Interruption for that hardware enable
Code Example # /* The simplest interrupt-driven program: * When Push button Key 1 is pressed, cause an interrupt * Each time, Toggle LED 3. (i.e. go on and off with each Key 1 press) */ .global _start _start: .equ LEDs, 0xFF200000 .equ KEY_BASE, 0xFF200050 la sp, 0x20000 # Initialize the Stack Pointer csrw mstatus, zero # turn off bit 3 of mstatus - # disable processor interrupts #(in case it was on, just being cautious, while we set everything else up) # Now, enable interrupts from the KEY device, # using the Interrupt Mask Register: Bit i of mask register on means # cause an interrupt when edge capture bit i goes to a 1 # This tells the device when to *request* an interrupt on wire IRQ18 la t1, KEY_BASE # address of KEY registers base into t1 li t0, 0b0010 # just want bit 1 -> Key 1 to have enabled interrupts sw t0, 8(t1) # Set interrupt enable in interrupt mask for Key 1 - # i.e. have it request an interrupt when edge on key 1 sw t0, 12(t1) # clear Edge Capture bit of Key 1 in case it is already on # Enable interrupts from the processor side - enabled in 2 ways: li t0, 0x40000 # 0x40000 corresponds to bit 18 of 32 bit word being 1 # (The Keys request interrupts on line 18) csrs mie, t0 # this sets bit 18 of the MIE to 1, # enabling interrupts specifically from KEYs la t0, interrupt_handler # put addr of interrupt handler routine into t0 csrw mtvec, t0 # set MTVEC to contain that address - # so proc knows where to go when interrupt happens li t0, 0b1000 # turn on bit three of register t0 csrs mstatus, t0 # use it to turn on bit 3 of MSTATUS - # the MIE bit to enable processor interrupts Main_loop: li t0, 1 # this loop doesn't do anything except set t0 # and t1, and we can check that the # interrupt program doesn't disturb them li t1, 2 j Main_loop # Just do that over and over /* this is where the processor will execute when interrupt occurs: */ interrupt_handler: # Note that, upon an interrupt, # the MIE bit in MSTATUS is set to 0, # preventing a further interrupt. # First reserve room on the stack for three words (3 words x # 4 bytes/word = 12) for the three registers we'll use t0, t1 and ra addi sp, sp, -12 sw t0, 0(sp) # Push t0 onto the stack sw t1, 4(sp) # Push t1 onto the stack sw ra, 8(sp) # Push ra onto the stack li t0, 0x7FFFFFFF # Next, check if the interrupt was caused # by devices we were expecting (KEYS in this case) # by looking at the code placed into the low 31 bits of MCAUSE csrr t1, mcause # read MCAUSE into t1 and t1, t1, t0 # "zero out" bit 31 (leave every other bit the same) li t0, 18 # code for KEYs in MCAUSE should be 18 bne t1, t0, end_interrupt # if MCAUSE low 31 bits aren't 18, # something's wrong, just return call KEY_ISR # otherwise call the KEY interrupt service routine # restore the registers that were used back from the stack end_interrupt: lw t0, 0(sp) lw t1, 4(sp) lw ra, 8(sp) addi sp, sp, 12 # move the stack pointer now that we've copied the values mret # return from interrupt - # this copies the MEPC register into the PC # it also restores the MIE bit back to be 1, re-enabling interrupts KEY_ISR: la t0, KEY_BASE # gets keys port address into t0 lw t1, 12(t0) # Load the edge capture register and check # if it is Key 1 pushed (just checking) andi t1, t1, 0b0010 # ... (Note: The provided images end here, the rest of the ISR to toggle the LED is missing)

Current and Current Densities # This unit is about Displacement Current, Convection Current and Conduction Current
Displacement Current # This is the current under Insulator, it is caused by the rate of change of the Electric Field
$$ \vec{J}_D = \frac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial t} $$
Convection Current # Current cause by the movement of Free Charges in space
$$ \vec J_{con}=\frac{\rho_v\Delta S\cdot \Delta l/\Delta t}{\Delta S}= \rho_v\cdot \vec u _v $$
$\rho_v$ : Charge Density $u_v$: Charge Drifting Speed This means $Current Density = ChargeDensity * Velocity$ Conduction Current # The Current cause by the moving Charge Carriers in conductor
$$ \vec{J}{conduction} = \rho{ve} \vec{u}e + \rho{vh} \vec{u}h=\rho{ve} (-\mu_e \vec{E}) + \rho_{vh} (\mu_h \vec{E}) = (-\rho_{ve} \mu_e + \rho_{vh} \mu_h) \vec{E} $$
That’s the movement of Electron and Holes, we can simplify this into
$$ \vec{J} = \sigma \vec{E} $$
Whereas $\sigma$ is Conductivity, $\vec E$ is Electric Field
Property of Materials # We characterise material by Conductivity $\sigma$: The ability for material to conduct current
Conductor # Conductor is the material having $\sigma »1$
Perfect Conductor # Perfect Conductor have $\sigma \rightarrow \infty$
As $\vec{J} = \sigma \vec{E}$, as Current Density has to be some finite number (Because the Energy need to be finite), thus as $\sigma \rightarrow \infty$, $\vec E \rightarrow 0$
This concludes that inside Perfect Conductor, there’s no Electric Field inside, while all Net Charges are on the surface Dielectric # Dielectric is the material having $\sigma «1$
Perfect Dielectric # Perfect Dielectric having $\sigma =0 \Rightarrow \vec J = 0$
This concludes that Ideal Dielectric’s Electric Field is zero Dielectric Breakdown # The material will have a Electric Field Threshold that when external Electric Field exceed it, the breakdown in material will occur
Semiconductors # $$ \sigma = (N_e \mu_e + N_h \mu_h) e $$
This means that the Semiconductor’s conductivity is depend on the density of Electric and Hole, and the N
Ex. # Behavior of materials under external Electric Field # Different material will present different behavior under an external Electric Field
Perfect Conductor under external Electric Field # Perfect Conductor has the property of $\sigma =\infty$, thus under Electric Field, this will creates two Electric Field in this case, an Internal one and a External one
The first $\vec E$ is pointing to the right, this will create a $-\vec F_E$ for Electrons in conductor As all the Electrons has been moved to the left side of conductor, this creates a second Internal $-\vec E$, thus the $\vec E_{net}$ is now zero And all the charges will distributed on the surface of the conductor
Conductor under external Electric Field # Unlike perfect conductor, we now only have finite $\sigma$ , the first thing to notice is that Internal Electric Field is no longer zero
As not all the Electrons can be pushed to the other side, this will cause $|\vec{E}{int}| < |\vec{E}{ext}|$, in order to measure the ability of this conductor blocking Electrons, we introduce Resistance
Resistance # The basic definition of Resistance is $R = \frac{V}{I}$, whereas
$V$: is the potential difference between two points, is the integral of two points $$ V = V_{P_+} - V_{P_-} = -\int_{P_-}^{P_+} \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l} $$
$I$: is the integral of current density across conductor cross area A $$ I = \iint_A \sigma\vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s} $$
Conductance # Conductance is just the reciprocal of Resistance
$$ G=\frac{1}{R}=\frac{I}{V} $$
Unit Conductance: Use Conductance to divided by length to get Unit Conductance $$ G’ = \frac{G}{l} = \frac{I}{V_{ab} \cdot l} $$
Joule’s Law # Joule’s Law indicate how Power dissipated in a conducting medium in the presence of an electrostatic field
$$ P = \iiint \sigma |\vec{E}|^2 dV $$
Behavior of Dielectrics # Inside Dielectrics, charges don’t move, but under the External Electric Field, it will cause a displacement, which is called Polarization
While there are two kinds of Molecules, Polar and Non-Polar ones, they also have different behavior under Electric Field
Polar Molecules # Non-Polar Molecules # When Non-Polar Molecule in under Electric Field, it will be extract into a Dipole
Notice that this $\vec P$ is parallel to the Electric Field $\vec E$ Polar Molecules # At the begining, there’s already a $\vec P$ in present, while after the effect of the Electric Field, there will be a Torque that spin the $\vec P$ to be parallel to the Electric Field
Dielectric Constant # Inside a conductor, the charges inside will be canceled out, where as the edges doesn’t, which forms the Bounded Charges $Q'$
This Bounded Charges can be further defined as Unit Bounded Charges $P$
Dielectric Breakdown # $$ \vec{P} = \varepsilon_0 \chi_e \vec{E} $$
Energy # When Electric Field is applying on a material, is the energy stored or lost?
Dissipation # For Conductors, under the collision of free electrons (that is the movement of them to form the current), this will transform electric potential into heat and deplete
$$ P = \iiint_V \sigma |E|^2 , dv $$
Thus the Electric Field will loss energy inside Conductor Storage # For Dielectrics, there’s no free electrons that the present of Electric Field only makes the molecules polarized, which after the disappear of Electric Field will retain balance
$$ W = \frac{1}{2} \iiint_V \vec{E} \cdot \vec{D} , dv $$
Thus energy will be stored inside Dielectrics ❗ Notice this is similar to the Hook’s Law
