We have already know how to use Fourier Series to analyze periodic signals by extract it into frequency domain
But what if the signal is aperiodic?
Then we should apply Fourier Transform instead
Fourier Transform # Derivation of the CT Fourier Transform # Suppose having a general CT Signal
Realize that a aperiodic signal is actually a periodic signal with infinite period
So we want to make some thing on the period part, steps we would like to do is
Window Signal to $[-T,T)$, then periodize it Compute CTFS of periodized signal Take the limit $T\rightarrow \infty$ ❗ So far the only “tool” we have is CTFS, so try to convert it into something we know
Windowing # Being with windowed one fragment
$$ x_{\text{fin}, T}(t) = x(t) \cdot [u(t + T) - u(t - T)] $$
Periodize # The repeat that fragment for infinite times
$$ x_{\text{per}, T}(t) = \sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty} x_{\text{fin}, T}(t - m(2T)) $$
CTFS # As the signal we have now is periodic, we can use CTFS now
Begin the CTFS with the Fundamental Frequency $\omega_0=2\pi/2T=\pi/T$
As always, the coefficient is
$$ \alpha_k = \frac{1}{2T} \int_{-T}^{T} x(t) e^{-jk\omega_0 t} dt $$
Now we would like to define a function $X_T$
$$ X_T(\mathbf{j}\omega) = \int_{-T}^{T} x(t)e^{-\mathbf{j}\omega t} \text{d}t $$
We notice that the CTFS coefficient is just sampling on this $X_T$ while divied by $2T$
$$ \alpha_k = \frac{1}{2T} X_T(jk\omega_0) $$
Now put this Coefficient back into the Fourier Series, which substitute $\frac{1}{2T} = \frac{\omega_0}{2\pi}$
$$ x_{\text{per}, T}(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} X_T(\mathbf{j}k\omega_0)e^{\mathbf{j}k\omega_0 t}\omega_0 $$
Notice this could be a Riemann Sum over the Frequency Domain
Here the Height is $X_T(\mathbf{j}k\omega)e^{\mathbf{j}k\omega t}$, while is in frequency domain
As all Riemann Sum can goes to Integral using limit, when $T\rightarrow \infty$, $\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T}\rightarrow 0$ this Riemann Sum then becomes to
$$ \lim_{T \to \infty} x_{\text{per}, T}(t) = x(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} X(\mathbf{j}\omega)e^{\mathbf{j}\omega t} \text{d}\omega $$
Recall the function $X_T$ has been defined as $X_T(\mathbf{j}\omega) = \int_{-T}^{T} x(t)e^{-\mathbf{j}\omega t} \text{d}t$, so as $T\rightarrow \infty$, this function then becomes
$$ X(j\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-j\omega t} dt $$
The CT Fourier Transform (CTFT) # The CTFT of a CT signal x it he complex-valued signal $X:\mathbb R\rightarrow\mathbb C$ defined pointwise by
$$ X(j\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)e^{-j\omega t} dt $$
Inverse CT Fourier Transform (Inverse CTFT) # The Inverse CTFT of a CT signal x it he complex-valued signal $X:\mathbb R\rightarrow\mathbb C$ defined pointwise by
$$ x(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} X(\mathbf{j}\omega)e^{\mathbf{j}\omega t} \text{d}\omega $$
CTFT Example # $$ x(t) = e^{-at}u(t), \quad a > 0 $$
As the result is a Complex Number, we want to analyze it using Magnitude and Phase $$ |X(j\omega)| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 + \omega^2}}, \quad \angle X(j\omega) = 0 - \tan^{-1}(\omega/a) = -\tan^{-1}(\omega/a) $$
Notice this general property that Amplitude is Even symmetry, whereas Phase is Odd Symmetry
CTFT Example: two-sided windowing signal # Consider the signal $x(t) = u(t + \frac{\tau}{2}) - u(t - \frac{\tau}{2})$, using CTFT we get
Signals of the form $\sin(x)/x$ is call the $sinc$ signal
CTFT Example: Shifted Impulse # Consider the delayed impulse $x(t)=\delta(t-\tau)$, its CTFT is
Having the amplitude of 1 and Phase of $-\omega\tau$
❗ If x is very concentrated in the time domain, the spectrum X will be very spread out the in frequency domain.
Inverse CTFT # Now having the Square Signal in Frequency Domain, we would like to do the inverse CTFT to find its signal in Time Domain
$$ \begin{aligned} X(\mathbf{j} \omega) &= u(\omega + \omega_{\text{b}}) - u(\omega - \omega_{\text{b}}) \ &= \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } -\omega_{\text{b}} \le \omega < \omega_{\text{b}} \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$
Partial Fraction Expansion # Sometimes Complex Rational Function need to be expand into those simple form, and this can be done by Partial Fraction
$$ X(\mathbf{j} \omega) = \frac{\mathbf{j} \omega}{(1 + \mathbf{j} \omega)(2 + \mathbf{j} \omega)} $$
Notice that if the nominator is greater than the denominator, than we should first subtract one the do the Partial Fraction on the rest
Existence of the CTFT for Finite Signals # Unfortunately, some CT signals do not have a spectrum, for example $x(t) = e^{at}u(t)$
$$ \begin{aligned} X(\mathbf{j} \omega) &= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{at} u(t) e^{-\mathbf{j} \omega t} ,\mathrm{d}t = \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{(a-\mathbf{j} \omega)t} ,\mathrm{d}t \ &= \left. \frac{1}{a - \mathbf{j} \omega} e^{(a-\mathbf{j} \omega)t} \right|_{0}^{\infty} = \infty \end{aligned} $$
Existence of the CTFT for finite action signal # If x has finite action, i.e., $x \in L1,$ then the CTFT $X(jω)$ is well-defined and satisfies $\lim_{\omega\rightarrow \pm \infty} |X(j\omega )|=0|$
This is a Sufficient but not Necessary condition
Existence of the CTFT for finite-energy signals # If $x$ has finite energy, i.e. $x \in L2$, then
X is well defined and has finite energy, $X \in L2,$ and The signal and its spectrum satisfy Parseval’s Relation $$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |x(t)|^2 dt = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} |X(j\omega)|^2 d\omega $$
A beautiful and surprising relationship between the energy of the signal and the energy of its spectrum
CTFT Example: The Complex Exponential # As both above are just sufficient condition, we will now analyse one does not have finite action nor finite energy, but is nonetheless CTFT-able
Consider the spectrum $X(j\omega)=2\pi\delta(\omega-\omega_0)$, we compute its CTFT to be
$$ x(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} 2\pi\delta(\omega-\omega_0)e^{j\omega t} d\omega=e^{j\omega_0t} $$
Thus those are a pair of CTFT
$$ x(t) = \underbrace{e^{\mathbf{j}\omega_0 t}}{\text{spread out in time}} \stackrel{\text{CTFT}}{\longleftrightarrow} X(\mathbf{j}\omega) = \underbrace{2\pi\delta(\omega - \omega_0)}{\text{concentrated in frequency}} $$
CTFT Example: A Periodic Signal # Let $x$ be a periodic CT signal with fundamental period $T_0$, and $\omega_0=2\pi/T_0$, we now represent x using the CTFS
$$ x(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} a_k e^{j k \omega_0 t} $$
Going term by term, the CTFT spectrum must be
$$ X(j\omega) = 2\pi \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} a_k \delta(\omega - k \omega_0) $$
Relationships between CTFT and CTFS # The CTFT and Signal Manipulations # Now we have calculated the spectrum X of some signal x, and we want to shift, scale or differential it
So we can use the properties of the CTFT to do shortcuts
Ex. # Since $x(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} X(j\omega)e^{j\omega t} d\omega$, thus $x(t-t_0)$ is
$$ x(t - t_0) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} X(j\omega)e^{j\omega (t - t_0)} d\omega= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left( X(j\omega) e^{-j\omega t_0} \right) e^{j\omega t} d\omega $$
CTFT Property: Magnitude and Phase # Here we mainly focus on Conjugation and Time-Scaling, that is
$x(t)^*. =X(-j\omega)^*$ $x(at)=\frac{1}{|a|} X(\mathbf{j}\omega/a)$ Now using the example of a song, we we play it backwards, that is $b(t) =s(-t)$
$$ B(\mathbf{j}\omega) = S(-\mathbf{j}\omega) = S(\mathbf{j}\omega)^* \implies |B(\mathbf{j}\omega)| = |S(\mathbf{j}\omega)| $$
This means that the Magnitude Spectrum of two song are same while the Phase, which indicate the time the frequency exist is unique
CTFT Example: Gaussian Distribution # For $\sigma >0$, consider the signal
$$ x(t) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}(t/\sigma)^2} $$
Knowing the fact that this Gaussian Distribution always have the area of 1
And this Function has the derivative of $\dot{x}(t) = x(t) \cdot \left( -\frac{t}{\sigma^2} \right) \implies \dot{x}(t) = -\frac{t}{\sigma^2}x(t)$
From the Table we can get two properties
$\dot{x}(t) \longleftrightarrow (j\omega)X(j\omega)$ $tx(t) \longleftrightarrow j\frac{d}{d\omega}X(j\omega)$ Then we can take CTFT on both side of Gaussian Distribution
$$ x(t) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-\frac{1}{2}(t/\sigma)^2} \stackrel{\text{CTFT}}{\longleftrightarrow} X(\mathbf{j}\omega) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\sigma\omega)^2} $$
Thus we can get
$$ X(j\omega) = e^{-\frac{1}{2}(\sigma\omega)^2} $$
So what this section is trying to say is that if Gaussian Distribution is thick in Time Domain, then it will be Wider in Frequency Domain
CTFT Properties: Conjugate Symmetry # If x is a real signal, meaning $x(t) ∈ R$ for all $t \in \mathbb R$, then the spectrum $X(jω)$ is conjugate symmetric, meaning $X(jω)∗ = X(−jω)$ for all $ω ∈ R$
Thus Magnitude is an Even Function, where Phase is an odd function
CTFT Properties: Multiplication # If we multiply two Signal $x(t)$ and $\hat x(t)$, then the new signal in time domain will then be
$$ y=x(t)\hat x(t) $$
Whereas its CTFT in Frequency domain will be
$$ Y(j\omega) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \tilde{X}(j\nu)X(j(\omega-\nu)) d\nu $$
Which is there Convolution divided by the $2\pi$
Example of Signal Multiplication: Amplitude Modulation # Having two signals, a Carrier $cos(\omega_ct)$ and a Baseband $x(t)$, their product in time domain is
$$ y(t) = \underbrace{\cos(\omega_c t)}{\text{“carrier”}} \cdot \underbrace{x(t)}{\text{“baseband”}} = \frac{1}{2} \left( e^{\mathbf{j}\omega_c t} + e^{-\mathbf{j}\omega_c t} \right) x(t) $$
Whereas the spectrum of cosine is $C(\mathbf{j}\omega) = 2\pi \frac{\delta(\omega - \omega_c) + \delta(\omega + \omega_c)}{2}$, thus the $Y(j\omega)$ is
$$ Y(\mathbf{j}\omega) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} C(\mathbf{j}\nu) X(\mathbf{j}(\omega - \nu)) \mathrm{d}\nu = \frac{1}{2} (X(\mathbf{j}(\omega - \omega_c) + X(\mathbf{j}(\omega + \omega_c)))) $$
In the figure above, $x(t)$ is the Baseband with the actual information we want to transfer, whereas the Modulated Signal is one with higher frequency but having the shape of $x(t)$
CTFT Properties: Convolution in time domain # Previously we mentioned the Multiplication in time domain is the Convolution in Frequency Domain
Now the Convolution in time domain just means the Multiplication in Frequency Domain
$$ Y(\mathbf{j}\omega) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \left[ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\tau) \tilde{x}(t - \tau) \mathrm{d}\tau \right] e^{-\mathbf{j}\omega t} \mathrm{d} t=X(\mathbf{j}\omega) \tilde{X}(\mathbf{j}\omega) $$
Discrete-Time Fourier Transform (DTFT) # Do the same thing as CTFT
First window the duration of $2N+1$ Periodize it Compute the DTFS Take the limit Then we can get DTFT as
$$ X(e^{j\omega}) = \sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty} x[n]e^{-j\omega n} $$
Also the Inverse DTFT is
$$ x[n] = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} X(e^{j\omega})e^{j\omega n} d\omega $$
Ex. # Ex. Right-sided decaying exponential # Periodic of DTFT Spectrum # Comparison of CTFT vs. DTFT # There is only one Fourier transform #

Electric Potential (Scalar) # The definition for Electric Potential is the work required to move a unit positive charge from A to B
$$ V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l} $$
Electric Potential by Point Charge # As Electric Potential is a work, we start with Work Done formula
$$ W = \int_{r_A}^{r_B} -q \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{l}=\int_{r_A}^{r_B}-qE(r)\hat rdr\hat r $$
Known that the Electric Field created by Point Charge is $\vec{E} = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2} \hat{r}$ $$ W = -\int_{r_A}^{r_B} \frac{qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2} dr=-\frac{qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0 }\int_{r_A}^{r_B} \frac{1}{r^2}dr= \frac{qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \left( \frac{1}{r_B} - \frac{1}{r_A} \right) $$
And the Potential Difference is the Work Done by Unit Charge, which is $$ V_{AB} = V_B - V_A = \frac{W}{q}=\frac{qQ}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \left( \frac{1}{r_B} - \frac{1}{r_A} \right)/q $$
Thus we can get the Potential Difference between two Point Charge is $$ V_B - V_A = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \left( \frac{1}{r_B} - \frac{1}{r_A} \right) $$
Absolute Electric Potential # Just like the GND in circuit, we always want to set up a reference point for Potential, that could be the point when $V_A =0$, which is $r_A\rightarrow \infty$
In such case, we will get the Potential Difference at a point as
$$ V(r) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} $$
Relation between Electric Field & the Electric Potential # Electric Field is a Vector Field, which is defined as the the opposite direction of gradient of Electric Potential Field
$$ \vec{E} = -\nabla V $$
So if we want to find the Electric Field of Point Charge what we should do is
Start with the Electric Potential of Point Charge $V(r) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r}$, then find its Gradient $$ \vec{E} = -\nabla \left( \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} \right)=-\frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\nabla \left( \frac{1}{r} \right) =-\frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \left( -\frac{1}{r^2} \hat{r} \right) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r^2} \hat{r} $$
❗ The property $\vec{E} = -\nabla V$ connects Electric Field and Electric Potential
Conservation Property of the Electrostatic Field # ❗ Voltage difference is the same regardless of the integration path
Equipotential Lines & Surfaces # Based on the property that
$$ V=\frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0r}\hat r $$
We know that as long as $r$ is the same, then $V$ remains constant, which is then a Equipotential Line & Surface Electric Potential of Different Model # Electric Potential of a Point Charge # Known from above that
$$ V(r) = \frac{Q}{4\pi\epsilon_0 r} $$
Electric Potential of Point Charges, is the Scalar Addition of Point Charges
$$ V(\vec{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{Q_i}{4\pi\epsilon_0 |\vec{r} - \vec{r}’_i|} $$
Electric Potential of an Electric Dipole # Notice there’s a Equation about $\nabla$ in Spherical Coordinate, which is
$$ \nabla f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial r} \hat{r} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} \hat{\theta} + \frac{1}{r \sin \theta} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \phi} \hat{\phi} $$
This Jacobian term will be mentioned again later Electric Potential of Continuous Charge Distributions # By using Integral, we can deal with more complicated Charge Distribution models
$$ V = \iiint \frac{\rho_v(\vec{r}’) , }{4\pi\epsilon_0 |\vec{r} - \vec{r}’|}dv' $$
$$ V = \iint \frac{\rho_s(\vec{r}’) , }{4\pi\epsilon_0 |\vec{r} - \vec{r}’|}ds' $$
$$ V = \int \frac{\rho_l(\vec{r}’) , }{4\pi\epsilon_0 |\vec{r} - \vec{r}’|}dl' $$
Electric Potential of a Conducting Shell (Surface) # The result can be verified by the Gauss’s Law that
Gradient Operator in Different Coordinate Systems # ❗ In Cylindrical or Spherical Coordinates, the Unit Vector’s Direction depends on the current position, which is not identical as Cartesian, the axis itself is changing. Under this case, we need to include extra term to fix this directional change, and that’s why there’s difference in Gradient (and other) Operator in different Coordinate Systems
Cartesian Coordinate # $$ \nabla f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \hat{x} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \hat{y} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \hat{z} $$
Cylindrical Coordinate # $$ \nabla f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial r} \hat{r} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \phi} \hat{\phi} + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} \hat{z} $$
Spherical Coordinate # $$ \nabla f = \frac{\partial f}{\partial r} \hat{r} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} \hat{\theta} + \frac{1}{r \sin \theta} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \phi} \hat{\phi} $$
Electrical Field # There’s several ways we define Electrical Field so far
1. Coulomb’s Law # Using the Charge Density Distribution $\rho_v$, while there’s no Symmetry for Gauss’s Law
$$ \vec{E} = \iiint \frac{\rho_v(\vec{r}’)(\vec{r} - \vec{r}’)}{4\pi\epsilon_0 |\vec{r} - \vec{r}’|^3} d v' $$
2. Gauss’s Law # When there’s a Symmetry, the Coulomb’s Law will be simplified into
$$ \oint_S \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s} = Q_{enc} $$
We first know the Charge Enclosed $Q_{enc}$ Then we find a Symmetry to simplify the integral $\oint_S \vec{D} \cdot d\vec{s}$ into $D_{\hat{u}} \cdot A_{Gauss}$ Then we can use $D = \frac{Q_{enc}}{A}$ to get the value of D, and Electric Field $\vec E$ 3. Gradient of Electric Potential # This method start with Electric Potential and find its Gradient to find the Vector Field $\vec E$
$$ \vec{E} = -\nabla V $$
Whereas the Electric Potential can be find by
$$ V = \iiint \frac{\rho_v(\vec{r}’) dv’}{4\pi\epsilon_0 |\vec{r} - \vec{r}’|} $$
4. Boundary Conditions # If we know the Boundary Conditions, then we can use the $\nabla^2 V$ to find V, then $\vec E$
Poisson’s & Laplace’s Equations # Starting from the Electrostatic Functions in Maxwell’s Equation
$$ \nabla \times \vec{E} = 0,\quad \nabla \cdot \vec{E} = \frac{\rho_v}{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r} $$
The first equations $\nabla \times \vec{E} = 0$ indicates that Electric Field is a Conversation (Irrational) Field, that its independent of the Path C, so that
$$ -\int _C\vec E\cdot \vec{dl}=\Delta V\Rightarrow \vec E= -\nabla V $$
Whereas for the second equation $\vec{E} = \frac{\rho_v}{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r}$, if we plug in $\vec E= -\nabla V$ , we get
$$ \nabla \cdot (-\nabla V) = \frac{\rho_v}{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r}\Rightarrow \nabla^2 V = -\frac{\rho_v}{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r} $$
Poisson’s Equation # $$ \nabla^2 V = -\frac{\rho_v}{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r} $$
Poisson’s Equations tells us that if there exist Free Charges $(\rho_v \neq 0)$, then the Rate of Change of Rate of Change of Electric Potential is depend on them
Laplace’s Equation # Whereas if there’s no Free Charges $(\rho_v=0)$, then Poisson’s Equation simplified into
$$ \nabla^2 V = 0 $$
Then the Electric Potential is then smooth over this region that the vacuum place’s Electric Potential Value equals to its Boundary’s average
Laplacian Operator in Different Coordinate Systems # Same as Gradient, Laplacian Operator has the same Jacobian terms
Cartesian # $$ \nabla^2 f = \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} $$
Cylindrical # $$ \nabla^2 f = \frac{1}{r} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \left( r \frac{\partial f}{\partial r} \right) + \frac{1}{r^2} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial \phi^2} + \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial z^2} $$
Spherical # $$ \nabla^2 f = \frac{1}{r^2} \frac{\partial}{\partial r} \left( r^2 \frac{\partial f}{\partial r} \right) + \frac{1}{r^2 \sin \theta} \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta} \left( \sin \theta \frac{\partial f}{\partial \theta} \right) + \frac{1}{r^2 \sin^2 \theta} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial \phi^2} $$

Linear circuit analysis techniques
Element, KCL, KVL, Nodal analysis # KCL # The algebraic sum of all currents entering and leaving a node is equal to zero
KVL # The algebraic sum of all voltages around any closed loop in a circuit is equal to zero
Super Node # When applying Nodal Analysis, if there’s a Voltage Source between two Nodes, then the current inside can’t be written, thus we need Super Node
We treat Two Nodes linked by Voltage Source as a Super Node Super Mesh # The same applies on Mesh Analysis, when having two Mesh sharing one Current Source, then a Super Mesh is needed
We discard the wire with the Current Source and treat the rest as one Mesh Superposition # The circuit we deal with are Linear, thus each Source can be analysis individually
Voltage Source: Short Circuit Current Source: Open Circuit Equivalent resistance # Any complicated circuit can be treated as one Resistance, and to find that Resistance, we have three methods
Inject Voltage Source # Discard the Source inside the circuit, i.e. short or open Apply a Voltage Source at AB Write out the current inside and thus find \(R=\frac vi\) Inject Current Source # The same with Above, but instead put a Current Source inside Direct Analysis # This Doesn’t work for circuit with Dependent Source Voltage division (for resistors connected in series) # $$ v_1 = \frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2} v,\quad v_2 = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} v
$$
Current division (for resistors connected in parallel) # $$ i_1 = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} i,\quad i_2 = \frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2} i $$
Thevenin/Norton equivalent circuit # The key concept of those two are, no matter how difficult the circuit is, when looking inside, it can always be simplified as a few elements
Thevenin # Thevenin simply the circuit into a Resistor and a Voltage Source, thus
$$ v=V_s+R_si $$
Norton # Norton simply the circuit into a Resistor Parallel a Current Source, thus
$$ i = \frac{v}{R_s} - i_s $$
Ex. Finding Equivalent Circuit # Maximum power transfer # As what’s being indicated in Thevenin, the whole circuit can be transfer into two elements
In such case, we would like to further investigate what should the Load Resistance \(R_L\) be to gain the maximum power from the circuit Knowing that \(i_L = \frac{V_s}{R_s + R_L}\), we can find the formula of Power is $$ P = R_L \cdot i_L^2 = R_L \left( \frac{V_s}{R_s + R_L} \right)^2 $$
This equation have the curve of Thus the Power gain its maximum when \(R_L=R_s\), thus $$ P_{max} = R_s \left( \frac{V_s}{2R_s} \right)^2 = \frac{V_s^2}{4R_s} $$
Circuit analysis with controlled source # Circuit with only dependent source # Those Circuit only have dependent sources, that they can be treated as a simple Resistor R, with no Voltage or Current Source inside
If we want to find the Value of the Resistor, we can A. Inject a Test Current \(i_{test}\)
B. Inject a Test Voltage \(v_{test}\)

Amplifier transfer characteristics # Differential Amplifier # Operational Amplifier # Operational Amplifier, has few main things to remember
Op Amp’s Properties # Virtual Short # The Open Loop Gain $A$, is a very Large Amplifier, that Ideally Infinite, this states that, based on the equation $V_{out}=A(V_p-V_n)$, the Positive and Negative Voltage has to be identical to make the output within the Operational Area
Thus Virtual Short States $$ V_{p}=V_{n} $$
Ideal Op Amp # An Ideal Op Amp have following assumptions
$$ R_{in}=\infty,\quad R_{out}=0,\quad A=\infty $$
Effects of finite open-loop Op Amp gain (A) # If an Op Amp is no longer Idea, then what will happened is that
Thus the Closed Loop Gain for Non-Ideal Op Amp is
$$ \frac{v_0}{v_s} = \frac{(R_1 + R_2) / R_2}{1 + \frac{(R_1 + R_2) / R_2}{A}} $$
Op amp analysis # Buffer # Buffer is the device to keep the Signal the same linking from two devices
The circuit above is a Voltage Divider with no Buffer, the Output Voltage is $$ V_o = \frac{R_L}{R_s + R_L} V_s $$
As we want to make $V_o=V_s$, the Value of two Resistors really matters in such case While if we put a Buffer in between, then $$ V_x = V_{\text{sig}} \cdot \frac{\infty}{R_{\text{sig}} + \infty} = V_{\text{sig}} $$
In such case, the input Signal remains the same While for the output part $$ V_{\text{out}} = V_o \cdot \frac{R_L}{R_{\text{out}} + R_L} \approx V_o $$
So that’s how A Buffer keeps the Voltage Inverting Amplifier # Inverting Amplifier has the Closed Loop Gain of
$$ \frac{v_o}{v_i} = -\frac{R_2}{R_1} $$
Inverting Amplifier in Cascade # If the input Voltage $v_i$ comes from another Circuit, the previous circuit’s Output Resistor and the Inverting Amplifier’s Resistor will form a Voltage Divider, having the effect
$$ V=\frac{R_1}{R_1+R_0} $$
To make the input Voltage V as same as possible, we then need to make $R_1$ as large as possible However, if we want to make an Amplifier, then the Closed Loop Gain is $R_2/R_1$, then $R_2$ has to be something even bigger, i.e. $100M\Omega$, this is kind of hard and will cause Distortion Thus it’s kind of hard for Inverting Amplifier to satisfied both at once Inverting summer # $$ v_o = -\left( \frac{R_F}{R_1}v_1 + \frac{R_F}{R_2}v_2 \right) $$
Non-Inverting Summer # $$ V_o = \frac{R_A + R_B}{R_A} \cdot \frac{V_1 + V_2}{2} $$
Differential amplifier or subtractor # $$ V_o = \left( \frac{1 + R_2/R_1}{1 + R_3/R_4} \right) \left( \frac{R_4}{R_3} \right) V_2 - \left( \frac{R_2}{R_1} \right) V_1 $$
To simplify into a subtractor, we will made $\frac{R_4}{R_3} = \frac{R_2}{R_1} = a$, thus $$ V_o = a(V_2 - V_1) $$
Capacitor # Parallel-Plate Capacitor is the most common seen model, its Capacitance is determine by
Capacitor have three important property in circuit
Open-Circuit Under DC Conditions Dynamic Effect Voltage Must be continuous over time Time Instant Capacitor Voltage vC(t) Resistor Voltage vR(t) Key Observation $0^-$ (Pre-switching) $0\text{V}$ $0\text{V}$ Initial relaxed state. $0^+$ (Post-switching) $0\text{V}$ $V_s$ Continuity: v_C cannot change instantaneously. $\infty$ (Steady State) $V_s$ $0$ Capacitor acts as an open circuit. Thus we can write it as a integral form
$$ v_C(t) = \frac{1}{C} \int_{-\infty}^{t} i(\tau) , d\tau = v_C(0) + \frac{1}{C} \int_{0}^{t} i(\tau) , d\tau $$
Power and Energy # $$ P_c(t) = v_c(t) \cdot i_c(t)= v_c(t) \cdot C \frac{dv_c(t)}{dt}= \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{1}{2} C v_c^2(t) \right) $$
This is the power of Capacitor
$$ u_c(t) = \frac{1}{2} C v_c^2(t) $$
Whereas the Energy it stores is the one inside derivative
This indicates that Power is the derivative of energy by time t ❗ Capacitors and inductors have kind of duality, i.e. Capacitor voltage $\iff$ Inductor current
Inductor # Inductor is actually a Solenoid with length L, the Inductance has been defined as
$$ L = \mu_0 n^2 \ell A $$
When the current go through the Solenoid, it will then creates a Magnetic Field that induct the EMF
$$ v_L(t) = L \frac{di_L(t)}{dt} $$
Property of Inductor # Is Short Circuit under DC Only have Voltage when Current is changing $i_L(t^-) = i_L(t^+)$ $$ i_L(t) = i_L(0) + \frac{1}{L} \int_{0}^{t} v_L(\tau) d\tau $$
Energy # $$ U_L(t) = \frac{1}{2} L i_L^2(t) $$
Series and Parallel Combinations # Dynamic Op Amp circuits # Using Capacitor and Inductor, we can create Op Amp with more operations
Inverting Integrator # To Find the Closed Gian, start with the KCL at the $V_-$ Node, with virtual short, that is
$$ i_c=-i_s $$
Also known from above that the current from a Capacitor is being defined as
$$ i_c=C \frac{dv_c(t)}{dt} $$
Combine the two equations to get that
$$ -i_s=C \frac{dv_c(t)}{dt}= -\frac{v_s}{R}\Rightarrow \frac{dv_c(t)}{dt} = -\frac{1}{RC} v_s $$
Integrate both side to get
$$ v_o(t) = -\frac{1}{RC} \int_{0}^{t} v_s(\tau) d\tau $$
Inverting Differentiator # Similarly, do the KCL at Node $V_-$
$$ C \frac{dv_s(t)}{dt} = -\frac{v_o}{R}\Rightarrow v_o(t) = -RC \frac{dv_s(t)}{dt} $$
Thus is a Differentiator

Recall Gauss’s Law in Integral Form: The Electric Flux pass through a surface only depends on the charges enclosed by this surface, in the form of

If there’s no Symmetry, then we have to use Coulomb’s Law which is the operator of Vector that is normally harder The commonly seen Symmetry Types are Spherical, Cylindrical, and Planar Electric Field of a Point Charge # So we can summarise the Electric Field created by a Point Charge as $$ \vec{D} = D_r \hat{r} = \frac{q}{4 \pi r^2} \hat{r},\quad \vec{E} = \frac{\vec{D}}{\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r} = \frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r} \frac{q}{r^2} \hat{r} $$
Electric Field of Infinite Long Charge Line # So the Electric Field created by Infinite Long Charge is $$ \vec{D}_\rho = \frac{\rho_l}{2 \pi \rho} \hat{\rho},\quad \vec{E} = \frac{\rho_l}{2 \pi \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \rho} \hat{\rho} $$
Electric Field of Infinite Uniform Surface # So the Electric Field for Infinite Uniform Surface is $$ \vec{D}_z = \frac{\rho_s}{2} \hat{z},\quad \vec{E} = \frac{\rho_s}{2 \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r} \hat{z} $$

$$ \begin{cases} \rho(r) = \rho_0 (r/R)^2 & \text{for } r \leq R \ \rho(r) = 0 & \text{for } r > R \end{cases} $$

Directives # Directives are not the code for CPU to run, instead, its a guidance for Assembler to order code
Directives start with an . Commonly seen Directive are .text , .data ,.align .text # Text Segment tells the Assembler that the following are runnable code that are read only
.data # Data Segment tells the Assembler that following code are data, like constant, and so on
.align # Alignment make sure the following code or data start with specific address, i.e. 4 or 8
Subroutines # Program Counter PC # Inside Processor, there’s a specific Register called PC, that is pointing to the next instruction’s address
Normally, PC increase by 4 each time, because the Processor we use is 32 bits Though we can manually change PC to address the instruction we want to call next, and that will be the case in Conditional Branch, or Subroutines Subroutines # Subroutines can also being interpreted by Functions, that can be reused for several times, consider this C program
int main(void){ int mysub(int p){ return(p+p); } int x,y; x = mysub(3); y = mysub(4); The above section indicated how PC works, while there’s a second Register tells the PC the original address to return to before calling the Subroutine (Function)
Now we can write the Assembly Code for the above C program
my_sub: add a0,a0,a0 ret li a0,3 call my-sub next: li a0,4 call my-sub done: j done Return Address # In Subroutines, they need to deal with he Return Address ra , that is the return address
The case is that, if A is calling B , then B return directly, everything is fine
But if A is calling B , and B is calling C , then the address of A will be overwrite
Stack - Data Structure # Thus we can use the Stack Data Structure to fix this problem
Having the property of $LIFO, Last In First Out$, Stack have two operations
Push: Put on top Pop: Remove from top Stack Pointer - Implementation of Stack # In NIOS V, A special Register x2 is designed as the top of a stack pointer
It is pointing to the address of the top word on the stack And we call it Stack Pointer or sp The Stack Pointer has the property of growing downwards (towards smaller addresses) in memory, so we init it in a higher memory address
In this course, we init sp at 0x20000 Notice that if sp is at 0x20000 , then it means the stack is empty Push in SP # Now let’s try to push a word 0x1234f678 into stack, that will be li t0, 0x1234f678
First we change the sp and allocate a memory for a word (4 Bytes) addi sp,sp,-4 Then we push the value into stack sw t0,(sp) Pop in SP # Now we are going to try to pop a word out, we basically do the reverse of push
First get the value of current sp lw t1,(sp) Then put sp back, notice that the value is not being deleted, but sp has been mov addi sp,sp,4 Code Example: Nested Subroutine Calls # # --- Initialization --- la sp, 0x20000 # Initialize stack pointer high in memory li a0, 1 # Load immediate value 1 into register a0 call sub_1 # Jump to sub_1; ra is set to 'done' address done: j done # Infinite loop once the program is finished # --- Subroutine 1 --- sub_1: addi sp, sp, -4 # Push ra onto stack: decrement stack pointer sw ra, (sp) # Save the return address (pointing to 'done') # ... logic for sub_1 ... call sub_2 # Call sub_2; ra is now overwritten with address in sub_1 # ... execution continues here after sub_2 returns ... lw ra, (sp) # Pop top of stack into ra just before returning addi sp, sp, 4 # Increment stack pointer to "remove" item ret # Return to the caller (PC <- ra) # --- Subroutine 2 --- sub_2: addi sp, sp, -4 # Push ra onto stack so we can call other subroutines sw ra, (sp) # Save ra (which currently points back to sub_1) # ... logic for sub_2 ... call sub_3 # Go off to sub_3, then come back # ... execution continues here after sub_3 returns ... lw ra, (sp) # Pop top of stack into ra addi sp, sp, 4 # Restore the stack pointer ret # Return to sub_1 (PC <- ra - the correct one!) # --- Subroutine 3 --- sub_3: # sub_3 would look similar if it called more functions # If it is a leaf function (calls no one), it may not need to save ra ret # Return to sub_2

Coulomb’s Law # Coulomb’s Law reveals the Force between two point Charges, it can be written in vector form
$$ \vec{F}{12} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r{12}^2} \frac{\vec{r}{12}}{|\vec{r}{12}|} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q_1 q_2}{|\vec{r}_{12}|^3} (\vec{r}_1 - \vec{r}_2) $$
Electric Field by Point Charge # Point Charges will creates Electric Field and that field have the Magnitude of Electric Force F
$$ \vec{E}q = \frac{\vec{F}{qq_t}}{q_t} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2} \hat{r} $$
And the result is given putting one Test Charge inside the Electric Field, and we can state that the Point Charge $q_t$ is in the presence of a Electric Field Superposition of Electric Fields # For several Electric Field, it follows the rule of Vector Addition
While each Charge’s effect on that reference point will be $$ \vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{q}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}’|^3} (\vec{r} - \vec{r}’) $$
By adding up those vectors, we can get he Total Electric Field $$ \vec{E}{total} = \vec{E}{q_1} + \vec{E}{q_2} + \dots + \vec{E}{q_n} $$
Ex. Superposition of Electric Fields # Electric Field due to Continuous Charge Densities # A Point Charge is being defined as a point with no volume and with charge $q$, its Electric Field is
$$ \vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \frac{q}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}’|^3} (\vec{r} - \vec{r}’) $$
When the Charges are no longer a point, but being described as Charge Density that evenly or unevenly distributed along a line, a surface or a volume, this Electric Field then need to be evaluate by the Integral, we get the Volume Charge Density’s Electric Field is $$ \vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \iiint \frac{\rho_v(\vec{r}’) (\vec{r} - \vec{r}’)}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}’|^3} dv' $$
They same apply on Surface and Line $$ \vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \iint \frac{\rho_s(\vec{r}’) (\vec{r} - \vec{r}’)}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}’|^3} ds’,\quad \vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \int \frac{\rho_l(\vec{r}’) (\vec{r} - \vec{r}’)}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}’|^3} dl' $$

Fourier Series # Now consider this case
we have being given an oscillation signal of an object after collision
This signal is kind of hard to be analysis, that it’s a Time Domain Signal with no features The way we do is try to build it based on Basis Signals and form a Weighted Sum $$ \hat{x} = \alpha_0\phi_0 + \alpha_1\phi_1 + \alpha_2\phi_2 + \dots = \sum_{k} \alpha_k\phi_k $$
And that is just the Principle of Fourier Analysis: The Transform between Time Domain and Frequency Domain Introductory example: An Even Periodic Signal # This is an Even Signal, thus we can choose $\cos$ as the Fundamental Component Thus we have $\phi_0(t) = \frac{1}{2}$ as DC Component, $\phi_1(t) = \cos(\omega_0 t)$ as Fundamental Component, and $\phi_2(t) = \cos(2\omega_0 t), \phi_3(t) = \cos(3\omega_0 t), \dots$ as Harmonic Components So the whole set to build up this Periodic Signal will then be $$ \left{ \frac{1}{2}, \cos(\omega_0 t), \cos(2\omega_0 t), \cos(3\omega_0 t), \dots \right} $$
Now we need to find a way to solve for the coefficient for the Linear Combination which is
$$ x(t) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{\ell=1}^{\infty} a_\ell \cos(\ell \omega_0 t) $$
Thus find those $a_0,a_1,a_2\dots$
The Final Result we achieved is that
$$ \frac{2}{T_0} \int_{-T_0/2}^{T_0/2} \cos(k\omega_0 t) \cos(\ell\omega_0 t) , dt = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } k = \ell \ 0 & \text{if } k \neq \ell \end{cases} $$
❗ This means that except the signal $\cos(k\omega_0t)$, every other signals will become zero after timing the $\cos(k\omega_0t)$ and take Integral
So now, for any Even Signal $x(t)$, we can apply the same method to extract cos signal at different frequency one by one
Ex. A Square Wave # Having the Signal $x_{fin}(t)$, we wish to approach this signal by Fourier Series
$$ x_{\text{fin}}(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } -\frac{\tau}{2} \le t \le \frac{\tau}{2} \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$
Notice that this Signal have Duty Cycle less than 1 (Time when signal is 1 is shorter)
First we want to calculate $a_0$, that is
$$ a_0 = \frac{2}{T_0} \int_{-\frac{T_0}{2}}^{\frac{T_0}{2}} x(t) , \text{d}t = \frac{2}{T_0} \int_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2} (1) , \text{d}t = \frac{2\tau}{T_0} $$
Secondly, find the general solution for $a_k$
$$ a_k = \frac{2}{T_0} \int_{-\frac{T_0}{2}}^{\frac{T_0}{2}} x(t) \cos(k\omega_0 t) dt = \frac{2}{T_0} \int_{-\tau/2}^{\tau/2} \cos(k\omega_0 t) dt $$
The bond for integral is $-\tau/2$ to $\tau/2$ because the function $x(t)$ is 1 during this fragment, and other are just zero that doesn’t change the value of the Integral, While the value of function is simply 1, so it can be simplify to RHS $$ = \frac{2}{T_0 k\omega_0} [\sin(k\omega_0 \tau/2) - \sin(-k\omega_0 \tau/2)] = \frac{2}{\pi k} \sin(k\omega_0 \tau/2) $$
Thus eventually we can get the Fourier Series for this signal to be $$ x(t) = \frac{\tau}{T_0} + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{2 \sin(k\omega_0 \tau/2)}{\pi k} \cos(k\omega_0 t) $$
And if we are doing an Approximation, that is only k terms of the Series, that will be $$ \hat{x}K(t) = \frac{\tau}{T_0} + \sum{k=1}^{K} \frac{2 \sin(k\omega_0 \tau/2)}{\pi k} \cos(k\omega_0 t) $$
Frequency Domain # After we extract the Square Wave from the Fourier Series, we can get its distribution over the frequency domain
On the right side, it indicate the coefficient of Harmonic Signal along k Thus we can use ${a_k}_{k=0}^\infty$ as the equivalenty representing of $x(t)$ in the Frequency Domain While ${a_k}_{k=0}^\infty$ is being called the Spectrum of x Fourier Series for odd Periodic Signals # For odd signals, the Series can be represent by similar method, but just that we change sin to cos
$$ x(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k \sin(k\omega_0 t),\quad b_k = \frac{2}{T_0} \int_{-T_0/2}^{T_0/2} x(t) \sin(k\omega_0 t) , dt $$
Fourier Series for Periodic Signals # For Signals that are neither even or odd, but periodic we can use the combination of even and odd, that is
$$ x(t) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k \cos(k\omega_0 t) + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k \sin(k\omega_0 t) $$
However, solving those two integrals turns out to be hard, so we introduce the concept of Complex Exponential Signals The Complex Exponential Fourier Series # When dealing with Real Fourier Series, we normally need to solve several equations to get the Series, while in Complex Exponential, instead, we can use Euler’s Formula
$$ e^{jk\omega_0 t} = \cos(k\omega_0 t) + j\sin(k\omega_0 t) $$
This formula change the problem from two Separate signal into one Complex Number on the Unit Circle in Complex Plane $$ \hat{x}(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \alpha_k e^{\mathbf{j}k\omega_0 t}, \quad \alpha_k \in \mathbb{C} $$
What this Formula States instead of $x(t) = \frac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k \cos(k\omega_0 t) + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k \sin(k\omega_0 t)$, is that we no longer use sin and cos as block to build the Signal, instead, we use $\phi_k(t) = e^{jk\omega_0t}$ However, changing into this more easier way, there are two challenges we need to face The fact that $e^{jk\omega_0 t} = \cos(k\omega_0 t) + j\sin(k\omega_0 t)$ has Imaginary Part, while in real life signal, we doesn’t have “Complex” Signal, thus we need to get rid of the Imaginary Part We need to produce both cos and sin, cause as indicated, a Periodic Signal need to be “building” on both cos and sin To get rid of the Imaginary Part, notice the fact that we are using the range of $\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}$ to form the series, this means that for each $k> 0$, there will be one $k<0$ to pair with it Based on Euler’s Formula, the Positive k will produce $$ (A+jB)(\cos \omega_0 t + j \sin \omega_0 t) = (A\cos - B\sin) + j(A\sin + B\cos) $$
While the Negative k will produce $$ (A-jB)(\cos \omega_0 t - j \sin \omega_0 t) = (A\cos - B\sin) - j(A\sin + B\cos) $$
By adding those up, we will get $$ 2(A\cos \omega_0 t - B\sin \omega_0 t) $$
Notice how this range $\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}$ both get rid of Imaginary part and produce both cos and sin
Continuous-Time Fourier Series (CTFS) # Let x be a periodic CT signal with fundamental period $T_0$ and angular frequency $\omega0 = 2π/T_0$, the complex numbers
$$ \alpha_k = \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{0}^{T_0} x(t)e^{-jk\omega_0t} dt $$
are called the Fourier Coefficients of x, and
$$ \hat{x}(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \alpha_k e^{jk\omega_0t} $$
is called the Continuous-Time Fourier Series (CTFS) of x
The integral can be taken in any interval of length $T_0$
Derivation of the coefficients via Approximation # Assume we don’t know the formula of $\alpha_k = \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{0}^{T_0} x(t)e^{-jk\omega_0t} dt$ so far, we are trying to use approximation to prove that the above formula is the best approximation coefficient
Consider a Finite number of terms of Fourier Series Expansion that $$ \hat{x}K(t) = \sum{k=-K}^{K} \alpha_k e^{\mathbf{j}k\omega_0 t} $$
We use MSE, Mean Square Error to evaluate the error which is $$ J(\alpha_{-K}, \dots, \alpha_K) = \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{0}^{T_0} |x(t) - \sum \alpha_k e^{jk\omega_0t}|^2 dt $$
By some derivation, we will found that $$ \alpha_k = \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{0}^{T_0} x(t)e^{-jk\omega_0t} dt $$
is exactly the CTFS coefficients we want for best possible approximation See Appendix A for Derivation
Example: sum of harmonic signals # Use CTFS to approximate signal
$$ x(t) = \cos(4\pi t) + 2 \sin(6\pi t) $$
Example: Square Wave # Notice that it takes high frequencies to make sharp corners
The CTFS and Signal Manipulations # Suppose having some CTFS Coefficients ${\alpha_k}_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}$, we can find the CTFS coefficients of simple manipulations, e.g. $3x(t) + 2$, $x(t - 5)$, $\text{Re}{x}$, $\frac{dx}{dt}(t)$ by properties of the CTFS
For example, $x(t) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \alpha_k e^{j k \omega_0 t}$, then $$ x(t - t_0) = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} \alpha_k e^{j k \omega_0 (t - t_0)}= \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} (\alpha_k e^{-j k \omega_0 t_0}) e^{j k \omega_0 t} $$
Which in result is just a mutiplication $\beta_k = \alpha_k e^{-j k \omega_0 t_0}$ All Manipulations can be conclude in this table Conjugate-Symmetry for real signals # Known that all signals in real life are Real-Valued, that means
$$ x(t)=x(t)^* $$
Known this property, we can then conclude the Symmetry of Real-Valued Signal in Frequency Domain, recall the CTFS coefficients
$$ a_k = \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{0}^{T_0} x(t)e^{-\mathbf{j}k\omega_0 t} , dt $$
It has the conjugate of $$ a_k^* = \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{0}^{T_0} x(t)^* (e^{-\mathbf{j}k\omega_0 t})^* , dt= \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{0}^{T_0} x(t) e^{\mathbf{j}k\omega_0 t} , dt
= a_{-k} $$
Known that $a_k^* = a_{-k}$, then we know that $|a_{-k}| = |a_k|$, and $\angle a_{-k} = -\angle a_k$ Existence of CTFS # Consider this function
$$ x_{\text{fin}}(t) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{t}, & \text{if } 0 < t \leq 1 \ 0, & \text{else} \end{cases} $$
Notice that when finding the 0th Fourier coefficient, it is $$ \alpha_0 = \frac{1}{1} \int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{t} , dt = \ln(1) - \ln(0) = +\infty $$
Existence of the CTFS # If $x$ has finite action, i.e. $x\in L_1^{per}$, then the Fourier coefficients $a_k = \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{0}^{T_0} x(t)e^{-\mathbf{j}k\omega_0 t} , dt$ are well defined and satisfy
$$ \lim_{k \to \pm\infty} |\alpha_k| = 0 $$
This is basically saying signal can’t be Infinite Large in Finite Time, Signal satisfied those conditions’s coefficient will have the following property
Well-Defined: Every $\alpha_k$ will be a finite value Decay: $\lim_{k \to \pm\infty} |\alpha_k| = 0$, that means the higer frequency term’s magnitude will become smaller Convergence of the CTFS # Knowing the Existence of CTFS, it means we can write out the coefficient
$$ a_k = \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{0}^{T_0} x(t)e^{-\mathbf{j}k\omega_0 t} , dt $$
However, it doesn’t means that this is guarantee to be converge to the original signal, thus need the further property of the Convergence of the CTFS
Let $e_K = \hat{x}_K - x$ denote the error between approximation and original signal, there are three kinds of convergence
Pointwise at time $t_0$ if $\lim_{k\rightarrow \infty}e_K(t_0)=0$ Uniformly if $\lim_{K\to\infty} |e_K|_\infty = 0$ In Energy if $\lim_{K\to\infty} |e_K|_2 = 0$ uniformly = amplitude of error goes to zero in energy = energy of error goes to zero ALL THOSE Convergence is under the assumption that $x \in L_1^{\text{per}}$
Pointwise Convergence of the CTFS # (i) If $x$ has a Continuous Derivative at time $t_0\in\mathbb R$, then $\hat x_K$ converges to x pointwise at $t_0$
(ii) Or if the left-side limits and right-side limits all exist at time $t_0 \in \mathbb R$, then
$$ \lim_{K\to\infty} \hat{x}_K(t_0) = \frac{1}{2}(x(t_0^-) + x(t_0^+)) $$
(i): Over interval where signal is smooth, then approximation converges pointwise
(ii): At jump discont. approximation converges to mid-point of discont.
Ex. A Square Wave # Approximation converges pointwise at all $t\neq\pm0.5$ Approximation converges to discontinuity midpoint at $t = \pm0.5$, which is 0.5 At $t=\pm 0.5$, the Ripple is called Gibb’s Phenomenon, it will never goes away Uniform Convergence of the CTFS # Uniform convergence requires stronger assumptions, an easy assumption is that the signal has a continuous derivative everywhere
If $x$ has a derivative which is continuous everywhere, then $\hat x_K$ converges to $x$ uniformly.
Ex. Signals for Uniform Convergence # This is signal $x(t) = t^3 - 3\pi t^2 + 2\pi^2 t$ that satisfies the assumption
However, in this this case , triangle wave doesn’t satisfies the condition, but on its frequency domain, it actually decay nicely as k increases
This means that there are weaker conditions for uniform convergence Weaker Condition for uniform Convergence
If x is continuous, and it its derivative is piecewise continuous and has only finitely many jumps of finite size over a period, then $\hat x_K$ converges to $x$ uniformly.
Convergence in Energy of the CTFS # If $x$ has finite energy, i.e. $x \in L_2^{\text{per}}$, then
(i) $\hat x_K$ converges to $x$ in energy
(ii) CTFS Coefficients have finite energy, i.e. $\alpha \in l_2$
(iii) The Signal and Coefficients satisfy Parseval’s Relation
$$ \frac{1}{T_0} \int_{0}^{T_0} |x(t)|^2 , dt = \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} |\alpha_k|^2\quad or \quad \frac{1}{T_0} |x|_2^2 = |\alpha|_2^2 $$
The discrete-time Fourier series (DTFS) # Any Periodical DT Signal can be express in a series containing the Complex Exponential Signal, that is we can express $x$ as
$$ x[n] = \sum_{k} a_k \phi_k[n] $$
Where as $\phi_k[n] = e^{j k \omega_0 n}$, $\omega_0 = 2\pi / N_0$ Thus the full DTFS can be written as $$ x[n] = \sum_{k=0}^{N_0-1} a_k e^{j k \omega_0 n} $$
Notice the range of k is from $0$ to $N_0-1$ Periodicity of DTFS # The reason why we only need $N_0-1$ numbers of k is because
$$ e^{j(N_0 \omega_0) n} = e^{j(2\pi)n} = e^{j(0)n} $$
$\omega_0 = 2\pi / N_0$
This is saying, when finding the $N_0$ harmonic frequency, its looks exactly the same as the $0$ one on discrete sampling point This can be proof by $$ \begin{aligned}\alpha_{k+N_0} &= \frac{1}{N_0} \sum_{n=0}^{N_0-1} x[n]e^{-\mathbf{j}(k+N_0)\omega_0 n} \&= \frac{1}{N_0} \sum_{n=0}^{N_0-1} x[n]e^{-\mathbf{j}k\omega_0 n} e^{-\mathbf{j}N_0\omega_0 n} \&= \frac{1}{N_0} \sum_{n=0}^{N_0-1} x[n]e^{-\mathbf{j}k\omega_0 n} e^{-\mathbf{j}N_0 \frac{2\pi}{N_0} n} \&= \frac{1}{N_0} \sum_{n=0}^{N_0-1} x[n]e^{-\mathbf{j}k\omega_0 n} \&= \alpha_k\end{aligned} $$
Orthogonality of complex exponentials # $$ \frac{1}{N_0} \sum_{n=0}^{N_0-1} e^{jm\omega_0n} e^{-jl\omega_0n} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } m = l + kN_0,k\in\mathbb Z \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} $$
DTFS Coefficient # $$ a_k = \frac{1}{N_0} \sum_{n=0}^{N_0-1} x[n] e^{-j k \omega_0 n},\quad k\in \mathbb Z $$
Ex. The Repeated Unit Impulse # The DTFS Coefficients are
$$ a_k = \frac{1}{N_0} \sum_{n=0}^{N_0-1} \delta[n] e^{-j k \omega_0 n} = \frac{1}{N_0} (1 \cdot e^{0} + 0 + \dots) = \frac{1}{N_0} $$
Notice by Orthogonality of Complex Exponentials, this extracts the value when $n=0$, thus $$ x[n] = \frac{1}{N_0} \sum_{k=0}^{N_0-1} e^{\mathbf{j} k \omega_0 n} $$
Ex 1. A growing Signal # Ex 2. The windowing Signal # Application: analysis of a real signal # This is a Signal sample at $f_s =48000~samples\cdot sec^{-1}$, where as the time interval is 2 seconds
If we Compute the DTFS coefficients and plot them, this is the chart
The first thing we notice is that the plot is symmetric about the midpoint
This is because the original signal $x(t)$ is a Real Signal, thus $|\alpha_k| = |\alpha_{N_0-k}|$

The Processor we are working with is called Nios V Processor
Nios V Processor # This is a processor from Intel with RISC-V Architecture
This is a 32 bit processor, that’s because it’s 32 bits wide Thus the address sent to memory is also 32 bits, this means that there are $2^{32}$ address locations We said that the word size of processor is 32 bits
In this case, the most information can be accessed is 32 bits, but we can access 16 bits (Halfword), or 8 bits Byte Addressable # In modern Computer, we give one Byte one Address
Image Memory as a lot of boxes, each box’s size is 8 bits, 1 Byte, in this case, each box will be given one unique Index (Address) As mentioned, the processor we are using are 32 bits wide, that means each time it’s going to get 4 bytes, that is $4\times 8 =32$
So each time we access memory, we will get this 32 bits (4 Bytes) Bar, Ex. A program that add three numbers from Memory # Now we have three numbers on Memory, that are 10,20,30 on (0x2C),(0x30),(0x34)
.data list: .word 10, 20, 30 # Define an array of 3 words (4 bytes each) answer: .word 0 # Reserve space for the final result .text .globl _start _start: # --- PHASE 1: LOAD DATA FROM MEMORY --- la t0, list # Load base address of 'list' into t0 lw t1, 0(t0) # Load 1st element (10) into t1 lw t2, 4(t0) # Load 2nd element (20) into t2 via offset 4 lw t3, 8(t0) # Load 3rd element (30) into t3 via offset 8 # --- PHASE 2: PERFORM CALCULATIONS --- add t2, t2, t1 # t2 = t2 + t1 (20 + 10 = 30) add t2, t2, t3 # t2 = t2 + t3 (30 + 30 = 60) # --- PHASE 3: STORE RESULT BACK TO MEMORY --- la t0, answer # Load address of 'answer' into t0 sw t2, 0(t0) # Store the final sum (60) into memory at 'answer' done: j done # Infinite loop to terminate execution flow The la and lw Instructions are called Executable Statements The .word 10 , is Assembler Directive Executable Statements # Those are the instructions CPU will do when the program is running
Assembler Directive # Assembler Directive are the things to show to Assembler, it means to Put Constant into memory into 32 bits at the next available location
In this case, we have
0x2C list = .word 10 0x30 .word 20 0x34 .word 30 0x38 answer: .word 0 la t0,list : Load Address (t0 <- list = 0x2c ) The la instruction actually include two encoded instructions, that is because both the instruction and the address are 32 bits, that makes we can’t give the 32 bits address and instruction at once, so we need two encoded instead Imagine this scenario, you ask a guy to take you to an address with 32 bits, however you only got 32 bits length of word to tell him, in this case you can’t give the Instruction of “Take me there” + “Address” at once
lw t1,(t0): Load the word from memory beginning at address given by t0 So t1 <- (t0) = (0x2c) = 10 () is just like Dereferencing a Pointer
lw t2,4(t0) : When we use 4(t0) , this is like a Index Offset, similar to the concept of array in C, t0 stores an address, and 4(t0) is then just referencing the word in 0x2c + 4 So t2 <- (0x30) = 20 lw t2,8(t0) : The same t3 <- (0x34) = 30 Now we are going to add those
add t2, t1, t2 # t2 = 10 + 20 = 30 add t2, t2, t3 # t2 = 30 + 30 = 60 la t0,answer sw t2,(t0) la t0,answer : load the Address of answer in Memory to Register t0 in Processor Then Store Word in t2 to the “Dereferenced Pointer” (t0) The reason why we can’t use sw t2,(answer) is because RISC-V only allows Register in brackets
Accessing Half Words & Bytes # As NIOS-V are byte accessible processor, that means we need to at least get one byte once
However, the fact that processors are all 4 bytes (32 bits) makes it hard to store more than one Half Word (2 Bytes) or Byte (1 Byte) into a Register So that means no matter the length of data we are choosing, i.e. Full Word, Half Word, or Byte, it’s gonna take the whole Register Recall that we Load Word using lw t2,(t3) , that is load the word t3 register is pointing to in the memory to register t2
We can do the same with Half Word using lh t2,(t3) Though as indicated, a Register is 32 bits, with only 16 bits stored, that makes the rest 16 bits left empty, so that we need to use Sign Extension to deal with the rest Sign Extension # When we want to increase the digit of a Binary Number without changing its value and Sign
Looked at the old Binary’s highest digit (Sign Digit) Change all before to the same value For example having 0000 0101 , that’s +5, if we want to extent it to 16 bits, it should be 0000 0000 0000 0101
So that’s what we do when storing Half Word into a Register
Though there are also method to leave the rest of Register unsigned, using lhu A,(B) Store Data from Register to Memory # The way storing Word, Half Word, and Byte into memory is kind of the same, which is using sw , sh ,and sb
Address for Data in Memory # If needed to store a word in memory, then its address need to be divisible by 4
Assume having a Memory with Address 0,1,2,3 If we want to store a word, then it’s address has to start on 0, 4, 8, 12, and can’t start with 1,2,3 The same apply for Half Word and Byte, Half Word has to start on 0,2,4,6, but Byte can be on any Move Instruction # Move Instruction # mv t3,t2 allows us to move the data in one Register t2 to t3
Having the General Form of mv rd,rs #rd <- rs Store Constant # If we want to store a constant for example 44 into Register, the we should use command li s3,44 #s3 <- 44
This constant 44 will be Encoded by assembler into 32 bit number and store into Register While this 44 is called Immediate Constant Immediate Constant # When dealing with constants, the command usually ends with a i
For example addi rd,rs,const #td <- ts + const Load Instruction # lw rd,D(rs1) #rd <- (rs1+D)
This load a 32 bit number into rd from memory address @ rs1+D D is also a 12 bit signed Immediate Constant encoded & Sign Extension Storing a Register # sw rs2,D(rs1)
Copy rs2 into Memory at address D+rs1 Logic Instruction # Logic & Shift Instruction are bitwise, they compare each bit one by one for the result
xxx rd,rs1,rs2 , xxxi rd,rs,Immed
xxx : one of AND, OR, XOR Ex. Logic AND Instruction # $$ \begin{aligned} &\text{and} \quad t_3, t_1, t_2 \ \ &001 \quad 011 \quad (t_1) \ \text{AND} \quad &001 \quad 101 \quad (t_2) \ \hline &001 \quad 001 \quad (t_3) \end{aligned} $$
Ex 2. Logic OR Instruction # $$ \begin{aligned} &\text{ori} \quad t_2, t_1, 0x7 \ \ &010 \quad 101 \quad (t_1) \ \text{OR} \quad &000 \quad 111 \quad (0x7) \ \hline &010 \quad 111 \quad (t_2) \end{aligned} $$
Shift Instruction # Shift Instruction are just like the >> in c++
srli t2,t1,3
Shift right t1 by Immediate Constant of digits i.e. if t1 is 110...110 , then it becomes 000110... , which means that the last three bits has been discarded after sll rd,rs1,rs2
There’s also a Shift Left Command sra rd,rs1,rs2
Keep the highest digit when shifting right

Scalar Field # $$ f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} $$
Scalar Field is used to describe the distribution of Scalar in space $\mathbb R^n$ Gradient of Scalar Field # $$ \nabla f(p) = \frac{\partial f(x, y, z)}{\partial x} \hat{x} + \frac{\partial f(x, y, z)}{\partial y} \hat{y} + \frac{\partial f(x, y, z)}{\partial z} \hat{z} $$
Taking the Gradient turns the Scalar Field into a Vector Field $\nabla f: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ Then the vector is pointing to the direction Having the largest rate of change Ex. Finding the Gradient of a Scalar Field # Electric Field & Electric Potential # $$ \vec{E} = -\nabla V $$
$V$ (Electric Potential): Scalar Field $\vec E$ (Electric Field): Vector Field Divergency of a Vector Field # Divergency is a scalar representing the strength of Divergency or Convergency at a given point
$$ \text{div } \vec{F} = \nabla \cdot \vec{F} = \frac{\partial F_x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial F_y}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial F_z}{\partial z} $$
$\nabla \cdot \vec{F}: \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$: Process of finding Divergency is finding a Scalar Field $\nabla \cdot \vec{F} > 0$: Source are going out at this point $\nabla \cdot \vec{F}< 0$: Sources are coming in at this point Gauss’ Divergence Theorem # $$ \iiint_V \text{div } \vec{F} , dv = \oiint_S \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{S} $$
❗ Divergence Theorem connect the Source inside the volume & Flux passing through the surface
Divergency Theorem Example # Evaluate $\iint \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{S}$ where $\vec{F} = xy\hat{x} - \frac{1}{2}y^2\hat{y} + z\hat{z}$ and the surface consists of the three surfaces of cylinder defined by $0 \le \rho \le 1, 0 \le \phi \le 2\pi, 0 \le z \le 1$
Curl of a Vector Field # $$ \nabla \times \vec{B} = \left( \frac{\partial B_z}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial B_y}{\partial z} \right) \hat{x} + \left( \frac{\partial B_x}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial B_z}{\partial x} \right) \hat{y} + \left( \frac{\partial B_y}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial B_x}{\partial y} \right) \hat{z} $$
❗ Curl is a Vector, it represent the Strength and the Direction of Circulation at a point
Curl of a Electric Field # $$ \nabla \times \vec{E} = 0 $$

Maxwell’s Equations described how Charge and Current form Electric and Magnetic Field, while indicate how Electric and Magnetic Field transfer into each other and how they propagate
Maxwell’s Equations # Maxwell’s Equations are actually the combination of four equations, each have their own name
1st: Gauss’s Law # ❗ Gauss’s Law: Charge forms Electric Field
$$ \nabla \cdot \vec{D} = \rho_v, \quad \nabla \cdot E = \frac{\rho_{v}}{\varepsilon_0} $$
$D$: Electric Flux Density $(c\cdot m^{-2})$ $\rho_v$: Volumetric Charge Density ($c\cdot m^{-3}$) Important Concept: $\vec D$ is the Electric Flux Density, it’s the real Field created, whereas $\vec E$ is the actual forced applied, they have the relationship of
$$ D = \varepsilon_0 E + P $$
In this formula, we treat the Displacement as the addition of two terms $$ \vec D = \varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_r \vec{E} $$
$\varepsilon_0$ : Free space Permittivity, a constant $\varepsilon_r$: Relative Permittivity, varies in different materials In this formula, we treat Displacement as the scaling of E after entering a material 2nd: Gauss’s Law for Magnetism # ❗ Gauss’s Law for Magnetism: There’s no signal Magnetic Pole
$$ \nabla \cdot \vec{B} = 0 $$
This law states that Magnetic Field Line is always a closed contour Important Concept: $\vec H$ is the Magnetic Field Strength, and $\vec B$ is the Magnetic Flux Density they are just same with the $\vec D$ and $\vec E$, having the relationship of
$$ \vec{B} = \mu_0 (\vec{H} + \vec{M}) $$
Treat $\vec B$ (Total Magnetic Field) = $\mu_0\vec H$ (Magnetic Field in vacuum) + $\mu_0\vec M$ (The contribution of material after being magnitized) $$ \vec B = \mu_0 \mu_r \vec H $$
$\mu_r$: Relative Permeability Or the Scaling of Magnetic Field after entering the material 3rd: Faraday’s Law of Induction # ❗ Faraday’s Law of Induction: Changing Magnetic Field will create Electric Field
$$ \nabla \times \vec{E} = -\frac{\partial \vec{B}}{\partial t} $$
$\vec B$: Magnetic Flux Density ($T$) 4th: Ampere-Maxwell Law # ❗ Ampere-Maxwell Law: Changing Electric Field will create Magnetic Field
$$ \nabla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J_f} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t} $$
$\vec J_F$: Free Current $\frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t}$: Displacement Current Important Concept: Here there’s two kind of current, knowing their difference is crucial for understanding this law
Starting with $\vec J_F$: this is formed by the free charges flowing inside wires, this will obviously creates a Magnetic Field around it Secondly, the $\frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t}$, this is the Electric Field Changed due to time, as this will also creates a Magnetic Field, we manually define this as the Displacement Current, where it’s actually a changed of the Electric Field Maxwell Equation under Static Case # This static means all terms with $\frac{\partial}{\partial t} = 0$ is now zero, and the Equations will be simplified into two separate fields: Electrostatic and Magnetrostatic
Electrostatic # $$ \nabla \cdot \mathbf{D} = \rho_v $$
The same $$ \nabla \times \mathbf{E} = 0 $$
❗ Static Electric Field is Irrational Field
Magnetostatic # $$ \nabla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0 $$
The same $$ \nabla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J_F} $$
As there’s no Electric Field change anymore, only current creating Magnetic Field is then the Free Current So under the assumption of Static, we can start with Electrostatic and Magnetostatic
Electrostatics # Now recall the 1st: Gauss’s Law: $\nabla \cdot \mathbf{D} = \rho_v$, this is the Differential Form of Gauss’s Law
Integral Form # Starting from the formula $\nabla \cdot \vec{D} = \rho_v$, take integral on both side to get
$$ \iiint_V (\nabla \cdot \vec{D}) dV = \iiint_V \rho_v dV $$
We known that the Divergence Theorem states that $\iiint_V (\nabla \cdot \vec{D}) dV = \iint_S \vec{D} \cdot d\mathbf{s}$, thus $$ \iint_S \vec{D} \cdot d\mathbf{s}=Q_{enclosed}\Rightarrow \iint \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{s} = \frac{Q_{enclosed}}{\varepsilon_r \varepsilon_0} $$
That is just the Most Common form of Gauss’s Law ❗ Gauss’ s Law (Integral Form): The Electric Flux pass through a surface only depends on the charges enclosed by this surface
Before applying this Integral Form of Gauss’s Law, we first need to figure out the Charge Distribution problem on the RHS, that’s $Q_{enclosed}$, we can apply integral to solve it
Ex. Charge Distribution Problem # An electron beam has a volumetric charge density described by $\rho_v = -5 \times 10^{-6} \exp(-10^{-5} \rho) \text{ C/m}^3$ over the region $0< \rho < 1$ and $0 < z < 4$
Magnetostatics # Starting from the Ampère’s Circuital Law with Maxwell’s Correction $\nabla \times \vec{H} = \vec{J}$
Integral From # Apply the same methodology, take the integral on both side of $\nabla \times \vec{H} = \vec{J}$ to get
$$ \iint_S (\nabla \times \vec{H}) \cdot d\vec{s} = \iint_S \vec{J} \cdot d\vec{s} $$
Notice the LHS can be substitute by Stokes’ Theorem into $\oint_L \vec{H} \cdot d\vec{l}$, thus $$ \oint_L \vec{H} \cdot d\vec{l} = I $$
And this is just Ampere’s Law, meaning that Current forms Magnetic Field surrounding it Current Density # Here we are still under the Static Maxwell’s Equation that the Ampère’s Circuital Law with Maxwell’s Correction
$$ \nabla \times \mathbf{H} = \underbrace{\mathbf{J}{cond} + \mathbf{J}{conv}}_{\mathbf{J}f (\text{Real Charge Movement})} + \underbrace{\frac{\partial \mathbf{D}}{\partial t}}{\text{Changing Electric Field}} $$
can be simplified into $\nabla \times \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{J}f=\mathbf{J}{cond} + \mathbf{J}_{conv}$
Here the $\vec J_f$ is actually the addition of two kinds of currents, Conduction and Convection Current Conduction Current # This current occurring inside conductor, it’s like elevator transferring charges
$$ \vec J =\sigma \vec E $$
The key point is that the Conduction Current Magnitude is depending on the $\sigma$, which is the Conductivity of material Convection Current # This Current is the movement of Charged Partial through vacuum space
$$ \vec{J}_{convection} =\frac{dQ}{dt}=\frac{\rho_vdx}{dt}= \rho_v \vec{v} $$
It follows the Kinetic Rules, that’s related to speed and density

Signals # Continuous-Time Signals # A continuous-time signal is a function of one (or more) independent variables which range over the real numbers $\mathbb R$
Discrete-Time Signals # A discrete-time signal is a function of one (or more) independent variables which range over the integers $\mathbb Z$
Time Shift # We can time-shift a CT signal x by $t_0\in \mathbb R$ to obtain $x(t − t_0)$
The same applies on DT signals Signal Convention # In time shift formula $x(t-t_0)$, or speicifcally for $t_0$ This means that the sign before $t_0$ is being kept as $-$
$x(t-t_0),t_0>0$ represent Right Shift, it’s a Delay in time $x(t-t_0),t_0<0$ represent Left Shift, it’s a Advance in time Scaling of Signal # we can time-scale a CT signal x by $\alpha \in \mathbb R$ to obtain $x(\alpha t)$
If $\alpha >0$, then its a Compress Otherwise its a Scaling Compressing in DT Signal # A issue of Compressing DT signal is that DT signal are only being sampling at $n\in \mathbb Z$
Thus if we Compress n by $\alpha$, this will create a fraction that no longer works Period # Periodic CT Signals # A CT signal $x$ is periodic if $x(t) = x(t + T)$ for some value $T > 0$ and all $t\in \mathbb R$
Fundamental Period # The smallest such value of T, denoted by $T_0$, is called the fundamental period of x
Period of a Constant CT Signal # As for a CT signal that stays constant, we would like to define it as periodic, but not with the period of 0, instead, it should have a period of $T_0=0^+$, that’s the limit approaching 0 from RHS Period Parameters # Other than period T, we still got other parameters that describe the Period
Frequency: $f_0(Hz)=\frac{1}{T_0}$, tells us how fast the signal repeats Angular Frequency: $w_0(rad\cdot sec^{-1})=2\pi f_0=\frac{2\pi}{T_0}$ Periodic DT Signals # A DT signal x is periodic if $x[n] = x[n + N]$ for some integer N ≥ 1 and all $n\in \mathbb Z$
The smallest such value of N, denoted by $N_0$, is called the Fundamental Period of x
❗ The addition of Periodic Signals does not guarantee a Periodic Signal
Support # Support of DT Signal # $$ supp(x) = {n \in \mathbb z~|~x[n] \neq 0} $$
The support tells you where the signal is non-zero
Support of CT Signal # $$ supp(x) = closure({t ∈ R | x(t) \neq 0}) $$
That is the smallest closed set containing the set ${t ∈ R | x(t) \neq 0}$
Ex. Support of CT Signal # If we a continuous function that is nonzero at $[0,1],[2,3]$, then its support is then $$ [0, 1] \cup [2, 3] $$
Notice that in this case
This function’s zero points are support, as setting them not support will break the continuity of the whole function Duration # In many applications, signals begin at some time and then continue
Right-Sided Signals # Right Sided CT Signals # Right-sided from time $T$ if $x(t) = 0$ for all $t < T$
Right Sided DT Signals # Right-sided from time $N$ if $x[n] = 0$ for all $n < N$
Periodic & Sampling # There’s two kind of signals, finite and infinite ones, as indicated,
Finite Signal # Finite Signals equals zero outside some bounded time interval
Or equivalently, we can say that $supp(x)$ is contained in a bounded interval
Sampling from Periodic Signal to Finite Signal # Periodic Signals are Infinite Signals that repeat itself, by sampling one period from it, we can get the Finite Signal
$$ x_{\mathrm{fin}}(t)=\begin{cases}x_{\mathrm{per}}(t), & 0 \le t < T_0 \0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$
Calculate the Fundamental Period of Periodic Signal # Ex. Calculate the FP # Periodic Extension # In the previous part, we’ve discussed about the basic definition of “Periodic”, but actually, we can tread “Periodic” as the concept of addition of Infinite Finite Signals
$$ x_{\mathrm{per}}(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty} x!\left(t-kT_0\right)=x(t+T_0)+x(t)+x(t-T_0)+\cdots $$
Odd & Even Signal # Odd & Even Signal’s definition is as same as the definition for odd & even functions
$$ x_{\text{even}}(t)=\frac{x(t)+x(-t)}{2},\quad{\text{odd}}(t)=\frac{x(t)-x(-t)}{2} $$
Any signal can be decompose into the form of
$$ x =x_{even}+x_{odd}=\frac{x(t)+x(-t)}{2}+\frac{x(t)-x(-t)}{2} $$
Measurement # Based on the perspective we treat a signal, we can Measure it in different ways
Size of Signal # In terms of Size, we can treat signal in Action, Energy and Amplitude
Action / L1 Norm # $$ |x|1 = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} |x(t)| dt $$
By inspection, this is the Integral of the absolute value of the signal Energy / L2 Norm # $$ |x|2^2 = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} |x(t)|^2 dt $$
Amplitude / L_Infinite Norm # $$ |x|\infty = \sup{t \in \mathbb{R}} |x(t)| $$
Supremum # Inside a set, there could be infinite Local Maximum, whereas the smallest Local Maximum is Supremum
Ex. Calculate the Norms # Given the signal
$$ i(t) = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}, I_0(t), \qquad I_0(t) = e^{-2t}, \quad t \ge 0 $$
$$ | i |_1= \int_0^{\infty} \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} e^{-2t}, dt= \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \left[ -\frac{1}{2} e^{-2t} \right]_0^{\infty}= \frac{1}{2},\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} $$
$$ | i |_2^2= \int_0^{\infty} \left( \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} e^{-2t} \right)^2 dt= \left( \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \right)^2\left[ -\frac{1}{4} e^{-4t} \right]_0^{\infty}= \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} \right)^2 $$
$$ | i |\infty= \max{t \ge 0} \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} e^{-2t}= \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} $$
Size of Periodic Signals # Periodic Signals have infinite length, so when we measure its length, we would like to take only one period and measure
Unit Step & Delta Function # Unit Step Function # $$ u(t) = \begin{cases} 1, & t \geq 0 \ 0, & t < 0 \end{cases} $$
The main usage for Unit Step Function are
1. Form Right-Sided Signal # By multiplying a signal with Unit Signal, this makes it become Right-Sided Signal
2. Build Square Signals # By using two Unit Signals and minus them, it form a Square Signal in a given time
$$ u(t - k) - u(t - 1 - k) $$
DT Unit Impulse Function # $$ \delta[n] = \begin{cases} 1, & n = 0 \ 0, & n \neq 0 \end{cases} $$
As indicated, this function’s value is being define with 1 at time $t=0$, while 0 all other times
This can be shifted by the shift by Time Shift method Any DT signal can be treated as the addition of scaling Impulse functions
Sampling using Impulse Function # Impulse Function can be apply on signals to sample the value of signal in a given time
CT Unit Impulse Function # In continuous case, the Impulse Function is unlike DT signal that has a given value of 1 at time t, instead, it’s actually a rectangle with area of 1
In this given area, first regard the value of $\Delta$, this rectangle’s area is given by $$ \text{Height} \times \text{Width} = (1/\Delta) \times \Delta = 1 $$
So we are now sure that under CT signal, this Impulse is just a rectangle with area of 1 Now check out the Height, in CT we don’t define the function to have a infinite height Instead, we define it as A Undefined Value Shifting in CT Signal # In DT, we say Sampling, cause sampling is a discrete behaviour, while in CT we use Shifting as its related to Integral and continuous, but they basically means the same
$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t)\delta(t - t_0) dt = x(t_0) $$
That is, when we use a signal $x(t)$ to times a Impulse Function at $t_0$ that is $\delta (t-t_0)$, the result will then be $x(t_0)$ Integral and Derivative of CT Impulse Function # Unit Step function, which looks like
is just the integral of Unit Impulse function that after $t=0$, the area suddenly becomes 1 and stay at one for the rest
Complex Signals # When learning about Complex Signals, we always want to start with the unit circle
The Sinusoidal Signal is being created when spinning around the Unit Circle, and the only variable is $\theta$, where as it’s equal $\omega_0t$, so that the x and y values can also being defined by that $\omega_0t$, thus we have $$ \theta(t) = \omega_0 t, \quad x(t) = \cos(\omega_0 t), \quad y(t) = \sin(\omega_0 t) $$
Whereas $\omega_0=2\pi f_0=\frac{2\pi}{T_0}$ Phase Shift # When the input is a AC Voltage, Capacitor will create a Phase Shift on its Current and Volatge
That being said, in this circuit $$ i(t) = \cos(\omega_0 t),\quad v(t)=\cos(\omega_0 t+\frac{\pi}{2}) $$
That is Current leads the Voltage Complex Number # Skipping the basic property for Complex Number, two formula needed are
$$ Re{z}=\frac{z+z^*}{z},\quad Im{z}=\frac{z-z^*}{zj} $$
Complex Exponential Signal # The Euler’s Formula indicated that
$$ e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta $$
Substitue $\theta$ to $\omega_0 t$ to get $$ z(t) = e^{j\omega_0 t} = \cos(\omega_0 t) + j\sin(\omega_0 t) $$
This give the way to express sin and cos by Complex Exponential $$ \sin(\omega_0 t) = \frac{e^{j\omega_0 t} - e^{-j\omega_0 t}}{2j},\quad \cos(\omega_0 t) = \frac{e^{j\omega_0 t} + e^{-j\omega_0 t}}{2} $$
Complex Exponential DT Signals # For Complex Exponential CT Signals, they are always Periodic, but for DT signals this doesn’t always hold, consider Signal
$$ x[n] = e^{j\omega n} $$
This signal is periodic when $\omega$ and $2\pi$’s ratio is a Rational Number See above image, the left signal has Angular Frequency of $\frac2\pi$, and the right’s is $\frac{5\pi}{6}$ The left side has the ratio of $\frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{\pi/2}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{4}$, and the right is $\frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{5\pi/6}{2\pi} = \frac{5}{12}$ Whereas in this case
The Angular Frequency is $\omega =1$, thus $\frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{1}{2\pi}$ A more formal definition for any DT signal $x[n] = e^{j\omega n}$ to be periodic would be
$$ e^{j\omega n} = e^{j\omega (n+N)}\quad for ~all ~n\in\mathbb Z $$
Expand to get $$ e^{j\omega n} = e^{j\omega (n+N)}=e^{j\omega n}\cdot e^{j\omega N} $$
Known that $e^{j2\pi k} = 1$, thus divided both side by $e^{j\omega n}$ to get $$ 1=e^{j2\pi k} = e^{j\omega N}\Rightarrow 2\pi k=\omega N\Rightarrow k=\frac{2\pi}{N} $$
$k$: Cycles needed in one period $N$: Sampled Points in one period Ex. Finding the periodicity of Complex Exponential DT Signals # Ex2. Finding the periodicity of Complex Exponential DT Signals # Ex3. Finding the periodicity of Complex Exponential DT Signals # Frequency-periodicity of DT Complex Exponentials # Above section discussed about the Periodicity of DT Complex Exponential $e^{j\omega n}$’s n, $n$ is the way we describe time in DT Complex Exponential
Now the Angular Frequency $\omega$ also has that Periodicity, which is
$$ e^{j(\omega + 2\pi)n} = e^{j\omega n} \cdot e^{j2\pi n} = e^{j\omega n} $$
This is because no matter what $n$ is, $e^{j2\pi n}$ is always 1 This states that DT Complex Exponential Signals’ Frequency are periodic with period of $2\pi$ i.e. $e^{j\frac{5}{6}\pi n} = e^{j\frac{17}{6}\pi n}$ Aliasing # Different continuous-time signals, when sampled, can produce the exact same discrete-time signal; this phenomenon is called aliasing
Notice that the sampled signal are the same from three different CT signals Nyquist Criterion # Aliasing is a problem when we are trying to sample CT signals, thus Nyquist Criterion states the way to sampling while avoiding Aliasing, and the statement is that to
Sampling minimum 2 times in one period can guarantee no aliasing That is $f_s > 2f_{max}$, e.x. If CT signal is T = 1 sec, that is f = 1Hz, so $f_{sam}=2Hz$ Periodicity of Discrete-Time Frequency # The Discrete Time Frequency is also periodic, that being said
k Formula Sequence $k=0$ $e^{j0}$ $[1, 1, 1, 1]$ $k=1$ $e^{j\frac{\pi}{2}n}$ $[1, j, -1, -j]$ $k=2$ $e^{j\pi n}$ $[1, -1, 1, -1]$ $k=3$ $e^{j\frac{3\pi}{2}n}$ $[1, -j, -1, j]$ $k=4$ $e^{j2\pi n}$ $[1, 1, 1, 1]$ Discrete-time complex exponential signals are periodic in frequency with a period of $2\pi$, which means that for a signal with a time-domain period of $N_0$, there are exactly $N_0$ distinct frequencies before the patterns begin to repeat

“In the nanosecond realm, volume is not just liquidity; it is information.”
Abstract # Market makers provide liquidity under the assumption that order flow is uninformed. However, when informed traders (insiders or superior latency arbitrageurs) enter the market, the probability of Adverse Selection spikes. This note explores the VPIN (Volume-Synchronized Probability of Informed Trading) metric as a real-time gauge for “toxic” order flow.
1. The Problem of Adverse Selection # In a standard limit order book (LOB), a market maker earns the spread ($S = P_{ask} - P_{bid}$). This profit is theoretically risk-free if and only if the price process is a random walk and incoming orders are uncorrelated.
However, if an incoming trader knows that the price will jump in the next $t+\Delta t$, the market maker selling to them is taking a guaranteed loss. This phenomenon is known as Toxic Flow.
2. Volume Bucketing: Time is Irrelevant # Traditional time-based bars (e.g., 1-minute candles) are flawed in HFT because market activity is not uniform. VPIN introduces the concept of Volume Buckets: sampling the market every time a specific volume $V$ changes hands.
Let $V$ be the volume bucket size. For each bucket $i$, we calculate the Buy Volume ($V_\tau^B$) and Sell Volume ($V_\tau^S$).
3. Calculating Order Imbalance (OI) # The core driver of toxicity is the absolute imbalance between buy and sell pressure within a volume bucket. The Order Imbalance ($OI$) for bucket $i$ is defined as:
$$ OI_i = | V_i^B - V_i^S | $$
To estimate VPIN, we smooth this imbalance over a rolling window of $n$ buckets. The formula derived by Easley, López de Prado, and O’Hara (2012) is:
$$ VPIN = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n} OI_{i-j}}{n \times V} $$
Where:
$n \times V$ is the total volume traded over the window (Average Daily Volume or a fraction thereof). High VPIN values (> 0.8) historically precede “Flash Crashes” or significant volatility regimes. 4. Python Implementation # Below is a vectorized implementation using Pandas to compute VPIN from a stream of tick data. Note that accurate trade classification (identifying whether a trade was a Buy or Sell) typically requires the Tick Test or Lee-Ready algorithm.
import numpy as np import pandas as pd def calculate_vpin(trades_df, bucket_volume, window_size=50): """ trades_df: DataFrame with columns ['price', 'volume', 'initiator'] initiator: 1 for buy, -1 for sell """ # 1. Assign trades to Volume Buckets trades_df['cum_vol'] = trades_df['volume'].cumsum() trades_df['bucket_id'] = (trades_df['cum_vol'] // bucket_volume).astype(int) # 2. Aggregation per Bucket # We split volume into Buy/Sell based on the initiator flag trades_df['buy_vol'] = np.where(trades_df['initiator'] == 1, trades_df['volume'], 0) trades_df['sell_vol'] = np.where(trades_df['initiator'] == -1, trades_df['volume'], 0) buckets = trades_df.groupby('bucket_id').agg({ 'buy_vol': 'sum', 'sell_vol': 'sum' }) # 3. Calculate Order Imbalance (OI) buckets['OI'] = (buckets['buy_vol'] - buckets['sell_vol']).abs() # 4. Calculate VPIN (Rolling sum of OI / Total Volume in Window) total_window_vol = bucket_volume * window_size buckets['VPIN'] = buckets['OI'].rolling(window=window_size).sum() / total_window_vol return buckets.dropna()
summary: Implementing the VPIN (Volume-Synchronized Probability of Informed Trading) metric to detect adverse selection risk in high-frequency order books.
title: Quantifying Order Flow Toxicity: A Microstructure Perspective

“In a world of noise, the signal is often hidden in the second derivative.”
核心摘要 # 在当前宏观流动性紧缩的背景下，资产价格的二阶导数（波动率）表现出明显的“跳跃-扩散”特征。本文通过随机微积分视角，探讨短期波动率曲率（Curvature）的异常变化如何预示市场流动性的枯竭。
1. 从几何布朗运动到非线性跳跃 # 传统的 Black-Scholes 模型假设波动率为常数，但在高频交易（HFT）环境中，价格更接近于一个带有跳跃项的随机过程。我们可以用以下随机微分方程（SDE）来描述：
$$dS_t = \mu S_t dt + \sigma(t, \omega) S_t dW_t + J_t dN_t$$
观察近期的标普 500 指数（SPX）走势，我们发现 $J_t$（跳跃项）的频率显著增加。这并非简单的市场情绪波动，而是反映了限价订单簿（LOB）中深度（Depth）的非对称性。当卖盘深度在极短时间内撤单，随机项 $dW_t$ 的系数 $\sigma$ 会发生政权转换（Regime Shift）。
2. 波动率期限结构的“反转”信号 # 目前 VIX 期货曲线表现出近端高度敏感的特征。通过对隐含波动率表面（IV Surface）的横截面分析，由于 Gamma 负对冲效应，Delta 中性组合的对冲成本正呈指数级上升。
凸性陷阱（Convexity Trap）：当市场处于“负 Gamma”状态时，做市商的对冲行为会放大价格波动，形成正反馈循环。 信号过滤：利用卡尔曼滤波（Kalman Filter）对噪声进行处理后，真实的波动率中枢已上移至 18.5 区域。 3. 给量化交易者的结论 # 在 ECE 的信号处理视角下，当前的震荡不是“白噪声”，而是具有长记忆性的“红噪声”。
策略调整：减少均值回归（Mean-reversion）头寸，增加对冲尾部风险的凸性头寸。 风险敞口：关注流动性共振点，防止在高频清算螺旋中出现非线性亏损。 技术实现：建议在回测中引入更复杂的随机波动率模型（如 Heston Model），以捕捉当前的肥尾（Fat-tail）风险。 Disclaimer: This document is for academic research and portfolio demonstration only. Not financial advice.
summary: 探讨在当前宏观流动性紧缩背景下，如何通过随机微积分视角观察波动率曲率的异常变化。
title: 波动率路径下的隐性结构：当前政权转换的随机性分析
